item.title: While Issuing Warnings About AI-Made Bioweapons, Anthropic Quietly Set Up an AI-Run, Robot-Operated Biology Lab Here in the US
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.72
Just one week after Anthropic released a report claiming to have shut down potential bioweapons development conducted by unnamed users of its Claude AI, details have now emerged that the AI firm has also been quietly running a robotically automated and AI-operated biology lab itself. Reuters reporters uncovered the project after speaking with two anonymous sources who explained that Anthropic wants to ramp up Claude AI’s ability to coordinate robotic lab assistants in the performance of science experiments with minimal human intervention. According to Reuters, Anthropic’s new autonomous “wet lab” is operating right now somewhere in the Bay Area. (Seems fine.) The plan appears to be pitched toward possible drug development. However, it will reportedly stop just short of the clinical trials that might put the firm in direct competition with pharmaceutical industry giants (presumably prospective Anthropic customers), according to Anthropic’s head of life sciences, Eric Kauderer-Abrams, who confirmed the lab’s existence to Reuters. “We believe that to do biology, the final test is still and will be for a while in real lab work,” Kauderer-Abrams told the wire service. “We absolutely are doing that today.” In vitro veritas Kauderer-Abrams went on to emphasize that nothing Anthropic is currently undertaking inside this previously undisclosed lab diverges from “what you would see in most biotech companies.” And there was already some prior indication that the firm was pursuing biotech opportunities. Earlier this summer, Anthropic touted its protein-design research, both “in silico” (meaning virtual or computation-based only) and “in vitro” (meaning outside complex living organisms, whether inside test tubes, petri dishes, or something else). But, for years, a desire to spur medical breakthroughs has been a persistent theme from the firm’s CEO, as Amodei has spoken candidly about his father’s tragic death from Hepatitis C just four years before a life-saving medication was first successfully tested on patients. As Amodei put it in some ambitious prognostications back in 2024: “AI-enabled biology and medicine will allow us to compress the progress that human biologists would have achieved over the next 50-100 years into 5-10 years.” Caveat promptor Despite those public statements, a spokesperson for Anthropic followed up with Reuters to underline that its new wet lab is not specifically pursuing drug discovery, but declined to get into any details. The firm’s life sciences head framed this more in terms of the project still being in its nascent phases. “We’re in the very early innings of using AI to automate the execution of lab work,” Kauderer-Abrams said, calling it “an area that has the potential to bring about meaningful acceleration in so many different processes.” While the debate on the safety and prudence of AI-assisted biotech R&D will likely stretch on years or even decades, it’s been a remarkably confusing week for the discourse. Last Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei announced that companies like his own should ‘pause’ further AI development in the face of myriad credible-to-alarmist concerns about the technology’s power to end human civilization as we know it. Soon thereafter, like addicts in the bargaining phase of denial, Amodei and his AI competitors appeared to land on the concept of “pacing the frontier” as a safety-conscious slowdown in AI research that doesn’t disrupt the precious tap of investor capital. Amodei specifically cited the threat of AI-assisted “bioterrorism” in his weekend blog post—following logically from his company’s own internal investigations into suspicious biological research by Claude users, albeit conveniently without ever mentioning Anthropic’s own bio lab. Of course, pharmaceutical research and development is not the same thing as bioweapon development, but there is so much overlap between the two that processes for one could easily be repurposed for the other, and that includes AI models trained for biological research. In a lengthy X post this week, MIT synthetic biologist Kevin Esvelt, long a voice of caution in this field, also weighed in. Esvelt, notable for his work advancing how CRISPR could be used to speed-up evolutionary selection via gene drives, revealed that an AI chatbot had recently suggested to him “a novel form of bioweapon” that he “hadn’t realized was possible.” Esvelt added that he ran his X post by Anthropic’s advanced version of Claude AI, Fable, for factchecking help, “triggering a classifier” in the process. Nice to know, at least, that one safeguard is working.

item.title: After Threatening Character.AI With Legal Action, Disney Puts Its CEO in Charge of Tech
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.64
Disney has turned to the head of the controversial AI company Character.AI to lead its tech efforts. The company announced Friday that Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand is joining Disney as a senior executive vice president and its first-ever chief technology officer. Anand will take up the newly created role on Oct. 2 and report directly to Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro. He’ll oversee the company’s enterprise technology, infrastructure, data and AI platforms, product, and engineering, to “modernize how Disney builds and delivers technology company-wide.” Several of Character.AI’s technical employees are also expected to join Anand at the media giant. Character.AI is an AI platform best known for letting users create and interact with chatbots based on fictional characters, celebrities, and original personas. In its own announcement Friday, Character.AI said Anand and the team joining him will help Disney connect fans with “its beloved stories and characters in new and innovative ways.” Character.AI said its app remains live and online and that it will share more information later about what comes next. “He is an expert builder and strategist, technical and product-minded, with sharp instincts for what fans actually want,” D’Amaro said in a press release. “He also has real enthusiasm and respect for Disney, a clear sense of where technology and creativity meet, and shares our belief that technology creates the most value when it helps people do their best work.” Interestingly, the hire comes just about a year after Disney threatened legal action against Character.AI. Disney sent the company a cease-and-desist letter in September 2025 demanding that it stop allowing users to create unauthorized chatbots based on Disney-owned characters. Character.AI ended up removing the characters, and the dispute did not escalate into a lawsuit. This new hire, along with Disney’s deal with OpenAI last year, makes it clear Disney isn’t necessarily opposed to people using AI to interact with its characters, as long as it has some control. But Character.AI has faced separate controversies that make Disney’s decision to bring in its CEO and some of its engineers in-house surprising. Earlier this year, Character.AI and Google agreed to settle multiple lawsuits brought by families who alleged their children suffered psychological harm after interacting with Character.AI chatbots. One lawsuit, brought by a Florida mother, alleged the app contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide. Another lawsuit, filed in Texas, alleged that Character.AI chatbots encouraged a 17-year-old to harm himself and told him that killing his parents would be an acceptable response to his parents’ screen-time restrictions. Character.AI announced major changes for younger users in October 2025, including new age checks and a ban on open-ended chats for users under 18. Anand joined Character.AI as CEO in June 2025. Before joining Character.AI, he served as president and chief product officer at fintech company Brex. He was also previously vice president of ads and business products at Facebook. Disney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Paramount Sets Dates for ‘Hearts Eyes’ and ‘Crawl’ Sequels
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.36
Paramount has a lot of movies it hopes will bring audiences in theaters, and it just planted some flags for a pair of upcoming horror flicks. Arriving next year on July 16, 2027 is Crawl 2, the sequel to the 2019 hit. Directed by the returning Alexandre Aja, the flick stars Emily Rudd and Mason Gooding as a duo stuck in New York during a hurricane that’s brought in some alligators ready to chomp down on anything they see. Production is currently underway in Hungary, and according to Deadline, the summer date was internally locked down prior to this announcement. Then, on February 4, 2028, Heart Eyes 2 will come to the masses. Moved up a week from its original mid-February date, the second movie will again by helmed by Josh Ruben, who directed the first. (Paramount handled the original’s distribution in most international territories, and has domestic rights for the sequel.) Being further out, plot details on the second movie are under wraps, but Olivia Holt is reportedly back as Ally. At time of writing, there’s no word on whether Gooding will be back as love interest Jay. Currently, Crawl 2 is sandwiched in between Warner Bros.’ Man of Tomorrow (July 9) and A Minecraft Movie Squared (July 23), with Paramount closing that month with A Quiet Place Part III on July 30. As for Heart Eyes 2, not a lot of movies have hard dates in 2028 just yet, but the genre films that do—like X-Men, Tangled, and Evil Dead Wrath—are weeks or even months away from February 11 that year. Paramount’s yearly track record is fairly solid when it comes to horror, and with Crawl 2 and Heart Eyes 2, that may continue. Want more io9 news?
