item.title: RIP to Cult Actor Gerrit Graham, Star of ‘Phantom of the Paradise’ and ‘Child’s Play 2’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.20
There are certain actors who pop up in multiple cult movies, sometimes as the lead, sometimes only in very small roles—but are always memorable, no matter where you see them. Gerrit Graham, who passed away this week at the age of 77, was one such performer; his career kicked off in the early ’70s and spanned decades of entertaining turns in movies and TV shows. If you’re a fan of Brian De Palma’s Phantom of the Paradise, Graham’s role as the flamboyant pop star Beef is forever emblazoned in your psyche. He also made an impression in the suddenly timely AI tale Demon Seed (1977); Robert Zemeckis’ satirical salesman saga Used Cars (1980), opposite Kurt Russell; the terrible but also wonderful National Lampoon’s Class Reunion, a 1982 black comedy set at “Lizzie Bordon High School;” post-Vietnam urban warriors action flick The Annihilators (1985); trashy “alien invasion by way of my satellite TV” romp TerrorVision (1986); splattery techno-horror delight Chopping Mall (1986); and CHUD II: Bud the CHUD (1989), in which he played the sewer-emergent title character. Graham also appeared in 1987 cult skateboarding film The Search for Animal Chin, endearing him to an entirely different demographic beyond midnight movie fiends. In 1990, he starred in Child’s Play 2 as a foster dad who takes in little Andy Barclay and ends up tangling with Chucky as a result. On the small screen, he had roles on Tales From the Crypt, Star Trek: Deep Space Nine and Voyager, and Babylon 5, among many others. According to Variety‘s report on Graham’s death, he was also a songwriter who collaborated with Bob Weir of the Grateful Dead and a screenwriter who penned episodes of the 1980s Twilight Zone, among additional credits. He will be greatly missed. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: Dyson’s Latest Robovac Is Ideal for People Who Don’t Care About Mop-Bots
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.21
Dyson has released three new robot vacuums this week: the $550 R1 Nurovi Dry, the $700 R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry, and the $1,200 R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub. And it’s actually the cheapest of those that caught my eye the most. Robot vacuums can be a very nice thing to have around the house, but high-end floor bot pricing has ballooned out of control lately, with some encroaching on the $2,000 marker. At the same time, some of these robots—I’m looking at you, Dreame Aqua10 Ultra Roller—can whiff so hard on the basics that it’s impossible to justify spending that cash. I don’t know about you, but I long for a cheaper, simpler robot vacuum that can still map my home, navigate well, and has good obstacle avoidance. That seems to sum up the R1 Nurovi Dry. The R1 features 21,000Pa suction, a mid-tier spec compared to some other robovacs that reach into the 30,000s and higher. But as Dyson chief engineer Jake Dyson is quoted as saying in a press release emailed to me this week, “Robotic cleaning isn’t just about suction power.” I’m inclined to agree, based on all of the various robot vacuums I’ve tested. For example, the best model I’ve tested for picking up dust and dirt remains the Matic robot vacuum, which only sucks air at 3,200Pa in its standard cleaning mode. So what does the R1 do instead? A cross-section render on the Dyson site (check it out below) shows a smaller channel that brings fine debris into one chamber, while a larger channel above it collects bigger chunks in another. The company also says it can “intelligently detect dust levels and floor types in real time” to adjust its suction power and cleaning behavior, and its self-emptying dock uses a cyclonic canister instead of a dust bag you’d have to replace every few months. The R1 has other premium-style features, including a side sweeping brush that reaches out to get into tight spaces the robot otherwise wouldn’t be able to reach. The company says in its press release that this brush has been “engineered at a precise angle” with a connector that “actively controls the pressure and direction of the brushes” to keep from flicking debris away from the robot, instead directing it into the robot’s path. I’ve seen similar claims from other robot vacuum makers, and I’d be interested to see how this plays out in real-world testing. Furthermore, Dyson says the R1 can climb up to 0.79-inch floor transitions and is fairly squat at 3.78 inches tall, meaning it can get under very low furniture. That’s not the shortest, but it’s pretty good—for comparison, the Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete stands at 3.12 inches tall when its periscope-like sensor cluster sinks into its body. But that’s a $1,700 vac-bot; I’ll take the extra half an inch to save $1,100. The R1 uses LiDAR for mapping and navigation, as well as “line lasers and edge sensors” for object avoidance. All of the above can be said for the R2 as well, which also features dual triangular mop pads that the company says can better get into edges and corners, while its dock washes the pads using 167-degree water. Meanwhile, the R3 adds AI vision cameras and uses UV light for “forensic checks” after cleaning “for full proof of a hygenic clean.” It also features 30,000Pa suction and a roller mop that extends to reach edges but lacks the articulating side brush of the other bots. The R1 Nurovi Dry and R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub are each available now on Dyson’s website. The R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry is exclusively available at Costco.

item.title: 4 subscriptions you can replace with a $10 ESP32
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.76
Even when you buy a product outright, you may still need to pay a subscription to access all of its features. These subscriptions can soon add up, but thankfully, there are alternatives. You can often avoid subscription fees with an inexpensive ESP32. Turn a Peloton into a subscription-free smart exercise bike SmartSpin2k can make even dumb spin bikes smart Peloton is a popular brand of smart exercise equipment, best known for its connected stationary bikes with a built-in touchscreen. The bikes cost upward of $1600, but many useful features require a subscription, and the All-Access membership currently costs $49.99 per month in the US. The membership gives you access to instructor-led classes, leaderboards, and more. An ESP32 can't replace the instructor-led training that Peloton offers, but it can help you make a Peloton bike useful even without a subscription. It can even turn a standard spin bike into a smart bike that matches many of the features Peloton and other expensive models offer. That's because an ESP32 is the brain inside the SmartSpin2k project. The SmartSpin2k is a simple device that you can buy ready-made or build yourself that uses the ESP32 and a stepper motor to let third-party fitness apps such as Zwift automatically control the resistance knob of your spin bike. When you're riding up a virtual hill in your training app, the resistance automatically increases to match. The SmartSpin2k PCB and wiring harness cost $110, or you can buy the finished product for $239. You can use it with a Peloton or many models of conventional spin bikes that cost significantly less than Peloton models. When you factor in the subscription savings for your Peloton sessions, you could save yourself a small fortune. Remote start your car without paying for it An ESP32 can press the same button that you do SmartSpin2k is a complex project with many parts. Sometimes, paying a subscription fee. Some cars have smart features that let you do things like start the car remotely or warm up the cabin before you get in on a cold day. Many car makers charge subscription fees for these types of features, with GM's OnStar Connect plan starting at $14.99 per month. If you have a spare key fob with remote features, there is a much simpler and far cheaper solution. You can hook up an ESP32 to the contacts beneath its buttons and simulate button presses remotely, using options such as ESPHome. You can then start your car remotely without a subscription, as long as your key fob is within range. You may want to consider ways to mitigate the additional security risks of giving your car keys remote access. Stop paying to store your security camera recordings An ESP32-CAM can detect motion and store recordings locally Many popular security camera and smart video doorbell brands offer some kind of subscription. A Ring subscription, for example, is required in order to play back video history, get person, package, and vehicle alerts, and more. If you want to cover more than one camera, the subscription fee is even higher. You can set up your own local security camera system using an ESP32 and some other hardware. For example, an ESP32-CAM combines an ESP32 chip with a camera module, giving you everything you need to capture images and video. Applications such as ESP32-CAM_MJPEG2SD allow you to capture video when motion is detected and save it locally to an SD card. Alternatively, you can stream the video to a computer running Frigate or other Network Video Recorder (NVR) software. You can then save all of your video on your local hard drives and access it when you need it. You don't need to pay a subscription, and none of the data needs to leave your home. Open your garage door remotely without paying Home Assistant and an ESP32 can do the same job Popular garage door opener brands, including Chamberlain and LiftMaster, use the myQ platform to let you open and close your garage door remotely. In some cases, taking full advantage of this platform requires a subscription. For example, the Connected Garage for Tesla integration can automatically open your garage when your Tesla approaches your garage and close it when you leave, but it comes with a $45 per year fee. The ratgdo (Rage Against the Garage Door Opener) project is a small, open-source garage door interface that allows you to remotely control your garage door without a subscription. ESP32-based versions can run ESPHome firmware and expose your garage door opener to Home Assistant without going via myQ's cloud service. You can then build your own automation that will open your garage door when you get home and close it when you leave. You get automatic garage door control without paying a subscription fee. An ESP32 alone often isn't enough In some cases, an ESP32 and a few wires are all you need, but if you want to replace a subscription, you'll often need additional hardware. The SmartSpin2k project, for example, requires significant outlay even if you're building it yourself. However, when you add up the ongoing cost of subscription fees, ESP32-based solutions could save you significant money in the long run.

item.title: 4 reasons some Android features are still off-limits to you
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.55
Are you also dealing with a particular kind of Android frustration I know too well? You find out your phone can do something, get excited to try it, and then find the feature nowhere. You check Settings, Google it, follow the instructions step by step, and still come up empty-handed. No setting. No toggle. Nothing. That’s because “available on Android” doesn’t necessarily mean “available on your phone.” Android features can be surprisingly selective. Two people can have Android phones, run the same software version, and still have access to different features. Strange, right? It’s the same, same — but somehow different. I’ve learned to check a few things before wasting time digging through Settings for a feature that may never show up. So, before you blame yourself — or your phone — here are four reasons some Android features can still be off-limits for you. Region locked Not every feature is global I noticed something was off when I started looking into Gemini in Chrome. I had a perfectly capable Android phone, and the feature simply wasn’t available to me. Google currently lists Gemini in Chrome on Android as available only in the U.S., so if you’re using an Android phone in India, you won’t have access to it, even if your device meets the other requirements. Google also says the feature is still rolling out gradually, so availability can depend on more than just your phone. This isn’t limited to Google’s features. Samsung also makes some Wallet features available only in certain countries or regions. Samsung Wallet can handle payment cards, boarding passes, tickets, and digital keys, but the features and content available can vary by country, device, carrier, and firmware. That’s what makes region restrictions so confusing. Apparently, your phone has a passport too. Hardware dependent Your phone can’t fake hardware I’ve had this happen when comparing Galaxy phones: I’d see my brother using a cool feature like Auto Zoom in FlexCam on his Galaxy Z Flip 6, grab my own Galaxy Z Fold 6, and expect to find the same option right away. After all, they’re both premium Samsung foldables. But that’s when I learned not to assume every Galaxy phone gets every feature. Samsung says some Galaxy AI and camera features are available only on selected devices. Hardware can make a bigger difference than you might expect. The processors, camera sensors, display, and other components can determine whether a feature is supported. In the case of Auto Zoom in FlexCam, the feature is designed around the Flip6’s FlexCam setup, where the phone can be partially folded and automatically adjust the zoom to keep you in frame. The Fold6 has a completely different form factor. Your phone can fake a lot with software, but it can’t fake hardware it simply doesn’t have. Software limited Don’t let your phone fall behind This one has caught me more than once. Sometimes, hardware isn’t the problem at all — the required software simply isn’t there yet. It’s a bit like having a perfectly good TV but missing the app you want to watch something on. The hardware is there, but the software hasn’t caught up. For example, I’ve opened Samsung’s Settings after seeing a useful feature in a tutorial, only to realize the person in the video was running a newer version of One UI. The menus looked familiar, but the option I was looking for was missing. The same thing can happen with Google apps. You might see someone using a new Gmail, Google Photos, or Google Messages feature, check your phone, and wonder why yours looks different. Updating the app or your phone can sometimes make all the difference. Sometimes your phone doesn’t need a new feature — it just needs to catch up. After all, in life and on your phone, staying up-to-date matters. Phased rollouts Wait for your turn This is probably the most annoying one because waiting around for a feature you already know exists is tedious. A feature can be officially announced, your phone can support it, and your software can be completely up to date, yet the feature still might not appear on your device. That’s because companies often roll out new features in stages instead of switching them on for everyone at once. A little patience, apparently, is part of the deal. I’ve seen this with Google and Samsung features. Google Messages is a good example. Google says Gemini in Messages is being released gradually, so even if your phone meets the requirements and your language and country are supported, you might not see it immediately. So I’d rather wait for the feature than panic over something that isn’t even in my control. Your phone might be innocent After all this, I’ve stopped assuming a missing Android feature means my phone is doing something wrong. Sometimes the feature is restricted where I live; sometimes my phone doesn’t have the hardware for it; sometimes my software needs to catch up; and sometimes I’m just waiting for my turn. So, the next time I see someone showing off a feature I can’t find, I’m not immediately going down a settings rabbit hole. It just means: not here, not on this phone, not yet.

item.title: Excel Easter eggs ended 24 years ago—but this open-source Space Invaders project keeps the fun alive
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.41
I've always liked the fact that older versions of Excel had hidden games tucked away inside them. Microsoft stopped doing that years ago, but Excel users never completely stopped having fun with spreadsheets. I recently found an open-source Space Invaders-style game that runs entirely inside Excel. Excel used to hide games in plain sight But the Easter eggs eventually disappeared Microsoft snuck some genuinely unexpected games into older versions of Excel. Excel 95 had the Hall of Tortured Souls, a Doom-style 3D maze, Excel 97 had a flight simulator (pictured above), and Excel 2000 had a driving game called Dev Hunter. But that tradition didn't last. In 2002, Bill Gates told Microsoft employees that Trustworthy Computing had become the company's highest priority, with a particular focus on security and reliability. Around the same time, newer versions of Excel stopped shipping with these kinds of hidden games. This meant we lost the intrigue and excitement of discovering that the spreadsheet program we use for budgets and reports contains an entirely unnecessary video game. Microsoft isn't the only company to have turned a spreadsheet into a place for games. Back in the 2000s, an OpenOffice Calc Easter egg let you play a Space Invaders clone directly in a spreadsheet. Two decades later, thanks to VBA and someone's hard work, I found myself doing essentially the same thing in Excel. Play "Space Defenders" in Excel Turn your spreadsheet into an arcade machine Evanml2030's Excel-SpaceInvader project on GitHub is an open-source VBA version of the classic arcade game. Download the macro-enabled Space Defenders workbook, open it in desktop Excel, and play directly inside the workbook. Macro-enabled Excel files can be malicious, so always double-check what you're opening first. I opened this file in Safe Mode (by holding Ctrl as I opened Excel) and inspected its VBA (Alt+F11) before I played it. For more details, scroll to the Security section below. It's much more recognizably Space Invaders than I expected. You move your ship from side to side, fire at the incoming enemies, and try to clear them before they reach you. The controls are simple: use the Left and Right Arrow keys to move and the Spacebar to fire. The game runs inside Excel's normal window, with the workbook effectively becoming the game screen. When you get hit, you're greeted with an abrupt "Uh oh, collision detected" alert, and you can click Launch to play again. On one playthrough, I did encounter a glitch where a falling object suddenly appeared next to my rocket and ended the game. Other than that, though, it worked excellently and played like a proper arcade game. How to get started If you've read the security information below and are comfortable proceeding, download the XLSM workbook from the project's GitHub page. In Windows File Explorer, right-click the file and select Properties. On the General tab, look under Security, check Unblock, and click OK. You'll also need to enable ActiveX controls in Excel for the game to work. Open a blank workbook, go to File > Options > Trust Center > Trust Center Settings > ActiveX Settings, select the option you want, and click OK. Once that's done, close the blank workbook, open the Space Defenders workbook, and enable its macros and ActiveX controls if prompted. Remember to change your ActiveX settings back when you've finished playing. This setting applies to Excel generally, rather than just this workbook, so leaving it changed can affect how Excel handles ActiveX controls in other files. There's a surprising amount of code behind it Excel is doing far more than displaying a few pictures For me, the interesting part was seeing how the game actually works. The VBA handles the game state, movement, enemies, bullets, collisions, timing, and the repeated updates needed to make everything appear to move smoothly. It uses DoEvents, which allows Excel to process other events while the game is running. Without that, a VBA routine that continually loops through the game would quickly make Excel feel unresponsive. The project also calls a couple of Windows API functions. GetAsyncKeyState, from user32.dll, is used to detect keyboard input, while QueryPerformanceCounter and QueryPerformanceFrequency, from kernel32.dll, are used for high-resolution timing. The graphics are handled in an especially Excel-ish way. The game dynamically creates Microsoft Forms Image.1 ActiveX controls and uses them to display the various sprites. In other words, those things flying around the screen aren't some special Excel game-rendering system. They're controls being created and manipulated by VBA. I find that more interesting than the fact that you can play the game itself. Someone has effectively built a small arcade-game framework inside a spreadsheet app. Security: Opening a macro-enabled file from the web In this case, I didn't find anything concerning Before playing, I inspected the workbook's VBA to see what it was actually doing. I didn't find code that launches external programs, makes network requests, reads or deletes files, modifies the Windows registry, or uses obvious code obfuscation. I also didn't find an automatic Workbook_Open() or Auto_Open() routine. The Windows API calls I found are used for the game itself: GetAsyncKeyState handles keyboard input, while QueryPerformanceCounter and QueryPerformanceFrequency provide high-resolution timing. The ActiveX controls are used to display the game's images. That doesn't mean you should automatically trust every macro-enabled Excel file you download. It means that, in this particular workbook, I didn't find anything that appeared to do anything beyond run the game. Microsoft disables ActiveX controls by default in Microsoft 365 and Office 2024, so you may stumble upon additional security warnings when opening the workbook. That's another good reason to treat downloaded macro-enabled files with caution. Excel is a playground You don't need to know VBA or build an entire game inside Excel to get creative with it. I've used Excel's humble grid to get creative in some surprisingly different ways, like making pixel art, planning a room, creating a stop-motion animation, designing a board game, and even mapping out a crochet pattern. You just have to stop thinking of Excel as somewhere you only put numbers.

item.title: How to set up a perfect “rescue USB” that can save any PC
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.84
When your PC's operating system gets corrupted, or if an update fails, or a drive gets damaged, you need to be ready—or be prepared to spend a lot of time trying to get it back up running. Thankfully, it's just as simple as grabbing a thumb drive and getting it up and running as a rescue drive. It's easy, and trust me, you'll thank us later. What's a rescue USB? Software repair tools on the go A rescue USB is basically an independent operating system stored on a flash drive. Unlike a standard external drive used solely for storing documents or backing up photos, a rescue USB is configured to bypass the computer’s primary hard drive entirely. When a computer encounters a critical failure—such as a corrupted Windows installation, a broken master boot record, or a severe malware infection—the internal operating system often becomes inaccessible. And in these scenarios, the computer cannot boot normally, rendering the data inside seemingly unreachable. This is where the rescue USB functions as a lifeline. By changing the boot order in the computer’s BIOS or UEFI settings, the machine loads the operating system residing on the USB stick rather than the faulty internal drive. Once booted, this environment provides a clean, stable interface that looks and feels much like a standard desktop. However, it comes pre-loaded with a specialized arsenal of software utilities designed specifically for troubleshooting. These environments often utilize lightweight versions of Linux or Windows PE (Pre-installation Environment). The tools included are vast and varied, ranging from disk partition managers and password reset utilities to antivirus scanners and hardware diagnostic tests. For instance, if a computer is overheating or crashing randomly, a rescue USB can run a memory test to check the RAM modules for physical defects without the interference of the main operating system. It acts as a bridge, allowing a user to interact with the hardware and files of a "dead" computer, providing the capability to diagnose the problem, repair the file system, or, in worst-case scenarios, extract critical data before performing a complete reinstall of the operating system. How do I set one up? A flash drive is all you need The requirements are pretty straightforward. A high-quality USB flash drive with at least 16GB or 32GB of storage is recommended to accommodate multiple tools and operating system images. The first step involves selecting the software that will make the drive bootable. While older methods required formatting the drive for a single specific tool using software like Rufus, modern solutions such as Ventoy have revolutionized the process. Ventoy allows the user to install a bootloader onto the USB drive once, after which the drive functions as a standard storage device where various disk image files, known as ISOs, can simply be copied and pasted directly into the folder structure. To begin the process, you need to download the installer for the chosen creation tool and plug the USB drive into a working computer. It is imperative to back up any existing data on the drive, as the initial installation of the bootloader will completely wipe and reformat the stick. Once the software has prepared the drive, though, you need the actual rescue disk images. Popular choices include Hiren’s BootCD PE, which offers a familiar Windows-like environment, or specialized Linux distributions like Ubuntu or SystemRescue. These ISO files are downloaded from their respective official websites. With the drive prepared by Ventoy, you simply drag and drop these ISO files onto the USB stick. No further extraction or complex configuration is required. When the USB is later plugged into a target computer, the boot menu will dynamically list every ISO file stored on the drive, allowing you to select the specific tool or operating system best suited for the immediate repair task. SanDisk Cruzer 8GB Flash Drive - Storage Capacity - 8GB - Compatible Devices - PCs and laptops - Suitable for - Portable apps, Linux installations Boot or install Linux on any PC with this super inexpensive USB 2.0 flash drive. Why should I have one? It's a cheap investment that'll save you in the future The primary reason is probably the immediate capability for disaster recovery and data preservation. Computer failures rarely occur at convenient times, and the difference between a minor annoyance and a catastrophic data loss often hinges on having the right tools immediately at hand. When an operating system refuses to boot due to a corrupted update or a "Blue Screen of Death," the data on the hard drive typically remains intact, yet inaccessible through normal means. With a rescue USB, a user can boot the machine into a live environment within minutes, navigate to the internal hard drive, and copy critical documents, family photos, or work projects to an external source. This ability to salvage data independently eliminates the panic associated with system crashes and removes the immediate need to pay for expensive professional data recovery services. A rescue USB also provides a secure environment for neutralizing severe security threats. Modern malware and ransomware can be incredibly persistent, often embedding themselves deep within the operating system processes to prevent antivirus software from removing them. By booting from a rescue USB, the malicious software on the internal drive remains dormant and inactive. This allows the user to run aggressive antivirus scans and removal tools on the infected drive without the malware being able to defend itself or spread further. No just for software repair Finally, beyond just virus removal, these drives are essential for hardware maintenance. They enable users to perform secure drive wipes before selling a computer, resize hard drive partitions to organize data better, or reset forgotten administrator passwords that would otherwise lock a user out of their own device. Possessing a rescue USB transforms a user from a passive victim of technology failure into an active administrator capable of diagnosing and resolving complex system issues. So yeah, it's a pretty good idea. Fire one up when you get a chance—it's better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it.

item.title: 4 ways to repurpose an old Kindle eReader
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.77
eReaders are particularly great gadgets because they tend to stay perfectly usable for a long time. However, there will eventually come a time when you want to upgrade. So what should you do with the old one? We have some ideas for you. Turn it into a smart home display The best feature of your old Kindle is the thing that made it so great for reading—the e-paper display. Since the e-paper only uses power when the screen changes, it’s a great device for a smart home dashboard. There’s an excellent guide from Matt Healy for setting this up with an old Kindle. It essentially just shows a web page, but it’s much easier to update the web page remotely than mess around on the Kindle itself. Attach this to your fridge and it’s a great little hub. Make an E-Paper clock If a full smart display feels like too much work, you can pare it down to the essentials. An e-paper clock is one of the coolest clocks you can have, offering extreme visibility without the annoying glow of an LCD or LED display. As long as your Kindle isn’t super ancient, you can literally just open up time.is in the browser and let it run. Sure, this isn't the most mind-blowing use for an e-paper display, but we're working within the confines of the stock software. Jailbreak it for full control In reality, there’s not a lot you can do with an old Kindle in its factory state. If you want true freedom and flexibility, you're going to have to jailbreak the thing. Doing this opens the door to far more than just custom home screens and new display hacks. Once liberated, you can install custom software and use the device for things Amazon never intended. The good news is it’s probably a lot easier to do this than you might think. Check out our full guide for a general walkthrough. Trade it in for a new one Alright, maybe you're a person who doesn't want to spend an afternoon tinkering with old tech. If you want the least painful path, you can repurpose your Kindle by using it to buy a new Kindle. Amazon offers a trade-in program that gives you an Amazon gift card and a nice 20% discount on a new Kindle. The discount is the real selling point here, though—Amazon typically offers only $5 for old Kindles. Don't let old Kindles go to waste! The takeaway here is that even the simplest, most limited tech can often be turned into something useful instead of gathering dust in a drawer. You got a little more mileage out of your money, and now you’re ready to start filling up your new e-reader with all the books you can handle.

item.title: You’re probably buying the wrong hard drive, and this 341,000-HDD study proves it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.68
When shopping for HDDs, it's all too easy to focus on the price and nothing else. Sure, the biggest drives tend to have eye-watering price tags, and not everyone needs 20+ terabytes of storage anyway ... but a recent study, based on a massive sample size, reveals that those drives might be well worth the added cost. In fact, Backblaze found that some of its largest HDDs failed the least out of its entire fleet. Backblaze's biggest HDDs are currently failing less And the sample size is huge Backblaze regularly reports on how its massive fleet of HDDs is doing, but one of its most recent reports reveals some interesting insights. Namely, that larger capacity may translate to better longevity for hard drives. The company analyzed more than 341,000 production hard drives in the first quarter of 2026. A huge chunk of those drives are of the enormous kind, with capacities of 20TB and more. The sample size is crucial here, because if, out of 86,000 drives, Backblaze is seeing encouraging trends, that has to mean something. While these 20+TB drives don't make up the majority of the fleet, Backblaze seems to be betting on them right now, as out of the 10,220 drives it deployed in Q1 2026, over 9,400 were above 20TB. That's roughly 92%. The most important finding comes down to the reliability of these humongous drives: Backblaze says that their AFR, or annualized failure rate, is just 0.85%. That's well under the average across the entire fleet, which sits at 1.24%. The way AFR works is that it accounts for how many days the drives were actually in service and annualizes the resulting failure rate, so it's more revealing than just comparing raw numbers of how many drives died vs. how many made it out unscathed. Backblaze also reported that its overall AFR improved from the first quarter of 2025, when it was at 1.42%. There's one enormous catch: these drives are still very young Drives you buy on the cheap are probably not Trusting an old HDD can end poorly for many reasons, and that's one important caveat we have to discuss to not make these 20TB+ HDDs look too exciting. The 20TB-and-larger models in the Q1 2026 report range from just a couple of months old to around 16 months on average. Compared to some of the smaller drives, some of which have been running for over five years, these new 20TB+ HDDs are basically babies. That gives them an advantage that might taper off when we look at these same figures in 10 years. A brand new HDD and an older drive don't exactly have the same odds of failing, especially when they're running 24/7 (as is the case here). On the other hand, a more recent Secure Data Recovery study revealed that roughly half of all failed drives sent to the company died in their first year of operation, but even this data has an important caveat: it only talks about drives that actually failed. Those that don't fail never reach the company, and thus aren't accounted for the way they are in Backblaze's data. I digress. Despite the potential age difference between Backblaze's chonky drives and those less capacious, the data is sound, because this isn't the only instance of it. Backblaze has previously compared its 20TB+ drives against older 14TB to 16TB models at similar points in their lives, and the newer, higher-capacity drives still looked competitive, if not slightly better. One 22TB drive is doing a lot of heavy lifting here Bigger doesn't automatically mean better Fun fact: The company seems to have a favorite drive. The WDC WUH722222ALE6L4 (22TB) now accounts for over 45,000 of Backblaze's units, and it only has a 0.38% AFR, which might have something to do with that preference. It also accounts for more than half of Backblaze's entire 20TB+ fleet. The data isn't a fluke, it seems. The drives averaged 16.1 months old, and the model's lifetime AFR was still only 0.58% across more than 22 million drive days; an impressive result when compared with the overall data. Still, there's a model that has an even better failure rate, although the sample size is much smaller, too. Toshiba's 24TB drives posted an excellent 0.22% AFR that quarter, measured across 7,203 HDDs. A cheap hard drive can still end up being the expensive choice Price per drive isn't the number I'd optimize for Going through these numbers does make me rethink my storage strategy a little bit. Most of my own strategy boils down to using what I already own. For instance, I've harvested HDDs from old consoles and laptops. I also tend to think that even tiny drives, such as a 120GB SATA, can have some use, provided you take good care of them and back up your files (those drives tend to be old, bordering on ancient, after all). When it comes to buying new drives, though, it's just not a good time to buy any, so when I did buy, I settled for 8TB. But looking at the prices now, as well as Backblaze's data, it does seem that those bigger drives might be the play. Of course, an important caveat: Do you even need 20TB+ of storage? Many people don't, and if you can't see yourself ever filling such a drive to, say, 70%, there's no need to spend more. These AFRs are low, no matter how you spin it, so it's not like a pricier drive is bound to live a longer life. The biggest drives are far from a gamble, they're just pricey I've heard people say that big HDDs are more prone to failure. I can't tell you based on my own experience, as I've been lucky enough to see very few drive failures in the last 20 years, and they've all been way smaller than 20TB. But Backblaze's data is just about the best sample size you can officially find, and it does reveal that 20TB+ HDDs are doing exceptionally well for now—so, at the very least, don't be afraid to buy them if you actually need them. Seagate Exos 22TB Buying a refurbished/recertified drive is a good way to get yourself lots of terabytes for cheap (well, relatively). The only issue is that those drives might not last as long as a brand-new drive would, so check and make sure they're in good condition.

item.title: This Ethernet cable test tells you more than a speed test ever will
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.40
If you feel like your internet is playing up, what's the first thing you do? A lot of us reach for the same tool: a speed test. Those things catch more than just slow internet; they also note your latency, and if there's packet loss, you'll see it because the speed test will take ages to complete (or it won't complete at all). And as long as it shows a number within our expectations, we shrug and assume the Wi-Fi is just having a bad day. A simple speed test, however, is not something anyone should be judging their whole network by. Even with a half-dead Ethernet cable, for example, your speed test can still give you a good result. If you actually want to test your setup, a bandwidth test is the better place to start. A speed test only ever checks your internet, not your cable It taps out the second you hit whatever your plan is selling you All a speed test does is measure the path from your device to a server on the internet, and it's completely capped by whatever internet plan you have. Ethernet cables, however, can move much faster than most plans, so a speed test will likely never stress it. If you do end up with a low number from a speed test, guessing the culprit can be pretty difficult. It could be your ISP, a VPN, a browser extension, a busy test server, congestion, an old router, or something else entirely. It's also worth going around and checking your Ethernet cables, since you could be dealing with something like a broken locking clip, a sharp bend, or a chewed cable. If you have pets, that can definitely happen; I still remember years ago, when my (then a puppy) dog chewed up my Ethernet cable in a fairly hidden-away spot. It took me a while to notice. There are honestly so many things that can cause a bad speed test result. It's not always your ISP (although in my case, it often is, but I'm unlucky when it comes to ISPs). The sneaky part is how a bad cable actually fails Gigabit needs all four pairs, and losing one won't kill the connection An Ethernet cable has eight wires inside, arranged as four twisted pairs. Full gigabit (the 1000BASE-T standard) needs all four of those pairs in working order, while older 100Mbps Fast Ethernet only needs two. So, if one pair gets damaged, your link can drop from 1Gbps down to 100Mbps but keep working all the same. Nothing disconnects, nothing throws an error, and the connection simply renegotiates itself down to stay stable. If things go really wrong, your adapter can even negotiate itself down to 2003-era speeds without you noticing a thing. The actual test: check your link speed, then run iPerf3 One number shows you the ceiling, the other shows you what you're getting The first thing to check is your link speed, also called the negotiated speed. On Windows, head to Settings, then Network & internet, then Ethernet, or just run Get-NetAdapter in PowerShell. If your PC has a gigabit port but the link only shows 100Mbps, then the problem is somewhere in your wiring rather than your internet. (Potentially. Maybe. Network troubleshooting is such a hassle, honestly.) Next, try out this great tool: iPerf3. I use it a lot. It's a free command-line utility that measures raw speed between two devices on your own network, with the internet completely out of the picture. Instead, it shows you the true ceiling of your cable, port, and network card. Install it on two devices (brew install iperf3 on Mac, Scoop or winget on Windows, apt on Linux). On one machine, run iperf3 -s to make it the server, then on the other, run iperf3 -c followed by the first machine's IP address. A healthy cable should give you around 900Mbps or more, so if you're crawling at under 100Mbps instead, you have discovered a faulty cable. Tack on -R to flip the direction, -t 30 for a longer run, or -i 1 to catch intermittent drops, and keep an eye on the "Retr" column, since a pile of retransmits usually means a flaky physical link. When the test finally points at the cable Swap first, tester second, replace third So, if these tests come up with bad results, the fix is pretty straightforward. First, verify the results by swapping in a short, working cable, and run the test again. If the numbers jump up, that cable is definitely the problem. It's the same trick I use for a cable that might simply be too long, where the signal degrades just enough to force those same slowdowns. A cheap cable tester (the $10 kind) is a good next step, since it instantly catches broken wires, shorts, and miswires. Just know it won't flag subtler issues like crosstalk, so a cable can technically "pass" and still choke at gigabit. As for replacements, Cat6 should be the default for anything new, but there's definitely no need to panic-buy Cat8 for a normal home. Honestly, plenty of the Cat5e cables you already own are still perfectly fine for gigabit, as long as they're in good shape. The speed test isn't useless, it's just answering a different question A speed test tells you if you're getting the internet speeds you're paying for, and that's something we all need to check at one point or another. Your link speed and an iPerf3 run, however, answer a completely different question: "Is my own wiring quietly holding me back?" Nothing lasts forever, so at some point, those Ethernet cables will be the ones causing the problems.

item.title: 4 innocent-looking Linux commands that can ruin your day
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.89
If you use Linux, you'll eventually want to get comfortable with the terminal. It streamlines your workflow and opens up a whole new way of computing that graphical apps simply can't match. This includes writing Bash scripts for system management and automation or administering a remote machine over SSH. That said, if you're just getting started and relying on online guides or AI chatbots for help, you need to be extra careful. Some commands can look completely harmless, but will break your system in seconds. Here are my top five picks for innocent-looking commands that you wouldn't think twice about but can completely ruin your day. rm -rf ~ /Downloads/old The most expensive typo you'll ever make The traditional dangerous version of this command goes like this: sudo rm -rf / Here, you're essentially running the remove (rm) command with elevated privileges and telling it to recursively (-r) and forcefully (-f) delete everything under /, the root of the filesystem. So, clearly, rm -rf can be dangerous, but it's not some forbidden command you should never touch. In fact, it's a standard way to delete a directory and everything inside it. Say you have an old Downloads folder you want to get rid of. The quickest way to do that is: rm -rf ~/Downloads/old The problem is that a single misplaced space can change everything. In the correct command, the tilde (~) and the path form one continuous string: ~/Downloads/old, which the shell expands to a path under your home directory, such as /home/dibakar/Downloads/old. But let's say you accidentally add a space after the tilde: rm -rf ~ /Downloads/old Now the shell sees two separate arguments. The first is ~, which expands to your entire home directory. So the command will now happily wipe out your documents, photos, configuration files, and everything else in your home directory, and then move on to the other path you specified. echo "a new line of text" > imp.config The difference between appending to a file and overwriting it If you're working in the terminal, one way to add a new line to a configuration file is to open it in a text editor like Nano or Micro and type it in. However, a faster way is to echo the same line straight into the file with a single command: echo "a new line of text" >> imp.config This command adds “a new line of text” to the bottom of the imp.config file. However, let's say you were in a hurry and mistyped it as: echo "a new line of text" > imp.config Now you've replaced the contents of your old imp.config file with a new file containing just one line: “a new line of text.” The only difference is that you typed “>” instead of “>>”. That's because the “>>” operator means append — it adds the command's output to the end of the file while leaving the existing contents intact. The single-arrow “>” operator, on the other hand, means write or overwrite. It creates a new file and writes the output to it, or, if a file with the same name already exists, replaces its contents with the new output. So, say imp.config originally had 10 lines of carefully written configuration, and you run the echo command with “>” instead of “>>”. Those 10 lines are gone. The file now contains exactly the one line you entered in the last command. I've personally done this to my .bashrc, which had hundreds of lines of customization built up over time. I'm not saying “>” is more dangerous than “>>”. Each operator has its place, and it's important to understand the difference so you can use them appropriately. sudo ufw enable It's the equivalent of locking yourself out of your own home This command is about as harmless as it gets on paper. It enables the firewall, which is genuinely good practice from a security standpoint and part of many routine setup checklists when configuring a new system. The problem shows up when you run it over SSH. Say, you're setting up a remote machine and type sudo ufw enable to start the firewall. If your SSH connection isn’t already allowed — which is unlikely on a new setup — the firewall will kick you out and prevent you from reconnecting. You'll need console or physical access to the machine to fix it. This can be a mild annoyance if the machine is in the next room, but a disaster if you're managing a server from another city, or worse, remoting into your home lab while on vacation. To avoid the mishap, first allow your SSH service through the firewall with sudo ufw allow ssh (or explicitly allow your custom SSH port), and only then run sudo ufw enable. This creates the firewall rule before the firewall is activated, so your SSH connection can continue through the firewall. :(){ :|:& };: Just don’t paste a command you can’t read Last but not least, we have the fork bomb. It's about as famous as rm -rf in the Linux community, but if you're a new user, you might have no idea it exists and could carelessly type it in. In fact, I've personally seen this used as a prank in online forums. Someone asked how to get fancy lettering (font ligatures) rendered in their terminal instead of the boring default text, and this evil–evil person told them to enter the fork bomb. On the surface, it almost feels logical that a weird string of symbols would render itself as fancy characters. However, what it'll actually do is rapidly consume system resources, slowing everything to a crawl and potentially making your system unusable. To understand why, here’s a quick overview of how it works: - :() declares a function with the name “:” - { :|:& } is the function body. Every time the function runs, it executes “:|:&” - :|:& creates a pipeline containing two calls to the function and runs that pipeline in the background - ; ends the function definition. - The final : calls the function for the first time. So it's essentially a function that keeps calling itself — where the first call becomes two, then two becomes four, then eight, then sixteen, and it just keeps going. The number of processes grows extremely rapidly until the system hits its limits. You’ll notice a severe slowdown or the system becoming entirely unresponsive. Now, the command itself doesn't delete your files or install malware, but recovering from the resulting lockup will require a hard reboot. This can cause problems if your system was in the middle of writing data — for example, during a system update, backup, or file transfer. Likewise, anything you opened but didn't save will likely be lost. It's rarely catastrophic, but it certainly turns into a nuisance.

item.title: These are the cheapest GPUs that can run DLSS 5 (you probably own one already)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.56
The first game with official DLSS 5 support, NBA 2K27, came out recently, and modders quickly took the DLSS 5 DLL file from the game and made it available to gamers around the world who own a newer NVIDIA GPU, allowing them to use DLSS 5 in a bunch of PC games with tools such as OptiScaler and DLSS 5 Swapper. While only the RTX 50 series is officially supported, at least for now, the two aforementioned utilities allow you to use DLSS 5 on older NVIDIA graphics cards as well. While a good chunk of NVIDIA GPUs can run DLSS 5 at playable frame rates, either officially or with mods, I've created a list of the most affordable NVIDIA cards that are widely available new and that you can run DLSS 5 on. Naturally, most are RTX 50 models, but I've also included a few RTX 40 cards as well. RTX 5050 The cheapest official route to DLSS 5, but it only just manages 1080p You can get an RTX 5050 new for about $300, but I recommend opting for a different card because the 5050 isn't that great, even for 1080p gaming. If you already own one, that's a different story, and you should definitely test DLSS 5 in games you own just to see the technology for yourself, even though it has a drastic frame rate hit. Now, while NBA 2K27 can run at playable frame rates at 1080p on an RTX 5050, reaching almost 60 FPS, you'll have to settle for 30ish frames per second or less in many other modern games. You'll also have a hard time using multi-frame generation along with DLSS 5 due to the card's limited 8GB memory buffer. But hey, the RTX 5050 can run DLSS 5, and at playable frame rates in some games, so why not try it out if you already own the card? RTX 5060 The minimum for a playable 1080p experience The RTX 5060 is the first decent choice for a 1080p experience. PC gamers have managed to get almost 60 frames per second running DLSS 5 at 1080p in a number of titles, which should be more than playable for many people. Some more demanding games will run slower, though, at about 40 FPS or lower. While this card's much more expensive than the RTX 5050, with the most affordable configs starting just north of $450 as of this writing, you're getting much higher performance that's enough to play many games with the modded DLSS 5 DLL. The only caveat, again, is that the card only has 8GB of RAM, which won't be enough for multi-frame generation running on top of DLSS 5 in games that use lots of video memory. That said, you should be able to run both frame gen and DLSS 5 in a wide range of games that aren't memory hogs. GIGABYTE GeForce RTX 5060 GAMING OC V2 - Memory Clock Speed - 2602MHz - Graphics RAM Size - 8GB A no-nonsense option for 1080p gaming, the RTX 5060 pairs 8GB of GDDR7 with NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture, while Gigabyte's triple-fan cooling setup keeps temperatures and noise in check through long gaming sessions. RTX 5060 Ti 8GB A bit faster than the RTX 5060 and a serviceable option for 1080p Now, while the 8GB version of the RTX 5060 Ti wasn't a great choice back when GPU prices were sane, it now makes sense to get one since you're getting a 15% performance bump compared to the RTX 5060 for about the same price bump. When it comes to playing games with DLSS 5, the performance boost should be enough for 60 FPS at 1080p in a lot of games, and about 40 FPS in more demanding titles. You will also be able to use frame generation in many modern titles, but multi-frame gen will be a no-go in games that devour VRAM. If you ask me, at current prices the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB is a better choice than the RTX 5060 if you can stretch your budget by about $50. RTX 5060 Ti 16GB The bare minimum for the 1440p resolution Thanks to its 16GB of VRAM, the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is the first option on this list capable of running games at 1440p with DLSS 5 enabled at playable frame rates. That said, the experience won't be perfect. You can expect about 40 FPS in most games where you can mod in DLSS 5, with 60 FPS and higher frame rates only being available with frame generation. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB has a major downside, though. It costs only about $60–$70 less than the RTX 5070, while the latter is about 30% faster. Sure, you're only getting 12GB of memory with the RTX 5070, but even 12GB should be enough for DLSS 5 and multi-frame gen at 1440p, with the RTX 5070 being less than 15% more expensive than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. If you're getting a new card, the RTX 5070 is a much better choice between the two. Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 Ti - Memory Clock Speed - 2632MHz - Graphics RAM Size - 8GB, 16GB Nvidia's RTX 5060 Ti (this time made by Asus) comes in two variants: 8GB and 16GB. The 16GB is a lot pricier, but with growing VRAM constraints, it remains the better pick. RTX 5070 The first decent choice for 1440p DLSS 5 gaming The RTX 5070 is the first card I'd actually recommend for 1440p DLSS 5 gaming. It's got enough oomph to run games at playable frame rates without the help of frame generation, and its 12GB of memory will hold down the fort at 1440p in most games, even with ray tracing enabled. While its price is highly inflated compared to the MSRP, this is the case for every NVIDIA card out there, so despite it being overpriced, it's still a solid choice if DLSS 5 support is a must. If not, you should consider getting the AMD RX 9070 XT, which packs 16GB of memory, is about 25% faster, and is actually cheaper than NVIDIA's card. I've been using an RX 9070 XT for about a year and a half now and can say that FSR 4 is almost as good as DLSS upscaling and that the card is an excellent choice for 1440p and 1440p ultrawide gaming. Gigabyte GeForce RTX 5070 Windforce - Graphics RAM Size - 12GB - Boost Clock Speed - 2600MHz Nvidia's RTX 5070 graphics card is one of the more balanced options in the RTX 50-series lineup. It gives you 12GB of VRAM, which is much more future-proof than the 8GB VRAM lower-tier cards offer, while also offering more cores and higher bandwidth than the RTX 5060 Ti. RTX 4060 and RTX 4060 Ti These RTX 40 cards aren't officially supported yet, but you can run DLSS 5 on them with mods Now, DLSS 5 isn't officially supported on older NVIDIA cards, but you can make it work with OptiScaler and DLSS 5 Swapper. When it comes to older NVIDIA cards you can still buy new, the RTX 4060 and RTX 4060 Ti are the cheapest out there that can run games with DLSS 5 at anything resembling playable frame rates. The RTX 4060 Ti is in a much better situation since it's about as fast as the RTX 5060, meaning you will get a playable DLSS 5 experience at 1080p in a wide range of modern games. On the flip side, the RTX 4060 is just a tad faster than the RTX 5050, meaning you shouldn't expect much more than 30 FPS with DLSS 5 enabled at 1080p, with more demanding games running even slower than that. Still, this is high enough to check just how DLSS 5 looks in action, so if you own an RTX 4060 and are interested in checking out NVIDIA's latest tech, feel free to test it. But if you want to get a new GPU for DLSS 5, neither the RTX 4060 nor the RTX 4060 Ti is worth it, unless you're ready to peruse the used market. You can run DLSS 5 on any RTX 20 card or newer, but most won't deliver playable frame rates Thanks to tools such as OptiScaler, RenoDX, and DLSS 5 Swapper, and the patched DLSS 5 DLL files, you can actually run DLSS 5 on every NVIDIA GPU starting with the RTX 20 series. Sure, the performance will be quite poor on many of the older cards; in fact, DLSS 5 will barely run on a good chunk of them. But hey, at least you can experience neural rendering firsthand and see what the fuss all is about.

item.title: I tested 3 paper-like Android tablets, and the winner isn't e-ink
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.38
As much as I enjoy digital books and comics, there is nothing quite like reading on paper—but I have neither the budget nor the space to amass physical copies of my digital library. This is why I've kept tabs on the state of paper-like Android tablets over the years. After comparing three devices that each take a different approach, here's what I would buy. A black and white E Ink tablet My BOOX Go 10.3 is great for books and manga, but color comics are a no-go When I read a digital copy of a novel on my super-thin BOOX Go 10.3, it's increasingly hard to argue that it isn't a superior experience to carrying around a physical book. The text looks as crisp as on paper, except I have complete freedom to change the size, font, and spacing. It's gentle on my eyes and ideal for reading outdoors. The device itself is paper-thin, which can't be said for the physical versions of the lengthy fantasy ebooks I'm currently reading (Adrian Tchaikovsky’s Epic Fantasy bundle has been a banger). Reading manga or other black and white comics on this device feels just as good. The lines are striking, providing amazing contrast without the eye strain that comes from staring at a mostly white OLED or LCD. If you have the opportunity to read Strangers in Paradise on a monochrome E Ink tablet, do it. Tragically, things tend to fall apart when I want to read my full-color comics. A monochromatic eReader like my BOOX Go can only render these in black and white, which loses much of the detail and often isn't fully legible. This leads me to try a color eReader instead. A color E Ink tablet I found the Bigme B10 an okay comic experience and worse for everything else My first color E Ink eReader was the BOOX Tab Ultra C. On that device, color E ink felt like reading newspaper prints. It's not a bad look, but it's also not the one that series like Saga or Monstress were designed for. These comics look much more accurately represented on the OLED screen of my Motorola Razr Fold than they do on an E Iink tablet. This year, I tried out a Bigme B10. Despite being a newer tablet with better specs, the technology hasn't evolved in the past few years. In fact, this purchase was a step backward. Bigme's software is so janky that I very quickly sold the device (Bigme’s return policy was too costly and time-consuming to bother). If anything, the color representation on the comics I wanted to read felt worse than I remembered and not worth the roughly $600 this device commanded. It gets worse. Color Kaleido 3 screens are incredibly dim, so they require a front light in all but direct light. Their lower contrast also makes ebooks less pleasant to read than they are on black and white eReaders. The end-result is a display that feels mediocre for books and comics alike. Yet while these generalizations are largely true, some brands make better modifications than others. I‘d say the Kindle Colorsoft technology stack results in a better reading experience than what I encountered with Bigme, but since I have no interest in getting locked into Amazon’s ecosystem, I needed to look elsewhere. Paper-like LCD It’s TCL NXTPAPER or bust I've heard about TCL's NXTPAPER displays for years, but I never quite convinced myself to pull the trigger. So I was happy to receive a review sample of the TCL Tab A1 Plus NXTPAPER, which is the right size and shape to compare with the E Ink Android tablets with which I am more familiar. TCL's approach to Android is quite minimal. It’s largely stock, with a few additions related almost exclusively to the display. The tablet does not activate an eEeader mode by default, but the difference is already striking when you first turn on a tablet. Colors look different on this matte display than on conventional tablets. They are less vivid, and, like the Frame TV on my wall, sometimes make the graphics look more like art (even if most of the time it doesn't). Things get interesting when you press the NXTPAPER button on the side of the device. This presents two additional options, a color e-paper mode and an "ink" one. The color option is much less vivid and feels comparable to an E Ink tablet, only it doesn't take on the low DPI look of a newspaper. This means modern comics retain the sharpness that their paper versions have, even if the colors are off. The higher refresh rate means I can turn pages and switch between comics more quickly. Reading ebooks on this tablet is less ideal. While the tablet does have advantages such as being readable in direct sunlight, it still feels like reading on an LCD. When a text file is only presenting words in black and white, there just isn't much nuance for TCL’s NXTPAPER stack to handle. It's fine, but I'm not noticing enough distinction to want to pick up this heavy tablet over my significantly lighter phone, even if I would still choose this over conventional Android tablets. For books, I‘d prefer to return to BOOX any day of the week. Unlike E Ink, NXTPAPER never quite feels identical to paper. Again, like my Frame TV, the backlight is the biggest tell. But perfection can be the enemy of the good, and there's something to be said for being close enough. NXTPAPER fails at being a drop-in replacement for paper, but it succeeds at offering a far more pleasant reading experience than conventional Android tablets and iPads. Which type of Android tablet is the better paper-like experience? E Ink excites me. I look forward to seeing how the technology progresses, and I get my hopes up whenever a new tablet is announced. Yet I continue to walk away disappointed. I have not yet seen an E Ink device that is best for all types of reading. If you’re committed enough, I would recommend a tablet like my BOOX Go 10.3 for ebooks, though any other black and white eReader will suffice. For color comics, E Ink just doesn’t quite do it for me just yet, and I’d recommend a TCL NXTPAPER tablet instead. That said, I personally have come to view a book-style foldable as the most ideal digital e-reading device. It’s lightweight, comfortable to hold for hours at a time, around the same size as a paperback, and large enough for comics.

item.title: 4 smart purchases to reduce your home energy usage
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.33
Energy costs are up, and the best way to lower your bill is to lower how much you use. There are multiple ways to go about that, and the right tech can help. Thermal Imaging Camera Find the air leaks through your home using your phone Heating and cooling are the two most energy-intensive things we do in our homes. We want heat to stay inside during winter and cool air to stay inside during summer. If that air leaks out, our heaters and air conditioners have to work harder to make up the difference. You can detect leaks by walking around the house and placing your hand near noticeable gaps to feel for air coming through. But this is neither the most efficient nor the most effective method. Instead, you can use a thermal imaging camera to detect temperature differences. These days, you can get a camera that plugs into your phone, allowing you to see the information on your large, high-resolution display. I have a few permissions. Instant hot water dispenser Waste less water and possibly use less energy Most of us know that central air and electric heaters are huge energy guzzlers. Not everyone knows that water heaters tend to follow behind as the next most energy-intensive thing in our home. Producing hot water is demanding, whether that's boiling water on a stove or turning on an electric kettle. I‘ve become enamored with instant hot water dispensers. A countertop hot water dispenser like the Waterdrop M6CG plugs into a regular wall outlet. Instead of boiling water like an electric kettle, it heats water instantly as it comes out and only runs for the short time it takes to fill a mug. Like an induction cooktop compared to an electric one, it saves energy by getting the job done faster. A built-in hot water dispenser like the Waterdrop K6 uses more power because it has its own tank that it needs to keep heated — but it has reduced my water usage by saving me from running my kitchen tap long enough to heat up. This also reduces how hard my electric water heater needs to work. A portable power station with solar panels Free energy that you can produce yourself The fastest way to recharge a portable power station is portable solar power. Many companies will even bundle the two together, saving you the research. Portable power stations save you money by reducing or eliminating your need to buy gas for a generator during a power outage. For people on time-of-use utility plans, these batteries can power electronics when energy costs are high and recharge when energy costs are low. Their capacity is now large enough to offload the charging of any number of portable electronics. A portable power station like the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 that you charge for a couple of hours on the weekend can then be used to charge your phone, laptop, and gaming handhelds throughout the week. SwitchBot Floor Circulator Fan A fan that can cool you off wherever you are and better circulate the air in your home I was fortunate enough to be able to design the home that I live in, and we intentionally placed ceiling fans in all the main living areas. These ceiling fans are not only an alternative to cranking up the central air, but they are a supplement that reduces how long our HVAC needs to run. They use so little power; by moving heat or air where it's needed, they save far more energy than leaving the HVAC to do that work alone. If you have ceiling fans, use them, but even in our home, we don't have a ceiling fan in every place that could benefit from airflow. This is why I've become quite enamored with battery-powered fans like SwitchBot's Floor Circulator Fan, which doesn't require an app despite being a SwitchBot product. It can run from wall power like any other fan, but it can also run on a battery for many hours at a time without using any wall power. It’s efficient enough that you could add it to a list of devices charged exclusively with a portable power station. Spend money to save money The list above contains hundreds of dollars worth of tech, and these devices won't save you anywhere near that much money over the course of a year. It cost my wife and me tens of thousands of dollars to eliminate our home electric bill by blanketing our roof with solar panels. Tech purchases don't save you money all at once, but they can change your thinking and lead to savings that add up in the long run.

item.title: I've run hundreds of Docker containers, but these 5 have never needed fixing
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.04
I've been homelabbing for over five years at this point, and it's safe to say I've run hundreds of Docker containers over the years. However, there are five stand-out containers in my homelab that I've simply never had to repair. Plex It's my media center of choice I'm a huge Plex advocate. I've tried Jellyfin in the past, but it just doesn't click with me like Plex does. Plex was the very first container I launched in my homelab back in January 2021, and I have been actively using Plex for over a decade at this point in some way, shape, or form. For me, Plex is the heart of my homelab. Without it, I wouldn't be writing about homelabbing content today. But, it's also one of the most stable apps in my homelab. I have never had an issue with it in all my years of running it. It just does what it needs to and doesn't complain. Any issues I've had have always been self-inflicted, like running it in a virtual machine and trying to pass through my integrated graphics from Proxmox to Plex—that was a nightmare, but not because of any fault with the Plex container. If I had to name my most reliable container in my homelab, it would definitely be Plex. Nginx Proxy Manager I couldn't run my homelab without it Nginx Proxy Manager, or NPM as it's also called, is right up there with Plex in its reliability. I prefer to use reverse proxies for my homelab's external access over Cloudflare Tunnels mainly because it's what I started with and what I know well. With NPM, I can add a new self-hosted reverse proxy in about 10 seconds because I'm so well-versed at it at this point. I have over two dozen reverse proxies running through it, and it's really never given me any problems. The few times I have had a problem, it typically had to do with something else on the network, and not NPM itself. NPM has been rock-steady for me and I've never had to really repair anything about it, outside of fixing a few Let's Encrypt certificates that got corrupted during a server move one time. Audiobookshelf This audiobook server has been rock-solid On this list, Audiobookshelf is one of the newer containers in my homelab, but it has become one of the most reliable containers in my homelab. If you've never heard of Audiobookshelf, it's an open-source Audible replacement, basically. It doesn't actually handle sourcing audiobooks like Audible does, but it handles the playback side of things. I left Audible about a year and a half ago for Audiobookshelf and haven't looked back. Like Plex, Audiobookshelf simply runs in the background and handles everything that I need it to without any fuss. I honestly haven't had a single problem with Audiobookshelf, which is pretty crazy considering it has over a dozen users on it and two separate libraries. Any problems that I've ever had were from third-party mobile apps, making the service itself something I've never had to fuss with. Tautulli It runs so smoothly I forget it's there most of the time Alongside Plex, I've been running Tautulli since the beginning of my homelab journey. It's a companion app to Plex and basically keeps a log of what was watched, when it was watched, who watched it, and what's being watched right now. Tautulli does a lot more than just that, but that's mainly what I use it for. I have never once had to mess with Tautulli after setting it up. It's just a reliable container that sits back and collects information for me. In fact, I had forgotten how long I have had Tautulli running because I rarely think about it. A few months ago, I needed to downsize my Plex server's catalog to save some space, and Tautulli started surfacing data from five or more years ago. It was impressive to me, and a testament to how reliable this container has been in my homelab. Speedtest-Tracker There when I need it, running when I'm not thinking about it Speedtest-Tracker is a container that I honestly don't think about often. I rarely check it, but I know that it runs reliably and is there when I need it. When would I need it? If I'm ever noticing slower networking speeds or other network-related issues, I can check Speedtest-Tracker to see what it is showing historically. Is this a one-off problem, or is my networking speed slower around the same time every day? Speedtest-Tracker just sits there, silently collecting data for me without me having to think about it at all. The best Docker containers are the ones you sometimes forget are even there I have plenty of Docker containers that I'm constantly messing with for one reason or another. Those containers are the ones that cause me the most headache. The best Docker containers in my homelab are the ones that I hardly ever think about, and I really think that's how every homelab should be.

item.title: Google’s Gemini went rogue and breached three companies
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.88
What you need to know - Google has apparently admitted that Gemini had escaped its testing environment and independently accessed systems belonging to three real companies. - A misconfigured internet connection was the initial opening, while a matching company name added to the confusion. - Gemini eventually stopped itself after recognizing that it was targeting real companies. - Google initially kept the incident quiet, arguing that Gemini self-corrected and caused no damage. Google's Gemini adds to the long list of AI models that have gone rogue. We have already seen similar digital jailbreaks handled by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in third-party safety testing. Now, it’s been revealed that Google’s Gemini model escaped its containment area in May, hacking its way into systems at three real companies, all on its own. The Wall Street Journal reports that the incident took place during a “capture the flag” exercise conducted by AI security firm Irregular. Gemini was intended to test a fictional company in a closed testing environment, but an unplanned internet connection gave it an escape. The fictional company also had a real business with the same name, creating another opening for confusion. Once online, Gemini found its way into three real companies. In one case it just kept guessing passwords until it got through. In two others, it found working credentials stored in public repositories and used them to access protected systems. It turns out that throughout the entire process, Gemini didn’t require any exotic movie-style exploits. It just combined elementary security vulnerabilities with the ability to search, decide, and persistently try, without a human directing each and every move. Google said Gemini stopped when it realized the targets were real companies and did not cause damage. In fact, while Anthropic’s Claude 4.7 kept going during a similar incident, Gemini backed off on its own volition. The impacted organizations were informed, although Irregular says the known testing issues were corrected weeks later. The search giant felt the incident didn't warrant a public announcement at the time because the AI self-corrected. But third-party researchers were not told until late July, and details are only now emerging after media inquiries pushed the issue. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android As AI agents gain broader access to the internet and computers, companies will need to establish tighter boundaries around what those systems can reach and clearer rules for what happens when those boundaries fail. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. He has been writing about consumer tech for as long as he can remember, and he has used a variety of Android phones since falling in love with Jelly Bean. item.title: Google Photos could soon be built much deeper into Samsung Gallery
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.70
What you need to know - Samsung's OneDrive Gallery integration is ending soon, but Google Photos appears ready to take its place. - A new Gallery Cloud Sync service has appeared on the Galaxy Store with support for backing up to Google Photos. - Samsung hasn't announced the Google Photos integration yet, but it could start rolling out within weeks. Samsung has started laying the groundwork for what appears to be the replacement for its outgoing OneDrive integration, and unsurprisingly, it's Google Photos. Earlier this year, Samsung announced that users would no longer be able to use OneDrive to back up photos and videos directly through the Samsung Gallery app. Until now, Galaxy users have been able to automatically sync their Gallery photos and videos with OneDrive without needing to use another app or service. However, that partnership is coming to an end later this month. And now, Samsung appears to be preparing its replacement with none other than Google Photos. X user Sandeep Adap has spotted a new Samsung service called "Gallery Cloud Sync" on the Galaxy Store, which appears to be designed to take over from the existing Gallery OneDrive Sync integration. The app listing says Gallery Cloud Sync will safely back up your memories, including photos and videos, to "Google Cloud" so you can access them across your devices. The mention of Google Cloud might sound slightly confusing, but it appears Samsung is actually referring to Google Photos here. User That Josh Guy on X was able to preview the upcoming functionality, which isn't live just yet, and found that Samsung Gallery will offer an option to sync directly with Google. The Gallery settings will reportedly show your available Google storage, let you choose which albums to sync, and offer controls to sync over Wi-Fi or while roaming. This could be a big change if you currently rely on OneDrive for Samsung Gallery backups, since you'll likely need to switch to Google Photos. That said, the overall experience should remain pretty similar, with the sync controls still built directly into the Gallery app. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The OneDrive sync option has already started disappearing from Samsung Gallery for some users and is expected to be discontinued completely later this month. Thankfully, Samsung's upcoming Google Photos integration looks like it could be an even more natural replacement. Samsung hasn't officially announced Galaxy Cloud Sync or started rolling out the Google Photos integration just yet. But with OneDrive support ending soon, we expect the new option to become available sometime later this month or in early October. Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. When he's not testing gadgets, he's either sipping chai, watching football, or playing cricket.
