There’s an entire industry of data brokers who hoover up oceans of public data, boil it down into complete personal profiles, and sell those profiles to people search sites, ad trackers, or even identity thieves. Stop the Bleeding: Easy Habits to Limit What You Share Now that we’ve established your personal data is likely strewn around the web, what can you do about it? For starters, rein in your own sharing. Make sure your social media accounts are configured so only your friends can see your posts. And even then, think twice before putting your address or other personal data in a post. Likewise, think about when you’re posting to a public discussion board—is there anything in your post that you wouldn’t want the world to see? This also applies to information you share with AI chatbots. Not only does the AI receive any private data you include, but it also makes its own inferences to extend that knowledge—often incorrectly. When filling out online registration forms, only fill required fields. And if a required field isn’t relevant to your interaction with the website, consider supplying false information. Clean Up the Damage: Specialized Tools to Delete Your Profile Earlier, I mentioned data brokers that collect public information and use it to create saleable personal profiles. There’s an entire industry of personal data removal tools devoted to finding your profiles on such sites and opting you out of their collections. These can be pricey, but some of the services will identify your exposure for free, leaving you to handle the opt-out process yourself. You’ll also find services that let you shop and interact online without revealing your actual email address. These temporary email services help you give a different email alias to each online merchant while still managing your email just as you’ve always done. Some even let you mask your credit card and phone number. Many websites require that you create a free account for full access. If you stop using the site, that account remains, potentially exposed if the site gets breached or acquired, or if it just decides to sell your data. Some security apps can search your email history to locate such accounts and aid in the process of closing those you don’t use. The Online Account Cleanup feature in McAfee+ reports on all the accounts found in your email—at the Ultimate pricing tier it automates closing out those accounts. PrivacyHawk offers a similar service. Ultimately, it’s nearly impossible to make use of the internet’s massive resources without leaving some traces. But if you stay alert, you can minimize what you reveal. And with the right tools, you can seriously shrink your digital footprint. About Our Expert When the IBM PC was new, I served as the president of the San Francisco PC User Group for three years. That’s how I met PCMag’s editorial team, who brought me on board in 1986. In the years since that fateful meeting, I’ve become PCMag’s expert on security, privacy, and identity protection, putting antivirus tools, security suites, and all kinds of security software through their paces. Before my current security gig, I supplied PCMag readers with tips and solutions on using popular applications, operating systems, and programming languages in my "User to User" and "Ask Neil" columns, which began in 1990 and ran for almost 20 years. Along the way, I wrote more than 40 utility articles, as well as Delphi Programming for Dummies and six other books covering DOS, Windows, and programming. I also reviewed thousands of products of all kinds, ranging from early Sierra Online adventure games to AOL’s precursor Q-Link. In the early 2000s, I turned my focus to security and the growing antivirus industry. After years of working with antivirus, I’m known throughout the security industry as an expert on evaluating antivirus tools. I serve as an advisory board member for the Anti-Malware Testing Standards Organization (AMTSO), an international nonprofit group dedicated to coordinating and improving testing of anti-malware solutions.

item.title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: To Upgrade or Not?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.62
Table of Contents Not everything at Apple's Surprise and Shine event was about the foldable iPhone Duo. There's plenty to be excited about with the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, especially if you're moving up from an older model. The two iPhones hardly differ from one another apart from screen size and battery life. And while they seem pretty similar to last year's iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, they have a performance edge that may be worth the bump. We've finished testing the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and have spent the last year dissecting the iPhone 17 Pro line. Here's how to decide whether upgrading to the 18 Pro is worth it for you. Full Specs | Apple iPhone 17 Pro | Apple iPhone 18 Pro | | |---|---|---| | Operating System | | | | Operating System | iOS 26 | iOS 27 | | CPU | | | | CPU | Apple A19 Pro | Apple A20 Pro | | Dimensions | | | | Dimensions | 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches | 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches | | Screen Size | | | | Screen Size | 6.3 inches | 6.3 inches | | Screen Resolution | | | | Screen Resolution | 2,622 by 1,206 pixels | 2622 by 1206 pixels | | Camera Resolution (Rear; Front-Facing) | | | | Camera Resolution (Rear; Front-Facing) | 48MP, 48MP, 48MP; 18MP | 48MP, 48MP, 48MP, 25MP | | Battery Life (As Tested) | | | | Battery Life (As Tested) | 27 hours, 42 minutes | TBD | Pricing: Increases Across the Board The iPhone 18 Pro lineup spans two models and various storage capacities. This is the first year that Apple is offering 2TB of storage with the smaller iPhone 18 Pro. Here's how it all breaks down: - iPhone 18 Pro: 256GB, $1,199; 512GB, $1,399; 1TB, $1,599; 2TB, $1,999 - iPhone 18 Pro Max: 256GB, $1,299; 512GB, $1,499; 1TB, $1,899; 2TB, $2,499 For comparison, here is last year's original pricing for the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max from when they debuted: - iPhone 17 Pro: 256GB, $1,099; 512GB, $1,299; 1TB, $1,499 - iPhone 17 Pro Max: 256GB, $1,199; 512GB, $1,399; 1TB, $1,599; 2TB, $1,999 In short, pricing is up $100 across the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, thanks to component shenanigans across the global supply chain. At the very least, 2TB of storage is now available on the smaller phone. Winner: iPhone 17 Pro. Design: Out With the Orange and In With the New There was nothing wrong with last year's iPhone 17 Pro redesign of the rear-shaped camera island, and it was clearly popular, as I see the orange phone in many hands. But the iPhone 18 Pro's colorways are simply outstanding compared with last year's offerings. Last year's special colors were Cosmic Orange and Deep Blue, but this year's are Glacier (an ice blue) and Burgundy (a wine red). Deep Black and Silver are also available for those who prefer something more conventional. Sizing hasn't changed between generations. The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro are both 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches (HWD). The iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 17 Pro Max are both 6.43 by 3.07 by 0.34 inches. If you want the lightest phone, it's last gen's iPhone 17 Pro at 7.27 ounces. The iPhone 18 Pro bumps the weight to 7.44 ounces, likely due to the added weight of the hard-thin polymer blades used in the camera's variable aperture. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the biggest honker of the four devices, and it's half an ounce heavier than last year's iPhone 17 Pro Max. It went from 8.22 ounces to 8.78 ounces. All iPhones share an IP68 water and dust rating. They all have an Action Button, Camera Control, MagSafe, wireless charging, and a USB-C port. Winner: Tie. The added weight is for a feature you'll use. Display: Nothing Different to See Here The new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max displays are the same size as last year's, with minor upgrades. They're 6.3-inch and 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR LTPO OLED displays, respectively, with unchanged resolution and pixel density. The most noticeable changes between the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max and its predecessors are the anti-reflective glass, improved outdoor contrast, and the Ceramic Shield 2 coating on the front. The Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro has been truncated. It's smaller than on the iPhone 17 Pro series. Now that it supports up to three Live Activities at a time, those tiny icons will still take up the extra space gained. Winner: iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max for the reinforcement with Ceramic Shield 2. Hardware: First 2nm Process The iPhone 18 Pro features the new A20 Pro. This is the first time Apple has built its silicon on a 2nm architecture, a major feat since it's a physically smaller processor. The A20 Pro is a six-core CPU with two performance cores and four efficiency cores. It pairs a seven-core GPU with neural accelerators for low-latency AI tasks. Performance-wise, Apple's A20 Pro is a major whopper over last generation's A19 Pro. In our Geekbench 6 tests, the iPhone 18 Pro scored 4,787 in single-core tests and 12,166 in multi-core tests, compared to the iPhone 17 Pro's 3,820 single-core and 9,820 multi-core scores. The iPhone 18 Pro Max scored 4,719 and 12,804, compared to the iPhone 17 Pro Max's 3,784 single-core and 9,734 multi-core scores. That's 24% and 32% better scores for each device, respectively. Those aren't small gains. On GPU-heavy gaming benchmarks, the A20 Pro delivers a substantial jump and even beats some current Android flagships. The iPhone 18 Pro Max achieved 48.8 frames per second (fps) at 8,143 frames in 3DMark, the synthetic benchmark we use to test graphics performance. It's about a 48% boost over the iPhone 17 Pro Max's 32.9fps at 5,487 frames. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro leads the lineup with 51.4fps at 8,579 frames, outpacing its predecessor and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, which scored 46.99fps at 7,847 frames. The iPhone 18 Pro can maintain a particularly high, consistent frame rate while gaming, likely helped in part by its revamped vapor chamber. For connectivity, the iPhone 18 Pro supports both sub-6GHz and mmWave 5G bands. However, in the U.S., only the iPhone 18 Pro uses Apple's custom C2 cellular modem. The iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a Qualcomm-made chip instead. The international versions of the series both use the C2 modem. It delivers on Apple's promise of faster uploads. Apple ditched the physical SIM completely in recent years. You won't see it on the iPhone 18 Pro. Both devices in the Pro line support up to two active eSIMs simultaneously, matching the iPhone 17 Pro. Winner: iPhone 18 Pro series. It's fast! Cameras: Variable Aperture Enters the Fold On the spec sheet, you'll see that the iPhone 17 Pro series and the iPhone 18 Pro series have similar camera sensors, at least in megapixels: a rear-facing triple 48MP array. But they differ in one key way: the iPhone 18 Pro is the only one with a variable aperture. It has a secondary 48MP Ultra Wide with the same 120-degree field of view as last year, plus a 48MP telephoto lens with an f/2.8 aperture and 4x optical zoom: an upgrade, but one with a few limitations. The iPhone 18 Pro series offers native manual Pro controls, where you can switch between four aperture presets (ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, ƒ/4.0). You can also change shutter speed, white balance, and follow with an on-screen exposure histogram. The Pro line can shoot video at up to 4K resolution at 120fps. The 18 Pro series is also the first to introduce Apple's Reference Image, which cryptographically signs the captured photo. You can use the Photos app to verify an image's originality or whether it's been touched by AI. Because it's encrypted at the hardware level, it's only available on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, though older iPhones can still identify the digital watermark. The front-facing camera remains mostly unchanged. Both generations have an 18MP front camera that can shoot 4K video at 60fps. However, the iPhone 18 Pro's selfie sensor is a 1:1 square that's twice the size of previous models. It now offers several wide-angle modes so that you can fit more of the scene behind you or friends on either side. You'll have to wait for our reviews to see whether the variable aperture makes a big difference. But the Pro line is currently the best Apple camera you can get in your pocket. Winner: iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max. Battery Life: We're Going Long Apple doesn't typically detail the battery capacities of its new iPhones, but we ran our battery benchmarks on the iPhone 18 Pro/Pro Max. The iPhone 18 Pro Max lasted 23 hours and 25 minutes of video playback. It's nearly ten hours behind its predecessor, but that could be due to a variety of factors. The anecdotal battery rundown managed nearly 50 hours of use with a few quick top-up sessions in the end. The Pro Max fared much better at 34 hours and 31 minutes. Charging speeds also shortened this round by about five minutes compared with the iPhone 17 Pro series. The iPhone 18 Pro charged to 49% in 15 minutes with a compatible 45W charger. It took 64 minutes to reach 100%. The iPhone 18 Pro Max reached 50% in 15 minutes with a compatible 60W charger. Wireless charging speeds on the iPhone 18 Pro series were increased to support 35W. Both models support MagSafe, Qi2, and Qi wireless charging. Winner: Tie. The iPhone is a long-lasting device overall. Which iPhone Pro is Right For You? The latest iPhone Pro is always a solid choice, but you don't need the brand-new model to get fast, reliable performance. The iPhone 17 Pro series was a strong launch last year. It was when Apple introduced the new rear camera island and began the journey toward better thermal dissipation. But the iPhone 18 Pro is the better choice simply because it delivers a major jump in performance with the A20 Pro, manual camera controls, and faster charging speeds. For now, here are a couple of things to consider if you are trying to decide on the iPhone 18 Pro series: - If you want the lightest, smallest Pro phone, it's the iPhone 18 Pro. - If you want the best camera capabilities possible, you can't go wrong with either iPhone 18 Pro size. The variable aperture alone is a neat feature, but the overall shooting and sensor improvements make the 18 Pro series a delight. - If you want endurance, the bigger iPhone 18 Pro Max has a larger battery to support the larger screen, so that it will last longer. The new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are on sale. They start at $1,199 and $1,299.

item.title: HubSpot Smart CRM Review: Comprehensive Contact Management for Bigger Businesses
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.53
HubSpot is one of the biggest names in CRM providers for large-scale companies, but it also offers the simpler, SMB-focused Smart CRM tool. The service, which you can now purchase independently of the company's other products, benefits from an excellent automation builder and several AI tools that streamline contact management. Moreover, the seemingly endless number of available add-ons makes Smart CRM easy to integrate into your existing business operations. However, the base plan is expensive, and some areas of the user experience could be more intuitive. HubSpot is worth considering for bigger businesses, but the extremely flexible Apptivo, the cost-effective Bigin by Zoho, and the exceptionally user-friendly Freshsales remain our Editors' Choice winners. HubSpot Smart CRM offers two plans: Professional and Enterprise. A free trial isn't available for either. Keep in mind that although you can pay monthly, that still locks you into an annual contract, with no option to cancel early. As such, you should subscribe only if you’re confident that you will use it for at least a year. HubSpot's free Marketing Hub plan lets you create contact lists and use their information to personalize marketing campaigns, but it only includes one deal pipeline, so it's not a viable long-term CRM solution. The Professional tier ($45 per user per month, billed annually) includes the full-featured AI agent hub, intent signals to enrich high-value customers, and contact enrichment to improve contact profiles. You can create 1,000 custom properties to connect specific data points to companies, contacts, or deals, with up to 40 calculated properties that roll up data from other fields to calculate things like commissions. Team management tools include the Breeze Assistant, 15 deal pipelines, up to 100 shared inboxes, and up to 75 reporting dashboards with the option to create up to 100 custom reports. Advanced AI agents and collaboration tools, such as a shared inbox, are also available, along with integrations with Slack and Salesforce. Enterprise ($75 per user per month, billed annually) adds AI insights on CRM index pages (in beta) and more advanced user management tools, such as multi-level team creation. Custom objects let you track virtually any passive data point in the CRM, while custom events let you track actions unique to your business. You also get a sandbox account for experimenting with aspects of the user experience. The calculated properties limit increases to 200; deal pipelines go up to 100; shared inboxes increase to 200; and the reporting dashboard limit increases to 100 dashboards with 500 custom reports. Both plans include access to an AI data agent for analyzing CRM data, a customer AI agent for answering customer questions, and a prospecting agent that builds personalized outreach for specific leads. However, each of these tools requires HubSpot AI credits. You get monthly allotments of AI credits with both plans (3,000 for Professional and 5,000 for Enterprise). If your company exceeds those allotments, you can buy more at a rate of $10 per 1,000 credits. HubSpot Smart CRM’s Professional tier is pricey for an entry-level plan on paper. Apptivo's and Zoho CRM's equivalents, respectively, cost $15 and $14 per user per month, billed annually. Even Insightly, one of the more expensive CRMs I’ve tested, maintains a base plan for $29 per user per month. However, the Professional plan's AI and automation features put it on par with—and in some cases, ahead of—similarly priced, high-end plans from other companies. Large businesses will likely find value in the sheer number of features you get with the Enterprise plan, but smaller companies should likely turn to more affordable plans from Apptivo, Bigin by Zoho CRM, and Freshsales. To sign up for Smart CRM, you need to create a HubSpot account using your name, email, and business name. HubSpot’s AI will ask you some basic questions to set up the core customer platform, with the option for you to configure things yourself. You can then request the upgrade to the Smart CRM product. Next, HubSpot’s AI will ask you additional questions and generate a custom CRM center based on your answers. This process is slightly more involved than signing up for other CRMs I’ve tested, but it's still largely straightforward. To add users, you can enter email addresses one at a time or via a CSV file. You can also set up permissions; a wide range of prebuilt options are available, such as sales reps and sales managers. You can create custom permissions presets in the settings area, too. HubSpot lets you import contacts from both CSV and Excel files. It won’t import contacts unless the spreadsheet contains specific fields, however, so your file must have separate columns for first and last names, for example. Otherwise, the requirements are pretty typical. Once you upload contacts, HubSpot maps them automatically to existing categories. The process is similar to what I’ve come to expect from top-ranking CRMs, such as Apptivo and Freshsales. The platform also supports advanced import options, meaning you can pull all of your existing CRM data—including deals and tasks—using a similarly automated mapping process. This can save you a significant amount of time if you’ve collected extensive and varied data. Of all the CRMs I’ve tested, only Pipedrive offers something similar, and its advanced import process isn’t as simple. Alternatively, you can sync data from dozens of other apps in the HubSpot Marketplace, such as MailChimp, Shopify, or Zoho CRM. Both one-way and two-way sync options are available. You can also hire a HubSpot CRM Data Migration Specialist for $500 to assist you. This process can take up to three weeks, but it might be worth it if you are bringing over a lot of data. The last setup step includes attaching an email address. This is a two-click process for Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 email addresses. You have to enter POP/SMTP settings if you use a different email provider. Adding a business VoIP system or any social media accounts is optional. The internal HubSpot Home page uses a simple black-and-white color scheme, with easy-to-read boxes displaying information about upcoming meetings and tasks. Navigating the site is simple, thanks to easily identifiable icons for key areas, such as contacts and reporting, in the left-hand toolbar. The “...” at the bottom of the toolbar lets you access other areas, such as the HubSpot Inbox. You can pin the tools you use most often to the main menu, as well as get rid of others you don't need. HubSpot displays quick digital tours and tutorial videos when you first log in to your account; you can skip them if you already have experience with CRMs. After that, you can get support 24/7 via email, live chat (with both an AI bot and human support options), or phone for both plans. Alternatively, you can consult HubSpot’s extensive knowledge base. Many CRMs, including Apptivo and Freshsales, limit some or all support channels to 24/5 access, making HubSpot noteworthy. Unlike Insightly CRM, HubSpot doesn’t separate leads and contacts. Instead, every contact receives a deal-stage indicator (such as New, Open, or Unqualified). By default, Smart CRM displays a table with all the key information about your contacts, including a column for recent updates that HubSpot's AI pulls from contact records. You can also add a Kanban view to understand the health of your pipeline and a calendar view to see your upcoming events at a glance. Contact profiles use a standard layout, with basic contact information on the right and a central area with more detailed records, including AI insights based on the contact’s interaction history. A collapsible sidebar displays companies, deals, and (if you’re also using HubSpot’s help desk system) tickets connected to the contact. Within a contact profile, you can modify contact records, move contacts through the pipeline, add a new deal or task, and send an email or make a call (if you have set up VoIP). Before you get into deals, it’s best to square away your pipelines. I found this the most confusing part of the Smart CRM experience, since there’s no individual tab for pipelines within the main area or the settings. I ended up asking the AI support bot for help, which directed me to the pipeline editor in Settings > Objects > Deals. Thankfully, the pipeline editor is highly intuitive, with options to edit the default pipeline or create a custom one. Deals, meanwhile, are simple to navigate even if you’ve never used a CRM before. This section uses a Kanban view by default, which means you can easily move deals forward in the pipeline just by dragging them. You can add calendar, report, or table views to see pipelines in different ways. Apptivo offers similar options. Both the card- and table-based views let you modify data directly and save whatever lists or views you need most often. That’s convenient for deals across multiple pipelines, deal packages, and long deals. And, as with contacts or companies, you can filter particularly long lists and create new data filters as you go. Breeze is what puts the “Smart” in HubSpot Smart CRM. It uses both in-house large language models and those from OpenAI to conduct company research, perform mundane tasks, trigger workflows, unify and enrich your data, and write blog posts, among many other functions. HubSpot divides functionality into two parts: Breeze Assistant and Agents. Breeze Assistant is available on both CRM plans. You can either select a prompt (such as “generate a report” or “summarize deal”) or type a custom request. Over time, Breeze Assistant learns about your company’s CRM needs. Additionally, it can perform data and contact enrichment, gathering information from your communications and the wider web to add key attributes, such as location and social media links, to contact profiles. I tested Breeze Assistant by asking various questions about my contacts, outside companies, and the platform itself. I found it helpful for researching potential and existing clients. The minimal information on my sample contacts somewhat limited my ability to test this feature, but Breeze Assistant still impressed me with excellent suggestions for nurturing leads. You can even ask Breeze Assistant to generate graphics and images for blog posts and collateral. However, since it relies on OpenAI's DALL-E, expect some of its infamous hallmarks to appear, like garbled text and people with more than five fingers. Compared with Zoho CRM’s Zia AI, I found the Breeze Assistant easier to talk with and more capable of understanding nuance. Of course, like any AI-powered assistant, you get back what you put into it. Note that some tasks are free, while others require varying amounts of AI credits; be sure to read up on AI credit usage for each task before using Breeze Assistant. Breeze Agents are what they sound like: AI-powered agents you can train to provide personalized outreach to prospects and clients. The Data Agent’s primary purpose is to create smart properties that generate specialized insights based on the information you select, such as a contact’s previous interactions or their public-facing website. Each prompt response from the Data Agent costs 10 AI credits. Other agents are available through HubSpot’s broader customer platform plans. All of these agents use AI credits per interaction, with the cost per credit varying by agent type and interaction complexity. HubSpot Smart CRM lets you set up multi-step workflows for automating various marketing tasks, with the option to start from a template, create a workflow from scratch, or build one with AI. Most templates are available only with a paid subscription to HubSpot’s broader customer platform, except for the “Create and assign tasks when a new deal is created” option. As such, you’ll likely end up creating most of your workflows. The workflow builder is a visual designer with a left-hand toolbar for adding elements such as triggers and actions to a flowchart. You can also ask AI to find and enter elements for you. The system is fairly intuitive and doesn't require coding knowledge. It’s also pretty similar to what I’ve found in other CRMs, such as Pipedrive. My one frustration here is the inclusion of templates you can’t actually use if you’re on the CRM-only plan. Clicking on these templates opens an upsell page in a new tab, which is highly distracting. The Inbox conveniently integrates all communications channels you’ve synced with HubSpot into one spot, including email, phone calls, and chats. You can sort through all of it here, and the list updates dynamically as new messages arrive. However, this area focuses on team communications, with no clear option for separating individual agents’ inboxes—something common in other CRMs like Freshsales. The email composer appears in an unusually small box in the right-hand corner and won’t let you enter your email’s subject or content until you’ve selected a recipient. After that, you get plenty of options, including typing out the email yourself, inserting a template or other content (such as articles from a knowledge base), or generating copy via HubSpot’s AI. The last choice is the least useful; it doesn’t offer the same range of tone or length options as similar tools from Pipedrive and others. The emails it created for me were highly generic. Template creation and bulk emailing are possible through Smart CRM, but both have severe limitations. You need to pay for HubSpot’s email marketing suite or purchase a third-party tool to create dynamic campaigns. Reports and dashboards are essentially the same thing in HubSpot. You can select one of several canned reports, modify it, and save it under a different name. Unlike many competing CRMs, HubSpot lets you create reports entirely from scratch. The custom report builder takes a little time to grasp, but it’s essentially a two-stage process. Stage one covers the basic data you’re looking to access (sales, marketing, service, and so on), as well as which subcategories you want (contacts or deals, for example, if your report is for sales). For the second stage, you move to a fairly intuitive report builder that lets you customize how data fields appear (e.g., a pie chart versus a bar chart). Additionally, you can use Breeze AI to generate custom reports. One oddity here is that there’s no immediately visible option for exporting your dashboards. Nonetheless, if you click the Share button and choose to email your report, the composer includes an area to select the file type (such as PNG or PDF) to convert it. I would prefer a one-step export option, something you get with Freshsales and Zoho CRM. You can get Smart CRM as part of the complete HubSpot customer platform or bundle it with individual HubSpot tools for email marketing, content management, and customer support. Together, these tools let you manage most of your business tasks in one place, though the cost of running them can be quite high. HubSpot Smart CRM also connects with various third-party apps, including email marketing tools (such as MailChimp), financial apps (such as QuickBooks and Stripe), Google and Microsoft Office apps, and social media platforms (such as Facebook and LinkedIn). Over 2,400 app integrations are available in the HubSpot Marketplace, making it one of the most versatile CRMs I’ve tested. HubSpot uses application-layer encryption to protect all user data, though it doesn’t state the specific protocol. HubSpot’s software and data centers also go through regular penetration testing and third-party audits to ensure its protocols are effective and meet the requirements of various security certifications, including HIPAA. You can see the details about certifications and incidents here. As mentioned, HubSpot’s permissions settings give you granular control over what each user can see and modify. You can also set up two-factor authentication and single sign-on to ensure the security of individual accounts. Additionally, you can control the data that HubSpot’s AI can access (though limiting this access may also reduce its functionality). Final Thoughts HubSpot Smart CRM - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. HubSpot Smart CRM offers effective tools for contact, lead, and deal management at scale. Its automated workflows and extensive Breeze AI tools are excellent for larger businesses looking to improve their customer management processes. We're also fans of its customizable report builder, comprehensive library of integrations, and excellent support resources. However, we recommend HubSpot only for expansive or growing organizations due to its high starting costs and occasional complexity. Smaller companies should instead choose among our Editors' Choice winners, including the highly customizable Apptivo, the very affordable Bigin by Zoho CRM, and the particularly intuitive Freshsales. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert I've been building websites and marketing campaigns for small businesses since 2010. I also run two businesses of my own: Hired Gunn Writing & Consulting and the Weeknight Writers group. I'm obsessed with testing new tools to improve and expand these businesses, and I've written about those I've tried for sites like CNET, CodeinWP/WPShout, and WinningWP.

item.title: Waymo Robotaxis Are Coming to Singapore, But Not Any Time Soon
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.90
Autonomous taxi rides run by Waymo are coming to Singapore, with testing in the country set to begin early next year. This announcement comes days after Waymo confirmed its launch in Tokyo, Japan, and a month after it detailed plans for Munich, Germany. Riders will have to wait until 2028 for Waymo to become available in Singapore. Alphabet has yet to say when in the year the service will be available, but it would mark Waymo's first launch in Southeast Asia. In the early months of next year, a series of Waymo test vehicles will be sent to Singapore to map locations and help accumulate data in what it calls “validation driving.” It begins its research process with manual driving, before moving to autonomous driving, with specialists available behind the wheel in case of emergencies. Waymo said, “We are confident that we will be able to meet Singapore’s high AV regulatory standards based on the significant real-world experience we have to-date and look forward to seeking the corresponding government approvals for future phases.” This comes days after Waymo announced plans to launch in its first Asian market: Tokyo. The ride-hailing service is set to launch in the Japanese city next year, made available through a partnership with Nihon Kotsu and GO. Testing in Tokyo first began in 2025, which explains the long wait for Singaporeans. Both Japan and Singapore differ greatly from US roads, where Waymo vehicles were first trained, including in weather conditions and traffic systems. Late last month, Waymo announced plans for robotaxis in Munich, Germany, marking its first European Union expansion. It is aiming to be up and running by the end of 2027. Waymo’s first international market is expected to be London, England. The brand says it’s on track to hit its target of launching vehicles in the city by the end of this year, but regulatory approval may delay Waymo and its robotaxi rivals' plans. In late August, Waymo’s head of policy and government affairs for the UK and Europe, Ben Loewenstein, told the Financial Times that the brand was “working through the safety approval process.” He said Waymo was waiting on Transport for London’s guidance on “how to earn their consent.” Earlier this year, Waymo launched in additional US cities, including Denver, Las Vegas, Tampa, and San Diego, bringing its total to 15. The wait for international Waymos on your next vacation may continue, but that’s not stopping it from keeping up with rivals like Tesla and Zoox. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Valve's Steam Frame Orders Begin Today. How to Snag the $1,059 VR Headset
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.67
Following a memory-related delay, Valve’s Steam Frame is finally ready to launch. The company will begin taking orders for the VR headset today. A 256GB version will be $1,059, and a 1TB model will cost $1,299. Both come with 16GB of Unified LPDDR5X RAM. How to Order the Steam Frame VR Headset To thwart resellers and bots, Valve is using a waitlist/reservation system. If you signed up and you're selected, you'll receive an email today with the option to purchase. “Based on the results of that randomization, you'll receive an email on September 17th letting you know you're either in the reservation queue or on the waitlist,” the company says. “If you're in the reservation queue, the model you signed up for has been reserved in your name. As units become available to ship, you'll receive an email with the option to purchase. The first batch of these emails will begin going out on September 18th. “You'll then have 72 hours to complete the purchase before we cancel your reservation and move on to the next person in the queue,” the company added. The product will be available on the Steam store for buyers in the US, Canada, Europe, and Australia. Customers in Japan, Taiwan, and Hong Kong will be able to purchase through Valve’s partner, Komodo. Valve's Steam Frame VR Headset Features Although the Steam Frame isn’t cheap, Valve is touting an array of enhancements and capabilities, including its design for both VR titles and non-VR games. “Designed for streaming, it can handle your entire Steam library. And it supports standalone play too, with over 100 games (and growing) already Steam Frame Standalone Verified,” it wrote in a blog post. The headset also features a 4-nanometer Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor and two 2,160-by-2,160 LCDs, each with a 72-144Hz refresh rate. In addition, the product relies on “inside-out tracking,” ditching external sensors, unlike the older Valve Index headset. Ahead of the launch, a few tech publications reviewed the headset. IGN notes, “The Steam Frame is probably one of the first VR headsets that can do everything right out of the box, from standalone gaming to streaming 2D games from your PC.” However, both IGN and CNET flagged the short battery life as a weakness. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Misleading AI-Generated Report 'Almost Started a War' With China
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.11
If you've used AI before, you know that it's not immune from mistakes, and hallucinations can easily crop up if you don't check the results. But though a large language model telling you to put glue on pizza might mean nothing more than a few laughs—not all uses of AI are so low stakes. The US military recently planned to take military action against a Chinese ship which it falsely believed to be transporting materials for a nuclear program to Iran, as a result of false information produced by an AI model, CNN reports. The report "almost started a war" according to one source. The US military had planned to intercept the vessel, according to four sources who spoke to the news outlet, but had realized the error shortly before the planned operation. Two other sources claimed that military officers were preparing to board the ship, while another said that the military were "in the air." The misleading report in question had reportedly been put together by a special operations command analyst using AI. The news comes as the Trump administration is making moves to incorporate AI into more parts of the military. In January, The Department of War released the Artificial Intelligence Acceleration Strategy, which outlined plans for the military to "become an 'AI-first' warfighting force across all domains," by unleashing experimentation, and eliminating "bureaucratic barriers." Many analysts within the military are concerned about pitfalls of expanding AI use for use cases like targeting, with one source telling CNN "there is no real guidance for how having a human in the loop will prevent civilian casualties or fratricide." Another source told CNN that: "AI allows you to get to a bad idea faster." The Department of War has yet to comment on the reports. The wisdom of fully incorporating AI into warfare has already been questioned by some research. In February 2024, a study from Georgia Institute of Technology, Stanford University, Northeastern University, and the Hoover Wargaming and Crisis Simulation Initiative played simulated wargames with five of the most common large language models. The researchers found that overall the LLMs acted more aggressively than humans, and in what they saw they developed greater "arms-race dynamics, leading to greater conflict, and in rare cases, even to the deployment of nuclear weapons." About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: AOC 16T20 Review: A Workable Portable Monitor for the Very Tightest Budgets
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.00
The AOC 16T20 ($69.99) is the least expensive portable monitor we've encountered in recent years. This compact, lightweight display is worth considering if you're cash-strapped and looking for a roomy auxiliary monitor for your home or for use on the road. (It's a 15.6-inch panel.) However, the trade-offs for its bargain-basement pricing include limitations in both features and performance. Its stand and navigation are primitive by portable monitor standards, and its peak brightness is low. For a bit more money (though still less than $100), you can get the Editors' Choice-award-winning MSI Pro MP165 E6, which includes a more tilt-adjustable stand and much higher brightness. Compact and lightweight, the 16T20 measures 8.8 by 14 by 0.4 inches (HWD) and weighs just 1.5 pounds, making it easy to travel with and fit in tight spaces. The 16T20's chassis has a matte-black front with fairly thin top and side bezels. These frame a 15.6-inch (diagonal) in-plane switching (IPS) screen with a resolution of 1,920 by 1,080 pixels (aka Full HD, FHD, or 1080p) and a 16:9 widescreen aspect ratio. AOC rates the vertical and horizontal viewing angles at up to 170 degrees, meaning you can view the screen from the side or above without significant degradation in brightness or color. Its refresh rate is 60Hz, typical of budget portables. The 16T20 comes with a wraparound, rigid, black protective cover, which doubles as a folding stand. The cover can be unfolded so that a strip magnetically attaches to the top of the panel's lid, while the monitor's lower edge can fit into either of two grooves in the cover's base, letting the screen rest at your choice of two tilt angles. Such "origami-style" folding stands, once common on lower-priced monitors, have largely been replaced by more rigid stands, such as the MSI Pro MP165 E6's built-in kickstand, that permit a much wider range of tilt angles. On the back of the monitor, below a large, silver AOC logo, are two holes for a 75mm VESA mount (bracket not included). At the bottom of the panel's left-hand edge are four buttons for controlling the monitor's on-screen display (OSD), along with a 3.5mm audio jack. I prefer a mini-joystick controller, such as the one found on the ViewSonic VG1655, but at the 16T20's price, I don't expect to find one. The 16T20 does have a pair of 1-watt speakers built in, but their output is unimpressive, hampered by rather tinny sound. On the right edge of the monitor are two USB-C ports, one for data and one for power, and one mini HDMI port. You may be able to use a single USB-C cable for both power and data; that worked fine in my testing with several laptops. The AOC includes one USB-C cable, but the 16T20 lacks a mini-HDMI-to-HDMI cable. Although I wouldn't call mini HDMI rare, it is atypical (except among portable monitors), so you may not have such a cable kicking around. Online retailers offer a number of them, starting at under $10, but one should have been included in the box. We tested brightness, contrast, and color coverage using a Klein K10-A colorimeter and Portrait Displays' CalMAN Ultimate 2026 software. AOC rates the 16T20's luminance at 250 nits (candelas per square meter); in our testing, it came up somewhat short, at 212 nits. The 16T20's advertised contrast ratio is 800:1; we measured it at a healthy 955:1. Most competitors have rated contrast ratios between 600:1 and 1,000:1. Lower-end IPS portable monitors generally have limited color coverage, and the 16T20 is no exception. We measured the 16T20's coverage of the sRGB color space, which is the universal color standard for websites and web-based art, at 50.7%. The panel's sRGB profile, as shown in the chromaticity (color quality and coverage) chart below, showed a pattern similar to many other sub-$200 portable monitors we have reviewed. The squares represent target color reference points, and the circles represent the actual measured color. In my ad hoc experiential testing of the 16T20, which includes viewing images from our photo test suite as well as selected video clips, I concluded that its image quality is typical of budget portable monitors. It will be usable for viewing web pages and office documents, as well as for casual viewing of photos and short videos. I noticed slight muting of the red tones, relative to other colors, in some of our images. (That's not uncommon with this sort of panel.) In general, the colors didn't really pop, partly due to the panel's relatively low brightness. So, although the 16T20 is not great for entertainment or photo work, it should be fine for general-purpose personal and business use. Final Thoughts AOC 16T20 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Listed at $69.99 and usually retailing for even less—at this writing, major online retailers are selling it for $49.99—the AOC 16T20 is one of the lowest-priced portable monitors we have encountered. It's a tempting choice for cash-strapped students and occasional business travel, but as you would expect from a display at its price, it comes with some trade-offs. Its feature set is basic; it uses a button-driven OSD; and its origami-style folding stand limits you to two tilt angles. Its screen is, in most ways, typical of budget monitors, with limited sRGB color coverage and modest brightness. And although it has both USB-C and mini HDMI ports, it doesn't include a mini HDMI-to-HDMI cable, which you probably don't have and will need to buy if you want to use that connection. Among under-$100 portable monitors, the 16T20 sells for about $10 less than the AOC 16T30. They are largely the same, except that the 16T30 replaces the 16T20's origami-style stand with a built-in kickstand, giving users much more flexibility in tilt angles, and it has slightly higher rated brightness and contrast. Listing at $95 but often retailing for less ($74, as of this writing), the Editors' Choice-winning MSI Pro MP165 E6 has a tilt-adjustable kickstand and a full-size HDMI port (with an included cable to match), but what really puts it over the top is its screen's brightness, well in excess of its rated luminance and more than twice as bright as the 16T20's panel. The MP165 E6 is our preferred sub-$100 monitor, but the AOC 16T20 will do in a pinch, especially if you're on a very tight budget. About Our Expert Since 2004, I have worked on PCMag’s hardware team, covering at various times printers, scanners, projectors, storage, and monitors. I currently focus my efforts on 3D printers, pro and productivity displays, and drives and SSDs of all sorts. Over the years, I have reviewed smart telescopes, iPad and iPhone science apps, plus the occasional camera, laptop, keyboard, and mouse. I've also written a host of articles about astronomy, space science, travel photography, and astrophotography for PCMag and its past and present sibling publications (among them, Mashable and ExtremeTech), as well as for the former PCMag Digital Edition.

item.title: How Did AI Send 1M Scams in 3 Days? 7 Brutal Security Stories Making Headlines This Week
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.90
There are two rules when it comes to cybersecurity news. First, there’s always something to talk about. Second, those things are often so irritating that you just want to go back to bed. Take this week, for example, when we reported on three different campaigns that compromised legitimate, trusted names to spread malware. Perhaps the biggest was that an HBO Max Reddit account was hijacked and began directing users to an app that was actually infostealer malware in disguise. Hot on the heels of that attack were the Iranian-affiliated hackers who used known security brands like Norton and KeePass to trick users into installing spyware. In this case, you may not need to worry about it as much, since the campaign is designed to target political dissidents, journalists, and activists opposed to the Iranian government. Even so, targeted malware attacks usually don’t stay targeted for long. For example, cybersecurity company Kaspersky published a warning this week that iTorrents.org, a public torrent repository, had been hijacked and was instead spreading malware, including a malware-laden version of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey that we mentioned a few weeks ago. As of right now, the site remains compromised. It’s not all bad news, though. I love sharing security-related wins when we find them, and this week we reported on law enforcement taking down one of the web’s most long-running DDoS sites. The site, NightmareStresser, posed as a legitimate tool that allowed users to stress test websites for reliability, but of course, for a modest fee, you could stress test hard enough to disrupt a site that didn’t belong to you, and that was the primary business model. Similarly, this week Bastille Networks, a security startup specializing in wireless intrusion detection, announced it had developed tools to detect nearby smart glasses, specifically for businesses and government agencies that want to keep them out of sensitive areas. Considering the reputation that pervert glasses have, we can only hope the tech becomes available to consumers soon, too. Now then, let’s take a look at what else is going on in the infosec world this week. Threat Actor Uses AI to Generate 1M Personalized Fraud Emails in 3 Days When we talk about how AI is a hacker’s favorite tool and how it supercharges malware campaigns, this is what we mean. Dark Reading reports that researchers at Microsoft tracked a phishing campaign in which an unknown threat actor sent over 1 million highly personalized phishing emails in less than three days, targeting payroll and accounts payable departments at companies worldwide with fake ServiceNow invoices and demanding payment for overdue bills. Even worse, because the threat actor used AI to draft the emails, they were often personalized with the actual names and roles of the target employees at the impacted companies, along with information about each company’s management. The emails even looked like they were part of a threaded conversation with other company representatives, making the email look like it was originally addressed to a company leader, who then directed the scammer to contact accounting to have the bill paid. Attacks like this play on the human element of security, creating a false sense of urgency and authority to encourage overworked, stressed-out employees to just do what the email asks rather than stop to verify its claims. It’s certainly creative, if not scary, and AI is making it easy for scammers to scale up such spear-phishing campaigns. Copyright Scammers Get Instagram Accounts Suspended and Demand Payment This isn’t so much a strict security story as it is a warning for anyone with an Instagram account they’d actually like to hold on to, and another example of social media platforms’ lax policy enforcement and overreliance on automated tools for reporting and moderation. Both the BBC and the Malwarebytes blog shared an alarming story about copyright scammers on Instagram weaponizing the platform’s automated reporting tools and “suspend first, verify later” approach to moderation by filing repeated false copyright strikes against accounts, getting them suspended, and then demanding payment via cryptocurrency to have the complaints withdrawn so the owner can get their accounts back. As with any ransom-style attack, there’s no guarantee that paying the ransom will actually get the attacker to withdraw the complaint, and even if they do, there’s no guarantee that Meta, the parent company of Instagram (and Facebook and WhatsApp), will restore the account. Malwarebytes reported that similar attacks have been occurring since 2023, and the platform hasn’t found a way to handle them. Meta says it restored the accounts the BBC reported, but let’s be honest: It shouldn’t take a media campaign to get a platform to listen to its users and to fight people who use its own tools to scam others. EFF: Privacy Considerations With AI Tools We’ve discussed before that AI and privacy don’t really go hand in hand, and we've even tested the most popular chatbots ourselves to see which ones store the most personal data. Since they’re so widely used, we also have tips to limit what ChatGPT and what Google Gemini know about you. But the folks over at the Electronic Frontier Foundation published a broad guide to AI privacy last month that dives much deeper, going into the differences between cloud-based AI and on-device AI, and reminding people that “do not train using my data” is not the same thing as “do not access my data and use it for other things,” which is easy to overlook. Opting out of one method of data handling doesn’t mean you’re successfully keeping your data private, unfortunately. The EFF guide also has specific links to disable AI training for individual tools, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and others. Additionally, it reminds people to consider how these services would handle law enforcement requests and if that should matter in your use case. Whether you’re an AI skeptic or a regular user, it’s worth bookmarking, if only as a reminder of how these platforms handle your data, from your prompts and queries to everything else they’re capable of collecting about you just based on your usage habits. Ask Our Expert: If Your Phone Is Stolen, Are Your Passkeys at Risk? Do you have a question about online privacy or security? I'm here to help! You can submit your question here, and I may answer it in an upcoming SecurityWatch column and newsletter. If you're not subscribed to the newsletter, head here to sign up, and check back each week for the latest updates from PCMag's security team. Now, on to this week's question! Sam F asks: “Can using passkeys on a phone be at risk if your unlocked phone is snatched out of your hand?” Hi Sam! Thanks for your question. If you’ve been nagged by pop-ups every time you log in to Amazon, PayPal, or even your bank lately to create a passkey for the site and stop using passwords (usually the messages say “sign in faster next time!”), you’re not alone. On the one hand, passkeys do make signing in to websites and services faster: They create a unique key pair, with the public key on the website to identify you and the private key on your device to verify that it’s really you logging in to your account. The downside is that while you don’t have to remember a passkey (and you can store them in a password manager), they’re susceptible to other kinds of attacks, like cookie hijacking and session stealing. To get to your question, though, if someone snatches your phone out of your hand and it’s unlocked, yes, whoever has your phone probably has your passkeys as well and can use them, assuming you don’t have your password manager or whatever tool you use to store the passkeys set to ask you to authenticate every time you use one. For example, I use Proton Pass for all of my passwords, and before I can log in to an app or website, I have to authenticate to unlock my vault. Still, just like my vault’s master password and those passkeys, it’s not like the burglar can use them after I’ve changed them or taken steps to disable them. A thief who runs off with my phone may have access to some open sessions before the phone locks itself (or before I lock and wipe it remotely, which you should do as soon as possible if your phone gets stolen). But when someone has physical access to your unlocked device, all bets are off, really. That’s not the fault of passkeys any more than it’s the fault of saved passwords or any other security measure that relies on your device to work. So don’t think of it as a limitation of passkeys—just remember that there’s a reason security experts admit there’s only so much you can do if someone has physical control of your device. About Our Expert I've been writing and editing stories for almost two decades that help people use technology and productivity techniques to work better, live better, and protect their privacy and personal data. As managing editor of PCMag's security team, it's my responsibility to ensure that our product advice is evidence-based, lab-tested, and serves our readers. I've been a technology journalist for close to 20 years, and I got my start freelancing here at PCMag before beginning a career that would lead me to become editor-in-chief of Lifehacker, a senior editor at The New York Times, and director of special projects at WIRED. I'm back at PCMag to lead our security team and renew my commitment to service journalism. I'm the author of Seen, Heard, and Paid: The New Work Rules for the Marginalized, a career and productivity book to help people of marginalized groups succeed in the workplace.

item.title: How to Stop AI Hacking? Some Companies Say the Answer Is More AI
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.58
With all the talk of automated AI hacking and alignment fears reaching a new level, a number of companies have proposed solutions to some of the booming technologies' biggest issues. Unsurprisingly, it's to add more AI to the loop, as TechCrunch reports. A number of startups are using AI defenses to address rogue agents. Apollo Research introduced its Watcher AI, which monitors a coding agent's work to ensure the tasks it's performing aren't malicious, that it avoids leaking any data, and that it doesn't delete anything important without explicit permission. Apollo's Watcher system then layers AI monitors. The first gives everything a quick pass, and if it spots any concerning behavior, it flags it and escalates it to a more capable monitor that can analyze it further. Only after that step does a human enter the loop to officially approve or reject the suggested actions. Meanwhile, rival company Goodfire offers another solution that examines an AI's internal activations rather than its output to detect whether it's engaged in nefarious activity. Following the Hugging Face attack, the CEO of Goodfire took to X to highlight how his company was doubling down on interpreting AI via the reasoning summary. He noted that it was specifically targeting improvements in AI safety in key areas, such as cybersecurity and bioengineering. Reasoning paths and summaries are techniques some AI developers have used in distillation attacks, in which a model maker trains their technology on another model's outputs. However, to counter such attacks, some AI developers are now making the reasoning summary less legible, making it harder to extract its true meaning. Not everyone believes AI is the solution to these problems. Other non-AI systems include more robust logs of agentic activities, which can then be interpreted using more traditional, non-AI tools, much as cybersecurity professionals have done for years. While security monitoring with AI might be easier, perhaps looping in some more traditional safety systems might be the smarter plan than relying on unproven automation. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Ultra 3: How Much 'Ultra' Do You Actually Get for $799?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.36
Table of Contents Apple didn't change the design of the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but what’s under the hood is a whole different story. Thanks to a new S11 chip, upgraded heart sensors, and impressive 74-hour battery life, the newest Ultra makes a serious case for your wrist. But with the Ultra 3 holding its ground, is it actually worth making the jump? If you're deciding between buying new or keeping your current watch, here's everything that actually changed. Full Specs | Apple Watch Ultra 4 | Apple Watch Ultra 3 | | |---|---|---| | Phone OS Compatibility | | | | Phone OS Compatibility | iOS | iOS | | Watch OS | | | | Watch OS | watchOS | watchOS | | Processor | | | | Processor | Apple S11 | Apple S10 | | Display Size | | | | Display Size | 1.9 inches | 1.9 inches | | Display Type | | | | Display Type | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | | Fitness Features | | | | Fitness Features | Blood Oxygen Monitor, ECG, Heart Rate Monitor, Accelerometer, GPS, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Light Sensor, Barometer, Pulse Oximeter | Blood Oxygen Monitor, ECG, Heart Rate Monitor, Accelerometer, GPS, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Light Sensor, Barometer | | Battery Life | | | | Battery Life | 74 hours (tested) | 63 hours (tested) | | Separate App Store | | | | Separate App Store | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | Price: Still Starts at $799 No changes here. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in one size (49mm), one casing material (titanium), and one wireless configuration (GPS and cellular) for $799, the same as the Ultra 3. That's for the Ultra 4 with an Alpine Loop, Trail Loop, or Ocean Band. If you want to be fancy, you can get the Ultra 4 with a Titanium Milanese Loop for $899, or spend anywhere from $1,499 to $3,149 for an Apple Watch Hermès Ultra 4, with an Hermès band and exclusive Hermès watch faces. Winner: Tie Design: Identical Look and Feel The Ultra 4 is nearly identical to its predecessor, with the exact same shape and measurements for its titanium body, and the same choice of natural titanium or black finishes. It's 1.5 grams heavier than the Ultra 3, but I implore you to notice the difference of a twentieth of an ounce on your wrist. In other words, they look and feel like the same watch. Winner: Tie Health and Fitness: Smarter Sensors and Readiness Scores Apple introduces its new S11 chip as the brains of the Ultra 4 and the Series 12, adding new AI and health features that the S10-equipped Ultra 3 lacks. For fitness, the Ultra 4 introduces a new holistic readiness score that assesses your overall state on a scale of 0 to 10 and offers a recommendation on how hard you should push yourself. An upcoming redesign of the iPhone Health app will have a Longevity tab for evaluating your Health Age, and tests to measure your balance, flexibility, and strength. The app will also let you incorporate new lab data from Quest Diagnostics for $119. Aside from the readiness score, the new app-based features will likely work on the Ultra 3 as well. In addition, Apple says that the S11 gives the Ultra 4 the most accurate step tracking of any smartwatch, with machine-learning algorithms that enable more precise distance measurements. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is also better at monitoring your heart rate thanks to upgraded optical and electrical heart sensors. Like the Series 12, the Ultra 4 can measure your heart rate every five seconds and checks heart rate variability (HRV) 24 times more often than the previous generations. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 AI Features: Audio Intelligence and Always-On Processing The S11 adds some new AI tricks to the Ultra 4 beyond holistic health tracking. It enables an upcoming Audio Intelligence feature, which lets the Ultra 4 and Series 12 listen throughout your day to provide AI summaries and guidance. It can recognize sounds and alert you to alarms and doorbells if you're hard of hearing, give you a Live Rewind text summary of the last 15 seconds of your conversation, and provide full recaps of those conversations after the fact. Apple claims that Audio Intelligence has several privacy measures to protect your data, including a dedicated hardware compartment on the S11 that processes audio internally. Apple also says it doesn't identify or attribute speakers in conversations and cuts out sensitive personal information. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Durability: Equally Equipped for Adventure No surprises here. The Ultra 3 is already a practically bulletproof smartwatch with a titanium body and a sapphire crystal display, tested to MIL-STD-810H standards. It comes with an IP6X dustproof rating, EN13319 diving certification, and depth capability up to 131 feet, and general water resistance up to 328 feet. The Ultra 4 offers all of those assurances, too. Winner: Tie Connectivity: Equal Signal Strength Everywhere This is another area where the Ultra 4 and Ultra 3 are equally well-equipped. Whichever generation you pick, you get dual-band Wi-Fi 4, Bluetooth 5.3, 5G, and LTE cellular connectivity, satellite connectivity, and precision L1/L5 dual-frequency GPS. Both watches also have Apple's ultra-wideband chip for precisely locating your phone nearby. Winner: Tie Battery Life: A Weekend-Ready Endurance Bump Apple is usually conservative in its battery life estimates; it claims the Ultra 3 can last up to 42 hours, but in our tests, it lasted 63 hours with the always-on display enabled. The Ultra 4 has an estimated battery life of up to 50 hours, and it similarly exceeded Apple's estimate, running for 74 hours before needing a charge. It hit that number without any kind of help from a power-saving mode, so you can safely take the Ultra 4 on a weekend trip and leave your charger behind. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 And The Winner Is... Apple Watch Ultra 4 The Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers substantial under-the-hood upgrades without raising the price, making it a strong value for serious athletes and outdoor adventurers. If you already own an Ultra 3, you can safely hold off unless you crave every extra hour of battery life or cutting-edge health tracking. Otherwise, the Ultra 4 is the clear, undisputed champion.

item.title: September's Best Laptops Deals From Apple, Dell, Lenovo, and More Will Save You Hundreds
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.26
If you've spent any time laptop shopping recently, you must have realized that prices are out of control. Skyrocketing demand for RAM has made prebuilt PCs more and more expensive, but we're here to help. The PCMag Deals team spends every day finding you the best offers on all kinds of tech, comparing specifications, real-world use cases, and historical prices to ensure that the laptop we recommend is worth every penny you pay for it. Below you'll see ten portable PCs that have been extensively tested and vetted by our experts using rigorous benchmarks, with detailed reviews that explain why each one is worth your time and money. I update this rundown regularly, so check back if you don't see the perfect machine for you right now. We've found the best laptops from all the major brands. These machines have clear screens, long battery life, and high-speed connectivity. Check out the latest discounts on laptops. If you're not as concerned about portability, check our list of the best desktop deals we've found for the month. Best Budget Laptop Deals These budget laptops cost less than $1,000 and can easily handle daily tasks. We focused on capable PCs that will last a while, avoiding underpowered e-waste. Our top budget laptop picks are a low-cost Dell with a good-sized screen and an affordable Lenovo that we've reviewed positively. If money's tight and you need an ultra-budget option, we'd recommend this Lenovo portable, which is currently on sale for $137 off at Best Buy, the lowest price we've seen all year. This is a great choice for students, as it has a fairly large 15-inch FHD display and a full-size keyboard for comfortable typing. Under the hood, you get a capable and price-conscious Intel Core i3 processor, coupled with 8GB of RAM. In our review, we were impressed by the light weight and good value for the money, although the 128GB of internal UFS storage is pretty skimpy. Use that money you'll save for an external flash drive. Best Buy has a super-deep discount on this Dell portable that makes it absolutely dominate the budget category. You'll have a hard time finding a laptop with a full 2K resolution touchscreen at this price, and it maintains a sleek, lightweight design despite the solid component loadout. While it's not suited for resource-intensive gaming or creative work, it'll more than handle daily productivity tasks, Web surfing, and video streaming without breaking a sweat. Also of note is its solid battery life, with Express Charge support letting you top it off quickly when it starts to run down. We wouldn't expect this machine to last long at this price, so if it fits your needs, snatch it up. Acer also makes reliable budget machines, and the Aspire Go 15 is a really solid unit at a nice price. You can read our extensive review to hear how it performs, but in short: even with less than cutting-edge components, it still knocked it out of the park in our productivity benchmarking, and the all-plastic build feels relatively sturdy. The FHD screen is decently sized, with Acer's BlueLight Shield eye protection for long periods of use. Port selection is also decent for a low-cost machine, with USB Type-C for both charging and data transfer. A dedicated Copilot key launches Windows 11's AI features with a single press. The $150 discount puts it into contention for sure. MacOS users are very loyal, but can end up spending more than comparable Windows models. We've got the lowest price on the latest MacBook Air, as well as an older-generation Pro that's affordable. It's not the deepest discount in the list, but being able to chop a hundred and fifty bucks off of the exceptional 2026 MacBook Air is well worth your attention. Apple's ultralight portable has long been one of our favorite laptops in the world, and the most recent iteration is no exception. In our review, it earned an Editors' Choice nod for boosted performance and exceptional style. The M5 processor is the star here, working closely with MacOS for terrific speed and stability in productivity tasks, creative work, and more. It remains the measuring stick by which we evaluate all other ultraportable laptops. This is a higher-end loadout with tons of storage and RAM. It's not the latest model, but the 2022 MacBook Pro is still an incredibly potent machine, well-suited for professionals on the go. You can read our review for all the details, but it earned an "Excellent" rating for its performance that easily outclassed Windows machines in the same price range, typically excellent build quality, and epic 22-hour battery life. This model has a larger 16-inch 3456 x 2234 Retina screen, but otherwise hits all the same ultraportable high notes. Just keep in mind that some of the more NPU-intensive Apple Intelligence functions might not run quite as swiftly here, but for $2099, it's a steal. Best Gaming Laptop Deals If you want to play your favorite PC games on the go, you need to invest in a machine with a dedicated GPU and pumped-up cooling. Gaming laptops usually cost over $1,000, but ultrabudget models are out there. A good gaming deal includes capable components and a screen with the resolution and refresh rate to do them justice. We've got a few gaming machines this month, including a low-priced HP portable and a big-screen Asus ROG model with some amazing silicon. Budget gamers need durable laptops that have just enough power to run today's top games. At retail price, we wouldn't choose this HP portable over comparable models, but a price drop of over $300 makes it an incredibly competitive machine for budget shoppers. We gave the Victus a "Good" rating in our review, noting that even though it didn't shine component-wise, the surprisingly good display and keyboard made up for it, making it a fine entry into the world of PC gaming. The RTX 3050 GPU isn't going to give you dazzling next-generation effects, but it'll handle most games in FHD at stable framerates. Battery life is also lengthy, and the fans are quiet and efficient. Our next step up is an Alienware machine that's seeing a ludicrous $750 price drop courtesy of Best Buy. While we haven't taken this one into the lab, we do have a review of the similar Alienware 16X, earning an "Excellent" rating for some of the same features this has, like a sharp screen with a fast refresh rate, along with a solid slate of components. While the RTX 5050 is the baby of Nvidia's current-gen Blackwell series of GPUs, it's still got the stuff and can pump out high framerates on all of the latest games. A full terabyte of internal storage is also very welcome at this price. Heat management is solid, with Alienware's Cryo-tech using a new thermal interface material to drop temperatures without overloading fans. You can put this up against just about any laptop in its price bracket and it will look great. Finally, here's a serious monster of a portable, an 18-inch monolith stuffed to the gills with high-end components for an extremely fair price. We have a solid review of the ROG Strix G18 that you can dive into for all the details, but the short version is this: it delivers on its promises of modern-era gaming with all the bells and whistles thanks to a potent RXT 5080 graphics card and a Core Ultra 9 processor to match. The sheer size of the beast means both the keyboard and touchpad are spacious, and it's also got room for plenty of ports. Battery life is also respectable, clocking over six hours of use on a single charge. We did wish that the IPS screen came with a higher resolution, but 2560 x 1600 is perfectly acceptable, especially with a $600 discount.
