item.title: I Outsmarted the 'World's Best' AI Detector in 30 Seconds
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.17
With tools that can pick out AI-generated images, music, text, and videos becoming increasingly vital for judging the authenticity of online content, Pangram has made headlines as the “gold standard” of AI detection (not to mention its own press release touting it as the "world's best"). But does its advertised claim of 99% accuracy hold up? Not exactly. Yes, Pangram consistently picks out AI content, but it also regularly gets things wrong. Below are my takeaways after extensive testing and research into the service. Using AI to Fight AI Pangram bills itself as “an AI detector that actually works” and, as mentioned, claims accuracy rates above 99% for text generated by just about every mainstream AI model, from ChatGPT to Qwen, and everything in between. It also has an AI image detection feature. Interestingly, Pangram itself uses proprietary AI models to power its detection tools. The company says its AI detection capabilities are a cut above the competition because third parties have independently verified its accuracy and reliability. It also cites its ability to detect content from all major AI models, its training on diverse datasets, years of company research, vast language support, and more. Pangram even claims that its tech is better at detecting AI content than humans, including text from tools that aim to humanize AI content to evade detection. These are bold claims, and some of Pangram’s underlying technology is indeed innovative. Take, for example, the focus on mirrored prompts. In these training scenarios, Pangram prompts a human to write something, then gives the same prompt to an AI model so it can train its models to understand the nuanced differences. This and other aspects of Pangram's development sound great on paper, but real-world performance and further exploration of the numbers reveal some flaws. Breaking the Detector: How I Tricked Pangram in Three Sentences If you think Pangram’s stated accuracy rates mean you’ll almost never see it get something wrong, that’s simply not the case. I’m not saying Pangram never works. It works most of the time, in fact, and it’s the most accurate AI detection tool I've tried. Unfortunately, that still just means it's the best among some clearly imperfect options. Keep in mind that Pangram requires submissions to be at least 50 words long to ensure accurate detection. To test the tool, I submitted a draft of the first section of this article after adding a sentence I generated using Gemini. Pangram failed to detect any AI content. Then, I added another sentence using Gemini, and Pangram still failed to detect it. Only after I added three sentences (going from an original 250 words to 311) did Pangram find anything amiss. However, it labeled only two sentences as AI-generated, one of which I wrote. When I rephrased the one AI-generated sentence it flagged, Pangram couldn’t detect anything. Pangram also says it can catch humanized text, but it’s easy to use humanization tools to fool it. For example, I generated a poem with GPT-5.6. Then, I searched for an “AI humanizer,” picked the first result that didn’t require an account, and had it ‘humanize’ ChatGPT’s poem. When I submitted that to Pangram, it called the poem 100% human-generated. Picture Imperfect: Simple Edits Fool Pangram's Image Detector Pangram primarily focuses on AI-generated text detection, but it can also detect AI images. The tool detected most AI-generated images in testing, but it still regularly makes mistakes. For example, relatively believable fake images can trip Pangram up. CNET published a fun article in 2023 that aimed to test your ability to spot AI images. One image (shown below) is of avocado toast with a strange-looking lime. Pangram called this image 100% human-generated, but it’s actually AI-generated. You can also fool Pangram by cleaning AI images with detection-evading tools. For example, I used Gemini’s Nano Banana model to crop an image. Though the image itself changed very little, editing images with Nano Banana attaches identifiable C2PA and SynthID markers. Pangram cited C2PA credentials when it called my image AI-generated. However, after I ran my edit through a free tool that makes it harder to detect and resubmitted it, Pangram considered it human-generated. What Pangram's '99% Accurate' Fine Print Isn't Telling You So, if Pangram still makes mistakes despite claiming such high detection accuracy, what gives? Fortunately, Pangram provides a ton of documentation about its testing. I appreciate this level of transparency, even though I still managed to pick out some deceptive quirks. For example, Pangram advertises 99.8% accuracy in detecting text generated by Anthropic’s Opus 5 model and cites a test it ran. But this claim doesn't encompass Opus 5 text edited by a human or humanized by a tool, among other things. Instead, it focuses solely on what Opus 5 spits out in response to prompts. Pangram tests some of the other things I mentioned separately, but they’re buried in its documentation. According to said documentation, Pangram can “detect humanized text as AI-generated 97.67% of the time and as either Mixed or AI-generated 98.83% of the time.” That's different from the 99.8% accuracy figure, but it's still close. However, other numbers indicate worse performance. For example, Pangram also measures its ability to detect AI-assisted text, which it correctly identifies only 55.01% of the time. That's a problem when the company primarily advertises the narrow scenario in which the 99.8% accuracy applies. Other published accuracy rates have different problems. For example, if you click on Pangram’s advertised 99.5% accuracy rate for Gemini 3 on its home page, it opens a page about the rather old Gemini 3 Pro model. This page also doesn't explain the 99.5% figure, unlike the linked pages for GPT-5.6 and Opus 5, which clearly do. If you check the aforementioned Pangram 4 documentation, it turns out the company also tested Gemini 3.1 Pro in preview and 3.5 Flash, where you can see a 99.5% false-negative rate. Nonetheless, that still doesn’t explain the listed accuracy rate for Gemini 3, which the company says it tested in November 2025 before the release of 3.1 Pro and 3.5 Flash. Also, these models still don’t represent “Gemini 3," which spans across not just more models but newer ones, such as 3.6 Flash, 3.7 Flash, and 3.8 Flash. Meanwhile, for GPT-5.6, Pangram went so far as to test each of its variants (Luna, Sol, and Terra), so the approach with Gemini feels especially lackluster. Although Pangram’s numbers aren't perfect, I have no reason to believe the company fabricated them. That’s great to see, but it only highlights the problem I’ve written about before with AI benchmarks: They just don’t translate well to real-world performance. In Pangram’s case, testing often shows truly exceptional (and improving) detection rates, but in practice, you can break the tool fairly easily. Cherry-Picked Results: The Reality Behind Independent Verification Beyond its in-house numbers, Pangram says it’s “proven the most reliable and accurate AI detector on the market by third-party researchers, including the University of Maryland and the University of Chicago.” This isn’t a lie, but that sentence makes the conclusions of the underlying research seem stronger than they are. For example, in the University of Maryland study, Pangram mentions comparing detection tools, including Pangram, against humans in spotting humanized AI-generated text. Pangram did the best among the tools and outperformed the humans individually in the test. However, humans still outperformed Pangram when voting as a group. This partially undermines Pangram’s claim that “independent studies have shown that Pangram's AI detection outperforms trained human readers in identifying AI-generated content.” In the University of Chicago study, Pangram mentions testing only three other AI detection tools alongside Pangram, which feels like an especially small selection given how many similar tools are available. Researchers at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel also tested only three other tools alongside Pangram, this time on lengthy academic papers. It’s not that this research doesn’t look good for Pangram, but it’s not necessarily conclusive proof of anything. Outside of research institutions, Pangram also cites other evaluations, too, such as David Gewirtz’s article on ZDNET about AI detection tools. Pangram quotes him as saying, “a newcomer to our tests that immediately soared into the winners' circle.” While Pangram performed well on his tests, Pangram doesn’t mention that Gewirtz’s article also said that “services marketed as AI content detectors are a mixed bag” and went on to conclude “[he] would advocate caution before relying on the results of any—or all—of these tools.” To be clear, these testimonies demonstrate good results for Pangram. I just don't appreciate how Pangram uses them to present an unrealistic expectation of its real-world performance. It still gets things wrong regularly, and false results can create real consequences for people. False Positives Can Ruin Lives: The Danger of Flawed Tools It’s increasingly difficult to distinguish what's real online, and AI is actively making the situation worse. Tools that claim to detect AI-generated content but can't do so perfectly just add to the confusion. For example, Substack recently announced the ability to scan posts using Pangram’s tech to determine how likely they are to be AI-generated. But what happens if you make your living by writing on Substack and Pangram incorrectly labels your work as partially or wholly AI-generated? Alternatively, what if Pangram provides cover for writers who mix their own content with AI-generated content by labeling it 100% human-generated? Substack allows you to report and remove scans on your work you believe are incorrect, but that’s not an ideal solution. And this goes well beyond Substack. Imagine a tenured English professor who doesn’t understand modern technology well, sending student essays to Pangram because their college partnered with Pangram. What happens when Pangram occasionally flags a completely authentic paper as AI-generated? Most people don’t know how to assess the reliability of AI detection tools, so it’s possible that such a scenario could result in an unfair failing grade and no recourse for the student. These dangers are why I’m so critical of AI detection tools like Pangram. I’d much prefer if Pangram were more up-front about what it can and can’t do well. There's No Gold Standard: Every AI Detector Should Be Doubted AI detection tools still aren't reliable in real-world scenarios, despite what their marketing and research say. Sure, if Pangram or a tool like it flags something as AI-generated, it can be evidence of something that might not be authentic, but these flags aren't infallible. And that’s essential to keep in mind, because putting too much trust in detection tools can lead to disastrous consequences. The best way to protect yourself is to learn exactly how companies derive their accuracy claims and maintain a healthy dose of skepticism about their results. About Our Expert I’ve been writing about consumer technology and video games for over a decade at a variety of publications, including Destructoid, GamesRadar+, Lifewire, PCGamesN, Trusted Reviews, and What Hi-Fi?, among many others. At PCMag, I review AI and productivity software—everything from chatbots to to-do list apps. In my free time, I’m likely cooking something, playing a game, or tinkering with my computer.

item.title: MSI Pro MP165 E6 Review: The Sub-$100 Portable Monitor to Beat
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.13
The MSI Pro MP165 E6 ($94.99), a 15.6-inch portable monitor, sells at a budget price and offers both USB Type-C and HDMI connectivity—indeed, it is one of the few portable monitors we have seen that integrates a full-size HDMI port. The MP165 E6 is small and lightweight, and comes with a carry bag made of stiff fabric. It has a built-in, tilt-adjustable kickstand that integrates a tripod socket, and its IPS screen offers good contrast and brightness. My extensive testing suggests that it is best for workaday tasks, rather than photo editing or movie watching. Still, it offers a lot for its price, and earns our Editors' Choice award as the best portable monitor for people on the tightest of budgets. The MP165 E6 has typical specs for a sub-$100 portable monitor, sporting a 15.6-inch full HD (1,920-by-1,080-pixel) in-plane switching (IPS) screen, which is aided by a matte, antiglare coating. The screen has a 16:9 aspect ratio, making it best for use with widescreen laptops. The panel is housed in a matte-black frame. On the monitor's left-hand edge are the ports: two USB-C and one HDMI. This is one of the few full-size HDMI ports I have seen on a portable monitor—many instead have mini HDMI ports, which are easier to fit in a thin frame. MSI includes both a USB-C cable and an HDMI cable in the box. You can connect the MP165 E6 to a power adapter via one of the USB-C ports, but in testing, it worked fine when it was bus-powered, drawing power solely from my laptop over the same USB-C connection it uses to transfer data via the DisplayPort Over USB Alternate Mode's protocol. On the right edge of the MP165 E6 are the power button, a three-way rocker switch for the on-screen display (OSD), and a 3.5mm headphone jack. The rocker works in tandem with the power button to let you navigate the OSD, though I found the controls awkward to manipulate. I would have preferred a mini-joystick controller, such as the one found on the Editors' Choice-winning ViewSonic VG1655. The MP165 E6 has dual built-in 1-watt speakers that are reasonably loud but of mediocre sound quality, which is about what we expect at this price. The MP165 E6 has a narrow built-in kickstand, which gives you fine control over the monitor's tilt angle. The stand also has a 0.25-inch threaded hole to fit a tripod. You'll also find holes in the back to support a 75mm VESA mount (bracket not included). We did our color and brightness testing using a Klein K10-A colorimeter and Portrait Displays' CalMAN Ultimate 2026 software. MSI rates the MP165 E6's peak luminance at 250 nits (candelas per square meter); in our testing, it was considerably brighter, tallying 335 nits. This should be fine for use in rooms with substantial ambient light, especially since the screen has an anti-glare matte finish. The MP165 E6's advertised contrast ratio is 1,000:1; we measured it at a slightly better 1,142:1. Sub-$100 portable monitors generally have rated contrast ratios ranging between 600:1 and 1,000:1, so this is good. As is the case with most sub-$200 IPS portable monitors, the MP165 E6 has limited color coverage. We measured its coverage of the sRGB color space, which is the universal color standard for websites and web-based art, at 51.7%. The panel's sRGB profile, as shown in the chromaticity (color quality and coverage) chart below, showed a pattern similar to many other budget portable monitor panels we have reviewed. The squares represent target color reference points, and the circles represent the actual measured color. In my ad hoc experiential testing, in which I view images from our photo test suite and some selected video clips, I concluded that the MP165 E6's color coverage is typical of a low-priced portable display. The overall impression? It's suitable for viewing web pages and office documents, as well as casual viewing of photos and short videos. I noticed that the red tones in some of our test images appeared a bit muted, which we frequently see with budget portable monitors. On the plus side are its high brightness and solid contrast. Final Thoughts MSI Pro MP165 E6 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. As a sub-$100 portable monitor, the MSI Pro MP165 E6 includes a basic feature set plus a couple of surprises: a full-size HDMI port and brightness well in excess of MSI's rating. Plus, its kickstand gives precise control over the panel's tilt angle. It's considerably brighter than the bargain-basement AOC 16T20, has a more functional stand, and includes all necessary cables. It's the best we've reviewed in its price range, and earns our Editors' Choice nod for budget portable monitors. For between $150 and $500, you could get a portable monitor with features such as a hinged stand, high refresh rate, stunning color coverage, a touch screen, a built-in battery, and even an OLED panel. But with the MP165 E6, you can both save cash and get a capable monitor. About Our Expert Since 2004, I have worked on PCMag’s hardware team, covering at various times printers, scanners, projectors, storage, and monitors. I currently focus my efforts on 3D printers, pro and productivity displays, and drives and SSDs of all sorts. Over the years, I have reviewed smart telescopes, iPad and iPhone science apps, plus the occasional camera, laptop, keyboard, and mouse. I've also written a host of articles about astronomy, space science, travel photography, and astrophotography for PCMag and its past and present sibling publications (among them, Mashable and ExtremeTech), as well as for the former PCMag Digital Edition.

item.title: Apple iPhone 13 vs. iPhone 18: How Performance and Features Have Changed in 5 Years
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.10
Table of Contents Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max deliver more power, take better photos, and last longer than ever. They also push your aging iPhone another rung down the ladder. The iPhone 13, released in 2021, remains the most widely used iPhone worldwide in 2026. That got me wondering: What exactly are iPhone 13 owners missing out on? Has Apple introduced enough meaningful upgrades to trigger serious FOMO, or are the changes unimportant to the average person? To figure this out, I did a deep dive into what five years of iPhone upgrades really get you. One caveat: The iPhone 13 is an entry-level model, while Apple only unveiled Pro models this year, so this isn’t exactly your typical apples-to-apples spec comparison. That aside, let's look at how much the iPhone has evolved over the past five years—and what you're sacrificing by holding on to your iPhone 13. Full Specs | Apple iPhone 18 Pro | Apple iPhone 13 | | |---|---|---| | Operating System | | | | Operating System | iOS 27 | iOS 15 | | CPU | | | | CPU | Apple A20 Pro | Apple A15 | | Dimensions | | | | Dimensions | 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches | 5.78 by 2.82 by .3 inches | | Screen Size | | | | Screen Size | 6.3 inches | 6.1 inches | | Screen Resolution | | | | Screen Resolution | 2622 by 1206 pixels | 2,532 by 1,170 pixels | | Camera Resolution (Rear; Front-Facing) | | | | Camera Resolution (Rear; Front-Facing) | 48MP, 48MP, 48MP, 25MP | 12MP, 12MP; 12MP | | Battery Life (As Tested) | | | | Battery Life (As Tested) | TBD | 15 hours | Design: 5 Years Later, It Still Holds Up Slap a case on it, and the iPhone 13 still looks and feels like it could be from 2026. Similar to the new iPhone 18 series, it’s got that iconic, squared-off silhouette, MagSafe support, and IP68 water-resistance rating. The iPhone 13 has an aluminum frame with a glass back, while the iPhone 18 Pro models feature an aluminum unibody design. The iPhone 13 has a 6.1-inch screen compared with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max’s larger 6.3- and 6.9-inch displays, respectively. All three phones use Apple's Ceramic Shield, though the latest iPhones step it up to Ceramic Shield 2. But the biggest changes start to show up once you turn the screen on. As a phone tester for six years, I vividly remember Apple boasting about the iPhone 13's "20% notch reduction" and feeling duped when I saw it for myself. It was narrower side to side but taller, meaning it dipped farther into the display. I wasn't a fan, so I'm relieved that we've moved on to the Dynamic Island, which debuted on the iPhone 14 Pro models. Designed to capture live, motion-rich information at a glance, the Dynamic Island is now smaller than ever on the iPhone 18 Pros (25% shorter than the 17 Pros). It still keeps you informed about what's going on in the background, whether you're navigating with Apple Maps, tracking your Uber driver's ETA, or keeping an eye on your Spotify playlist—it just stays more out of your way. What's nice is that it now supports up to three live activities, instead of just two. No, Dynamic Island isn't a must-have feature, but it’s a nice-to-have convenience. Is it going to change your life? Probably not. It’s definitely not a reason to ditch your iPhone 13, but having useful, glanceable information floating at the top of your screen is more useful than staring at an intrusive black box. You can also stick this one on the "not upgrade worthy" list, but Apple has been shaving down the bezels over the past five years. For example, when the iPhone 16 Pro models launched, Apple boasted that they featured the thinnest borders of any Apple product, a claim it later made again with the iPhone 17 and iPhone 17 Air. The iPhone 18 series continues to sport an ultra-slim display frame, allowing for more screen real estate. However, if you prefer more bezel space to rest your thumbs, this may not matter much to you. Apple's stubborn insistence on keeping base iPhones at 60Hz while budget Android phones offer zippier refresh rates has always baffled me. After the iPhone 13 series launched, it took Apple four product generations to finally expand ProMotion to its base models. The iPhone 17 lineup was the first to feature a 120Hz variable refresh rate at a lower price. If 60Hz is all you’ve ever known, you probably won’t miss what you’ve never seen. Speaking from experience, higher refresh rates make scrolling smoother, animations more fluid, and the entire phone feel snappier. The screens are also brighter than ever. Cameras: The Biggest Hardware Gap Between Generations Sorry, but your iPhone 13's camera is aging fast. The entire iPhone 13 lineup, including the Pro models, has a lower-res 12MP main camera. That's not even close to the phones of 2026. The iPhone 18 models feature Apple's best camera system to date. Their 48MP main cameras now have a showstopping variable aperture feature, which means the lens can adjust its light-gathering capabilities based on the shooting conditions. For example, in low light, it's supposed to soak up as much light as possible. However, in bright sunlight, photos should show reduced glare and blown-out highlights if the aperture is stopped down. The iPhone 13’s 12MP selfie camera is pretty dated, too. You're missing out on the higher-res 18MP front-facing camera for sharper, more detailed pictures. Moreover, the latest iPhones have a square selfie camera sensor that lets you take portrait or landscape selfies without rotating the phone. The iPhone 13 has a 12MP ultrawide camera, and while it's solid, it cannot tackle macro work. The latest iPhones can focus on ultra-close objects using the 48MP ultrawide lens. Further, the iPhone 13 lacks a dedicated telephoto camera, so you're missing the iPhone 18 Pro's ability to get 8x closer to distant subjects without relying on digital cropping. If you're a content creator, you're limiting yourself. The iPhone 13 lacks features such as Action Mode and 4K Cinematic Mode, and it also lacks support for ProRAW and ProRes, which are needed for advanced video editing. New to the iPhone 18 Pro models, you’re also missing smart-focus tracking, an AI feature that locks onto moving subjects, and Pro Controls, which lets you customize the camera app for quicker access to your most-used settings. Serious video shooters are missing out big time. Ports: Ditching Lightning for Universal USB-C Convenience Perhaps the most convincing case for upgrading comes down to ports. The iPhone 13 is locked to Apple’s proprietary Lightning ecosystem. USB-C is now the global standard, so holding onto a Lightning port is self-sabotage. If you ever need to borrow a charger these days, you'll likely be handed a USB-C cable, not a Lightning cable, leaving you high and dry. Plus, when traveling, you need to bring an extra cable just to accommodate your iPhone 13. Why do this to yourself when you can juice up all your devices with a single cord? You don’t need to purchase a $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro to ditch the Lightning port, but you should at least consider a refurbished or used model from the iPhone 15 series, the first lineup to make the leap to USB-C after Apple was forced to change course. Your iPhone 13 is missing the Action Button, a customizable shortcut key that replaced the age-old mute switch. Making its debut in the iPhone 15 lineup, the Action Button lets you assign quick shortcuts to your favorite features. For example, you can map it to trigger the flashlight, launch the camera app, record a voice memo, run custom Apple Shortcuts, and more. It's incredibly helpful. Your iPhone 13 also lacks the Camera Control feature that was introduced on the iPhone 16. This capacitive button gives you instant access to the camera to snap photos, capture video, or tweak settings such as exposure, depth of field, and zoom. Meanwhile, on your iPhone 13, you have to use the screen to execute these actions. Although I find the Action Button useful for firing up Shazam when I hear an unfamiliar song, I still haven’t gotten used to Camera Control beyond launching the Camera app. For actions like zooming, I find the on-screen controls easier and more intuitive. iPhone 13 owners narrowly escaped Apple’s SIM tray purge. When Apple launched the iPhone 14 lineup, it killed off the physical SIM slot on US iPhones, leaving eSIM as the only option. As a frequent traveler, I miss the old-school approach. I’d buy a SIM abroad, pop it into my phone, and be on my way with a local number and cell service. Setting up an eSIM without solid Wi-Fi is a nightmare. Trust me; I know from experience. The iPhone 13 supports both eSIM and physical SIM. If you're in the US, the latest iPhones remain eSIM-only. Processor and Software Features: A20 Pro Speed Gains and Apple Intelligence Support The iPhone 13 launched during a much simpler time: The AI craze hadn't hit yet. The 13's A15 Bionic chip doesn't have to handle much beyond running apps and some photo and video processing. The iPhone 18 Pro models are running the most advanced version of Apple Intelligence (Apple's AI suite). The A20 Pro chip, engineered on a 2nm process, has more memory bandwidth to support Apple's ballooning AI ambitions, including the new-and-improved Siri. The A20 Pro chip has a dedicated vapor chamber to improve thermal performance under demanding workloads, giving it a leg up for AI. Even though it can run iOS 27, the iPhone 13 does not support Apple Intelligence, which may be a plus for users with AI fatigue. Day-to-day performance has also jumped. When we tested the iPhone 13 five years ago, it blew competitors away with Geekbench scores of 1,721 (single-core) and 4,629 (multi-core). The iPhone 18 Pro models are running 3x faster than that. Battery Life: You Gain 14 Hours and Fast 60W Charging The iPhone 13, packed with a 3,227mAh battery, ran for 19 hours in our battery tests; it barely lasts an entire day. Fast forward to 2026, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max ran for 34 hours and 31 minutes in testing. You're starving yourself of potentially 14 hours of extra battery life by holding on to the iPhone 13. That's a huge deal. Moreover, the iPhone 13 charges at a slow 20W rate. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro Max charges at 60W. It can reach a 50% charge in just 15 minutes, which we confirmed in testing. Whoa! You're missing out, iPhone 13 users. Verdict: Is It Finally Time to Trade in Your iPhone 13? Yes, it’s finally time to retire that iPhone 13. Upgrading to the iPhone 18 Pro gets you off the Lightning leash, gives you hours of extra battery life, and puts a vastly superior camera system in your pocket. Plus, you can get some good carrier incentives on a trade-in. If you don't want to drop $1,200 (or more) on the latest Pro model, you should at least aim for an iPhone 15 Pro or newer. This will unlock Apple Intelligence, USB-C, upgraded cameras, and the freedom to roam without a portable battery.

item.title: Asus ProArt P16 (2026) Review: A Dream Laptop for Creative Pros
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.76
As a category, content creator laptops are a relatively recent niche, but Asus has been refining its ProArt series for years. The latest flagship 16-inch machine, the ProArt P16, is an expensive system for demanding professionals (starts at $3,999.99; $5,499.99 as tested). The design is the same as the previous edition, but Asus has introduced much more powerful Nvidia GeForce RTX 50 series graphics chips this time around. For demanding media and creative workloads, these upgraded graphics options—combined with fast AMD Ryzen AI 9 processing and a boatload of RAM—are ideal. In addition, these components are housed in a premium build and paired with a stunning 4K OLED touch display, making the new Asus ProArt P16 an Editors' Choice winner among high-end content creator laptops, replacing the older model. The ProArt P16 is available in two configurations, but whichever you choose, it is an expensive system. The same AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 processor and 64GB memory capacity are used across both models, but the other specs are tied to the different SKUs—they're not interchangeable. The $3,999.99 base system comes with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 GPU, a 2TB SSD, and a 16-inch 60Hz OLED touch screen with a 3,840-by-2,400-pixel resolution (4K, but in the 16:10 aspect ratio). The previous P16 ran on Nvidia's GeForce RTX 40 series GPUs, so this is a generational upgrade in graphics performance. Our review model is the pricier configuration, listed at $5,499.99, which includes an upgrade to an RTX 5090 GPU, a 120Hz version of the same display, and 4TB of SSD storage (implemented as two 2TB drives). The RTX 5090 should deliver significantly more power than the RTX 5070, though only the most demanding users, such as video editors, animators, engineers, architects, or designers, should seek that level of performance. Considering the cost, make sure you need the added muscle and storage. Given that, this system is excellent for strenuous creative workloads, and about as good as it gets among consumer laptops. The Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 CPU is a 12-core and 24-thread beast for crunching through demanding workloads and multitasking. The GPU is the top-end chip in the RTX stack, rivaled only by roughly equivalent Nvidia professional chips outside of the RTX lineup, which are more suited to workstations. The full testing details are in the performance section below. The ProArt P16 may aim at a niche audience, but its design is a chef's kiss for creative power users. The design is identical to last year's model; it’s all about the spec bump. The all-metal build looks sharp, with its heft (4.1 pounds) adding to the premium feel. Despite the power on hand, the ProArt 16's a surprisingly thin system, measuring 0.68 by 14 by 9.7 inches (HWD). You may not want to carry this machine with you multiple times a day unless necessary, but it's hardly immobile. On that note, the brilliant, roomy Lumina Pro OLED delivers a monitor-like experience. The brightness and vibrancy drew me in at first glance, and it quickly became clear that this is a screen fit for creative professionals. Our model has a 16-inch screen with a native resolution of 3,840 by 2,400 pixels (4K in its 16:10 aspect ratio), a 120Hz refresh rate (with variable refresh rate support), and touch technology. Our full testing data is further below, but we measured 448 nits at maximum brightness, and the laptop's rated up to 1,600 nits for HDR content. If you want a true monitor experience, note that laptops generally max out around 18 inches; for 20 inches and up, you’ll need an external display, so be sure this size won’t be a detriment to your workflow. Be warned that this glossy display is more prone to glare than matte displays, so you may stare back at your own face in bright environments. In addition to the screen, the ProArt P16's inputs and connectivity options are also suitable for creatives. The keyboard is comfortable, with noticeable travel and satisfying feedback for a non-mechanical keyboard—enjoyable enough for any user. A few keys, like Backspace, are slightly truncated, which doesn't feel necessary on a big 16-inch laptop. However, the truncated keys allow for sizable speaker grilles on either side of the keyboard, which are joined by four more speakers within the system. The forward-most, up-firing speakers are particularly noticeable, and the laptop pumps out strong sound quality that holds up at higher volumes. It’s the touchpad that has the true creator-centric feature: the DialPad, a circular touchpad that lets you easily select and switch among in-application editing tools. We’ve seen the DialPad on previous ProArt systems, first in a physical dial form and more recently in this circular touchpad iteration. It's located in the top-left corner of the touchpad, within easy reach for quickly switching among tools, colors, brush sizes, and more in your favorite creative applications. I'm no digital artist, so I can’t test how it fits into a creative's workflow. Still, I found it simple to use in my test sessions. The average user likely has no need for the DialPad, but for creative pros, it puts frequently accessed tools and options right at your fingertips, with some customization options available. If you're constantly swapping brushes or other tools, you can put them front and center by pressing the wheel and scrolling the circle to pan through your options. I miss the feel of the physical dial on older models, but this works fine, too. As for connectivity, the ProArt P16 includes one USB Type-C connection (USB4 with power delivery and data speeds up to 40Gbps), an HDMI 2.1 port, and a USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A port on its left side. On the right side, it has another USB Type-C port (this one a 3.2 Gen 2 port with power delivery and data speeds up to 10Gbps), another USB Type-A port, and an SD Express 7.0 card reader. This is a wide-ranging set of options, so you should find everything you need. The PC also includes a 1080p camera, which delivers sharp video quality and balances lighting well in dimmer environments. The wireless connectivity options include Bluetooth 5.4 and Wi-Fi 7. Asus bundles a fair amount of AI features into this system, and your mileage will vary on how helpful you find them. For example, MuseTree (an AI-powered image generator found on several Asus systems) returns, and you'll also find StoryCube, which organizes and searches all of your local media. The ProArt Creator Hub software contains most of these apps and other creator-friendly settings. The MyAsus application focuses more on device and system settings. To gauge the ProArt P16's performance, we ran it through our standard benchmark suite and compared the results with those of other laptops. You can see the names and specs of these systems below. In this group, I included two current high-end Windows options: the Framework Laptop 16 ($3,198 as tested) and the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Ultra ($3,799.99 as tested). I also selected the 16-inch Apple MacBook Pro with the M5 Max chip ($6,149 as tested) as a high-power alternative. This is the very top-end MacBook option, and most users won't need the ultra-potent and pricey M5 Max chip, but it is a worthy alternative in a roughly similar price range. Finally, the previous ProArt P16 ($2,699.99 as tested) is included here to demonstrate generational improvement, though it's important to note that its RTX 4070 GPU is far from a 1:1 leap to an RTX 5090. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the HandBrake 1.8 video transcoder to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess through a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. I should say up front that all of these laptops are fast, so the scores are at least good. Compared against one another, there is some separation that varies from test to test. For instance, the ProArt P16's PCMark 10 score led the group (though the MacBook couldn't run this and some other Windows-based tests), and its Photoshop result was the second-highest. However, its Handbrake result underwhelmed. When there is an outlier, it's the MacBook Pro with its M5 Max, which posted several of the best scores. All in all, while not the undisputed fastest we've tested in this bunch, the ProArt P16 can power through tough content-creation tasks. We challenge all systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. The ProArt P16 and its RTX 5090, configured at 120W TDP, push some of the highest scores, giving the system an advantage in this field for graphics-intensive workloads. Not all users need as much graphics muscle as processing speed, but plenty of editors, animators, engineers, and other workers will lean on a strong GPU. The M5 Max is a different story; most integrated solutions can't keep up with discrete GPUs like the RTX 5090, but Apple's top-tier chip is up to the task. The laptop's performance is objectively strong, but that's a given in this tier. As shown by the Framework Laptop 16 and MacBook Pro, other systems can offer more graphics muscle, even if the RTX 5090 is the top spec on paper. Thicker and larger laptops have even more thermal headroom for improved performance; we often see these differences in thin gaming laptops versus 18-inch gaming laptops, even when they have the same GPU. The ProArt P16 delivers strong graphics power, but it just isn't an unabashed chart-topper, which may be disappointing given the price and the RTX 5090's on-paper specs. As for the older ProArt P16 versus this version, you can see how much more overall muscle resides in the 2026 edition. Part of that is due to the former's RTX xx70 tier being unable to compete with the latter's RTX xx90 tier—a gulf that stretches across GPU generations. I didn't test the current ProArt P16's RTX 5070 model, but it would likely show some graphics improvement over the previous laptop (though not as much as one powered by the tested RTX 5090). More so than during the processing tests, the graphics test (and my anecdotal gaming) made the system run quite hot. It's not uncomfortable to use the keyboard, but the area above the keyboard gets quite toasty, as does the bottom panel; beware lap use under heavy load! As an aside, this is a capable gaming machine even at high resolutions. In testing thermal performance, I ran Cyberpunk 2077 at 1440p with the ray-tracing ultra preset. The RPG moved at roughly 60 frames per second. This is a demanding game and setting, so most titles will be even easier to run (plus AMD's FSR upscaling technology can boost frame rates further). We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with the display brightness set to 50% and the audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). The battery life was only decent, neither especially short nor long. As you can see, some of the alternatives ran laps around its near-10-hour result. Still, that’s long enough to last off the charger for moderate use in a cafe or airport. The type of work this laptop is intended for is usually completed at a desk when plugged in, after all. Final Thoughts Asus ProArt P16 (2026) - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The updated Asus ProArt P16 is a familiar face, offering few changes from the prior edition. The good news is that we were big fans of that model, and this iteration features superior graphics performance thanks to Nvidia's GeForce RTX 50 series, supplanting the RTX 40-series options. The rest of the premium features—from an attractive metal build, a beautiful 4K OLED screen, the DialPad, and software enhancements—all return, making this a leading option for creative professionals. Take that all together, and the 2026 Asus ProArt P16 earns an Editors' Choice award for high-end content creation laptops. About Our Expert I’ve been a consumer PC expert at PCMag for 10 years, and I love PC gaming. I've played games on my computer for as long as I can remember, which eventually (as it does for many) led me to build and upgrade my own desktops to this day. Through my years at PCMag, I've tested and reviewed many, many dozens of laptops and desktops, and I am always happy to recommend a PC for your needs and budget.

item.title: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11 Review: A Snapdragon Workhorse With Just a Little Sizzle
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.72
The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x won't blow you away, but it offers something hard to find right now: a decent everyday laptop with helpful features and potent enough silicon for less than $1,000 ($969.99 as tested). As you'd expect, it comes up short against the competition in some spots, such as underwhelming graphics capabilities and a lackluster design. The machine also packs a Snapdragon Arm processor, so you may encounter edge-case compatibility issues with x86-based apps. All told, the IdeaPad Slim 5x strikes a mostly successful balance between performance and affordability, while including some nifty upgrades that don't cost a fortune. Still, if you’re looking for a more premium design for a close or sometimes lower price, check out the HP OmniBook 5 14, our Editors' Choice pick for midrange ultraportable laptops. I tested the IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11's base configuration, which runs $969.99 and comes with an Arm-based six-core/six-thread Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus (X2P-42-100) processor with integrated Qualcomm Adreno (X2-45) graphics, 16GB of LPDDR5x memory, a 512GB solid-state drive, a 15.3-inch display, and a 54.7-watt-hour battery. The IPS panel has a native resolution of 1,920 by 1,200 pixels (1200p), and it supports up to 120Hz refresh and touch input. You can double the RAM for $300 more and boost the storage to 1TB for another $200, while an extra $30 will score you a 2,560-by-1,600-pixel 165Hz OLED display (without touch support)—a feature you should absolutely grab if given the choice. Same with the $10 upgrade that will boost the battery capacity to 70 watt-hours. Selecting all of these options brings you to $1,509.99, still relatively midrange but entering MacBook Air and Dell XPS territory. The IdeaPad Slim 5x isn’t designed for a premium market, so the build quality isn’t necessarily top-notch. I could tell in the seams of the build as I held it, and in the feel of the diving-board touchpad. First, the laptop measures 0.61 by 9.3 by 13.4 inches and weighs 3.28 pounds, so it’s less portable than a 14-inch device, even though the screen-space difference here isn’t all that significant. The hinges are fairly stiff, as well, so opening it up with one hand is a challenge, though the webcam lip on the lid helps. The only real embellishment you'll see on the outside of the laptop is a Lenovo logo. Likewise, Lenovo sells only one color, Cloud Grey, which is about as exciting as it sounds. The IdeaPad's IPS display simply can’t compete with an OLED panel, so, as I said before, definitely consider upgrading to the sharper and more colorful screen. It's only $30! The IPS comes limited to 1200p, and while the 120Hz refresh is welcome, it doesn’t have anywhere near the color vibrancy of OLED laptops you can find for about the same price (like this one). The larger footprint on the IdeaPad Slim 5x gives it room for two 2-watt Dolby Audio-certified up-firing speakers flanking the keyboard. They deliver some booming audio for a laptop in this price range. (Just don’t expect miracles in the bass department.) The IdeaPad Slim 5x serves up a spacious keyboard. Unlike some other laptops at this size, it doesn't come with a 10-key number pad, which might be a drawback for some. However, I prefer this setup since it allows for better top-firing speakers and more room for the main key layout. The keyboard provides deep enough travel and makes for comfortable typing over extended periods. The buttonless touchpad works well enough. It's wide and spacious, with minimal flex when left- and right-clicking. However, it might take some getting used to, since it isn’t quite centered below the keyboard, but on the space bar. For the webcam, Lenovo supplies a 1080p IR camera with a physical privacy shutter for extra security. It supports Windows Hello and can record video at 30 frames per second at 1080p. The image quality is surprisingly high, and for most users, it’ll be more than enough for video calls with friends and family, not to mention job interviews. Lenovo served up two 5Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A ports, with one always-on connection for device power delivery, on the right side. The laptop's left side includes two 10Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C ports with up to 65-watt power delivery and DisplayPort 1.4 video output. Finally, Lenovo installed an HDMI 2.1 port and a 3.5mm audio/mic combo jack on the left side, along with a Micro SD card reader on the right. For connectivity, the laptop includes Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 hardware, giving the laptop an edge over a lot of last-generation devices. The laptop lacks a wired Ethernet port, but that's a rare one these days, anyway. To gauge the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x’s performance on specific tasks, such as content creation and common productivity apps, I’ve compared it with several competing ultralights to see how it measures up. These include the Apple MacBook Air 13-inch ($1,299 as tested, $1,499 for a 15-inch with the same specs), followed by our $1,419.99 Dell 14S review configuration. Next, we have our current Editors' Choice pick for best Windows laptop for most people, the $899.99 HP OmniBook 5 14, as well as the Intel "Wildcat Lake"-based Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15 (tested at $1,299, but down to just under $1,000 in places). Our first group of tests represents workloads such as content creation, office productivity, and raw CPU speeds. Our go-to overall productivity and storage test, PCMark 10, is not yet Snapdragon-compatible, so we focused on core-stressing tests and media tasks. The three primary tests presented below are CPU-centric or processor-intensive. Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the transcoding freeware HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Additionally, we have encountered issues with Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators Adobe Photoshop 25 test on systems with Qualcomm Arm processors, so we’ve skipped it here until we resolve the issues. In testing, the IdeaPad Slim 5x outperformed much of its competition in both multi-core and single-core performance, as measured in Cinebench 2024 and Geekbench 6.3. It couldn't keep up with the M5 MacBook Air, though, lagging well behind it across all tests. Considering the MacBook's steep pricing—and even more for the 15-inch version—the IdeaPad turned in respectable results for the price. All of this comes with one big caveat, though. The Snapdragon X2 Plus turned in generally fast processor performance when running native Arm apps, but that may not hold when running x86-based apps through Windows’ Prism emulation. Most Windows apps were originally developed for x86 microcode-based processors made by Intel and AMD, and this code can't run on an Arm-based processor like Qualcomm’s Snapdragon line. To get around this, Windows 11 uses an x86 emulation layer called Prism, which translates an app’s x86 code into Arm code in real time. This allows these apps to run on Arm chips, but this added layer introduces latency into the code that can affect an app’s performance, sometimes significantly. However, distinguishing between the Arm and x86 versions of an app can be challenging, leading to unforeseen performance hits. In Cinebench 2024, for example, running the x86 version of the app through emulation drastically reduces performance compared with running the Arm version, with up to 39% lower multi-core performance and up to 34% lower single-core performance. That’s not to say every x86 app will have that kind of performance loss, but it shows how significant this performance hit can be, so it’s essential to always make sure you are downloading the Arm version of an app wherever possible to see the best performance out of this laptop. We challenge all systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. The IdeaPad 5x turned in fairly weak graphics performance, but not the worst on the list. It especially struggled with ray tracing, as you can see in 3DMark’s Solar Bay benchmark. So, if you're involved in computer gaming or advanced creative work, the MacBook Air 13-inch or 15-inch will be a much better choice. While we wouldn't directly compare the two, a similarly priced gaming laptop will perform much better for gaming, regardless. Specific game compatibility with Arm processors should also factor into your decision here if you're a gamer. We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with display brightness at 50% and audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we also use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). On our endurance test, Qualcomm's well-documented Snapdragon X power efficiency came through once again, giving the IdeaPad 5x just shy of a full day’s worth of juice (23 hours and 56 minutes). That beat the latest MacBook Air 13-inch by several hours, but the Dell 14S took the crown here with an astounding 38 hours and 29 minutes. The Lenovo's IPS panel, though, was strictly middling. It features 100% sRGB color-gamut coverage, which is important for web and general app color coverage, and a shiny 424 nits of max brightness. However, its measurements of 78% for Adobe RGB and 79% for DCI-P3 color coverage—essential for photo editing and watching movies, respectively—can’t keep up with the competition. If you’re looking at buying this laptop, opt for the OLED panel. It’s well worth the extra $30, which still keeps the price just under $1,000. Final Thoughts Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Weak graphics performance, a lackluster design, and a ho-hum display are significant drawbacks for the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11. However, the laptop’s upsides are hard to ignore, thanks to fast native Arm app performance (which covers most apps most people use every day), plentiful ports, and all-day battery life. For the price, this IdeaPad strikes an effective balance between performance and value, something that’s difficult to find in the laptop market right now. However, we've already found an even better-presented version of this package in the HP OmniBook 5 14, our Editors' Choice pick in the midrange laptop category. About Our Expert John (he/him) is a programmer, gamer, activist, and Brooklyn College alum currently living in Brooklyn, New York. Named by the CTA as a CES 2020 Media Trailblazer for his science and technology reporting, John specializes in all areas of computer science, including industry news, hardware reviews, and PC gaming. He's also well-versed in general science writing and the social impact of the tech industry. John has a Bachelor’s degree in English and a Master’s degree in Computer Science. You can usually find him on Bluesky, where you’ll get his hot takes on stuff, as well as his reposts of content that is almost as good as the worst stuff you used to be able to find on Vine. Beyond PC gaming, he spends his evenings building digital circuits, multiboxing Linux kernels, and coding shell scripts.

item.title: FAA: Laser Attacks on Planes Are Down, but They're Still Far Too High
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.40
Pointing a laser pen at the sky might seem harmless, but it can be extremely dangerous: distracting and even blinding pilots. Since 2010 laser strikes have plagued US aircraft, with experts chalking up the problem to easily available cheap laser pens, and people either not knowing or not caring about the risks it entails. Though thankfully these types of incidents haven’t caused any crashes, the FAA says pilots have reported 328 injuries since it started tracking the number in 2010. But the good news is that laser strikes against aircraft are down again this year, for the third time running, falling 24 percent year-on-year to 4,470 through July 2026 according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). This represents a huge decrease compared to 2023's all-time high of 13,304. The FAA chalked up the recent improvements to its ongoing outreach and training with local, state, and federal law enforcement. California recorded the most incidents overall with 614, while Texas recorded 445. Per capita Hawaii was the worst impacted state, with 5.09 incidents per 100,000 people, followed by New Mexico and Colorado. The FAA reminds the public about the dangers of holiday laser-light displays ahead of the upcoming holiday season. "The concentrated laser beams reach much farther than homeowners may realize and have the potential of distracting or temporarily blinding pilots," read the announcement. Pointing lasers at an aircraft is a serious federal crime. The FAA imposes fines of up to $11,000 for a single violation and up to $30,800 for multiple violations. Meanwhile, what it calls severe violations can result in up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, alongside additional state and local penalties. The FAA encourages people to report all incidents to [email protected], or local law enforcement, with your name, contact information, and the date, time, location, and description of the incident. About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: Microsoft spreads its version of DLSS to more Intel laptops
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.76
There’s more than one kind of optimized upscaling for games. Nvidia does it (DLSS), AMD does it (FSR), Intel does it (XeSS). And you might be surprised to hear that Microsoft does it, right there in Windows. Auto Super Resolution has been quietly spreading out to more and more hardware, and this week it comes to laptops and desktops with the latest chips. That’s not just a big deal for Core Ultra Series 3 laptops, which are the newest and coolest thing on a Best Buy shelf that no one can afford. It’s a big deal for the Arc G3 series, which are the chips in the coolest handheld gaming PCs that no one can afford, like the Predator Atlas 8. The majority of these devices are coming with Windows, so while FSR and XeSS are both options, it’s interesting to get an upscaling tool from the native operating system. It’s also enhanced by NPUs, so finally they can do something if you’re not trying to generate slop. Microsoft says that you can try out Auto SR with any game using DirectX 10 or later, but it’ll shine on “texture-heavy games at higher resolutions and graphics settings.” Interestingly, the promotional page is pushing users to bump up the settings quality and get the same or slightly better framerate, rather than going for a pure performance win. While only still images are shown, an Assassin’s Creed Shadows image shows more foliage on an Ultra High setting with approximately the same framerate. Auto SR also has some growing pains. It’s still trained on very specific input and output performance targets capping out at 1080p, and might get wonky at other resolutions. It also upscales the entire image, so even Microsoft says that “text & fine line UI detail appear ‘fainter.'” In fact it’s still recommending XeSS and other upscalers when the game explicitly supports them. If you’re on a Panther Lake laptop or handheld, you can download the Auto Super Resolution package to try it out.

item.title: Asus ProArt KD300 review: A tiny keyboard with big features
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.26
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - A high-quality feel - Smart touch control - Smooth and flexible with settings - Good battery life Cons - Cramped key layout - Unclear what the ‘professional’ angle is Our Verdict I’ve no idea what makes the ProArt a keyboard specifically for professionals, and the extra-compact layout won’t be to everyone’s taste. But it’s backed by a smart and user-friendly system, and the quality is undeniable. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Price When Reviewed $165 Best Prices Today: Asus Proart KD300 It’s hard to find good mechanical keyboards that aren’t marketed as “gaming keyboards,” but this one from Asus is just that. ProArt is their brand for creative gear, primarily monitors and laptops, but also this keyboard and a mouse that I’ve also tested. When I look at what Asus says about the ProArt KD300 online, I’m met with phrases such as “inspires boundless creativity” and “expressive control.” What exactly is particularly expressive and inspiring about the keyboard is, in fact, rather unclear. One of the noteworthy features is said to be its format. This is an extra-compact keyboard with a so-called 65 percent layout, which means it’s small in size and lacks some keys. There’s no numeric keypad on the side, nor even a row of function keys above. Mattias Inghe Cramped but well-built Everything is very well built and the chassis is sturdy, but it’s lighter than many competing keyboards, even compared to similarly small ones. The keys are low-profile, but with full travel and linear switches without a mechanical click. They trigger early when pressed, allowing you to type quickly. There is some clicking sound when pressing and releasing the keys, but it’s not excessively noisy. The point of the compact design is supposedly to free up more desk space for other things, such as a graphics tablet, mouse, cameras, and a microphone. I’m not sure if it’s worth it — I’ve never felt short of desk space — but that’s up to you. For some reason, this type of more compact keyboard is popular. Personally, I always prefer more keys. It’s not that the functions are inaccessible. There are F1 to F12 functions, media controls, window management in Windows, screenshot, and brightness and volume controls, but all via Fn combinations. These functions and more are printed on the front edge of the keys. They’re hard to see without good lighting in the room, but they’re there. The backlight doesn’t illuminate them, only the main characters in the center of the top row. Mattias Inghe Lots of features, plenty of flexibility You can also access other features this way, such as controlling the RGB backlighting with colors and effects, a macro function, and switching between paired devices. You can connect up to five devices, using a combination of Bluetooth, a USB receiver, and USB-C. In addition to the buttons on the top, there’s also a touch strip along the back edge of the keyboard. This gives you quick control over things like volume, screen brightness, the media player, and customizable swipe and click gestures. These are configured in Gearlink, Asus’s web-based interface. You simply browse to it from the computer that you’re connected to, so you don’t need to install any app. Here, you can change the function of absolutely every button and save your settings in different profiles. You get easier access to the backlight and control over power consumption. There are plenty of options for customization for both productivity and gaming, but it’s entirely manual — you’ll need to design your own setups. Mattias Inghe Can last for weeks It’s all powered by a 4,000mAh rechargeable battery, which, according to Asus, should last for “up to 16 months” without backlighting and 100 days with it. But of course, that depends on how much you use it during that time. In any case, you won’t need to hunt for a charging cable straight away. During my week-long test, the battery level dropped by 5 percent. But then I was using the laptop and keyboard rather sporadically. That’s still very good, though. If you appreciate an extra-compact keyboard — perhaps because you want to be close to your mouse or your desk is a bit cramped — this is one of the better ones you can buy. It offers surprisingly high functionality, a nice sense of quality, and precise keystrokes. The angle, specifically marketed as a keyboard for creative work, feels rather contrived. It’s a somewhat limiting solution as a text-input device and typing tool, and it doesn’t offer anything extra in terms of control for creative software. But that doesn’t stop it from being really good, if you’re comfortable with the format. Specifications Product name: Asus ProArt KD300 Manufacturer: Asus Connectivity: Bluetooth, 2.4 GHz RF, USB-C Battery: 4,000mAh built-in rechargeable Layout: 65% QWERTY keyboard Key type: Low-profile, ROG RX Red switches Number of keys: 68 Other: Device switch, touch panel, RGB backlighting System requirements: Device with USB or Bluetooth and Windows or Mac OS Dimensions: 30.56 x 10.9 x 2.68 cm Weight: 595 grams

item.title: Your monitor says it has HDR. That might not mean much
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.70
Imagine you just bought a brand-new monitor that prominently advertises its HDR capabilities. You hop over to YouTube and stream the first “4K HDR” video you find… but it looks washed out or barely any different from the non-HDR display you had before. It’s a common problem. HDR is touted everywhere on monitor spec sheets, but a lot of those badges don’t really mean much when the monitor itself isn’t capable of actually showing HDR. Real HDR needs the right hardware to deliver what the sticker on the box promises. If your monitor doesn’t have adequate brightness, it isn’t going to be able to produce those specular highlights that make HDR movies and TV shows really pop. If its contrast ratio is weak, it isn’t going to be able to deliver dark, inky blacks with real detail. If it doesn’t have enough dimming zones (or individual OLED pixel control), it’s going to struggle with halos and crushed shadows. Yup, lots of monitors promise HDR but fail to deliver. Here’s what’s happening and how you can avoid being duped. Real HDR vs. expectations HDR technology is widely misunderstood, and that’s at least partially responsible for why so many “HDR” monitors disappoint. It’s often marketed as a simple way to brighten highlights, darken shadows, and make colors look extra vibrant—but that’s not really what it’s doing. It’s just one example of how gaming monitor specs can deceive you. HDR is more about preserving a wider range of brightness and color information from the original source material. It then relies on the display to reproduce that wider range, and that’s why the display’s actual hardware and specifications are so important. With SDR (non-HDR) content, the signal has to contain all the details for highlights, midtones, and shadows in a narrower brightness range. That’s what results in SDR content losing detail in the extremes, with ultra-bright or extra-dark areas blending together and leaving detail compressed. If you’ve ever found yourself squinting to see the characters in a dark scene, this is partly why that problem occurs. Mattias Inghe A good HDR monitor gives the signal enough breadth to properly display the original image without losing detail at the extremes. Dark scenes can still look dark while allowing even darker shadowy figures to move within them, and bright elements in the clouds aren’t washed out just because a silhouette is moving in the foreground. Here’s the main takeaway: In order for HDR to be effective, the monitor needs to be capable of generating the brightness and high-contrast shadows that these HDR scenes demand. “Fake” HDR in monitors The Samsung Odyssey G55C is a fast and affordable gaming monitor with a 1440p IPS panel and HDR10 support. But while it might be able to technically handle an HDR signal, its hardware can’t back it up. It lacks local dimming, so blooming and halos occur. Its brightness is limited to a mere 300 nits, which just isn’t enough to meaningfully display bright highlights. Contrast is decent enough for an IPS monitor, but it can’t deliver the dark-scene details that higher-end monitors can. That’s why the best gaming monitors offer a lot more brightness than that. Samsung/Amazon Another example is Dell’s Alienware AW3225DM, which supports HDR and even has VESA DisplayHDR 400 certification. But many reviewers note that local dimming is poor and its 400-nit brightness is unimpressive, leaving highlights that fail to pop off the screen. And its contrast when local dimming is enabled—something you can’t turn off when it’s receiving an HDR signal—is worse than SDR mode. Even high-end monitors aren’t immune to this issue, with some that are lauded for their “HDR support” only delivering it conditionally or with notable caveats. For example, Dell’s Alienware AW3225QF is one of the most well-reviewed gaming monitors ever made, and its QD-OLED panel delivers fantastic colors, contrast, and brightness for OLED. Yet while on paper it can deliver 1,000 nits, it’s only VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black certified because it can only manage 1,000 nits on smaller screen segments. With a full-screen HDR image, it can only deliver around 250 nits. That’s one reason why we dinged it a star in our review of it. Matt Smith I have this monitor, by the way. It’s utterly gorgeous in SDR and still great in HDR with rich colors and deep shadows. But it’s a gaming monitor first and foremost, and it’s the buttery smooth 4K frame rates, high contrast, and snappy response time that I enjoy most. For watching HDR movies, I still prefer a big, bright OLED or Mini-LED TV. (Learn more about why Mini-LED is the future, not OLED.) What you need for true HDR Realistically, most affordable monitors can only push 300 to 400 nits of brightness, and that just won’t suffice for anything but the most basic HDR. They may be able to accept an HDR signal, but they won’t have enough brightness headroom to make those highlights look dramatically brighter. Even a VESA DisplayHDR 400 rating should be considered basic HDR compatibility and not true HDR support. Higher brightness ratings, particularly those backed by VESA like DisplayHDR 600, are notably more impressive and are likely to deliver the kind of vibrancy you’re looking for with HDR. Above that, you have DisplayHDR 1000 which is where HDR really becomes more convincing. With 1,000 nits of brightness, you have the headroom necessary to go bright without forcing the whole image to flatten out. That’s why my colleague recommends 1,000 minimum for HDR performance. Samsung But brightness isn’t the full story. You also need strong contrast and precise control to handle entire scenes with both bright and dark elements, especially if they cross over one another. The per-pixel control of OLED and the many local dimming zones of Mini-LED both make a huge difference to how light and dark interact on screen, and that higher contrast really helps pull out the details needed for HDR. And if you’re buying OLED, consider the type of OLED panel you’re getting. QD-OLED tends to offer more vibrant colors, but you can lose some of the contrast in brighter rooms. More traditional WOLED designs are often brighter and have more high-contrast shadows at the expense of more impressive color saturation. Sometimes it’s just Windows’ fault A major caveat to all of this HDR talk is that, even after years of work, updates, and readily available calibration tools, Windows 11 doesn’t handle HDR as well as one would hope. First, you need to make sure HDR is enabled in your monitor settings and within Windows itself. You should also run the Windows HDR Calibration app to fine tune your settings. But even then, issues can crop up. A quick search on Reddit for your monitor’s name/model followed by “HDR settings” will likely turn up all sorts of threads and replies where new monitor owners are pulling their hair out. Jon Martindale / Foundry And then there’s Windows Auto HDR, a neat OS feature for gamers who want to play older games that don’t have HDR support on monitors that do have HDR support. It effectively tone maps the SDR signal to better fit an HDR display’s capabilities. It’s not as good as native HDR support, especially with games where the look was supposed to be flatter, but it’s a nice-to-have option for supported games and monitors. Suffice it to say, your HDR experience will vary depending on your specific monitor, the hardware within it, the monitor’s settings, your Windows settings, your eyeballs, and your personal tastes. HDR isn’t black and white. Some monitors are much better at displaying it than others, even if they all say they support HDR. Ignore the vague “HDR10” and “HDR supported” and “VESA DisplayHDR 400” terms and marketing materials. Look at the raw specifications. If HDR matters to you, make sure the monitor you’re buying really has the brightness and hardware to power it. Don’t just take a manufacturer at its word. Further reading: The best monitors for 4K, HDR, and more

item.title: Block every ad and tracker for life with AdGuard’s $11 family plan
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.11
TL;DR: AdGuard’s Family plan blocks ads, trackers, and malware across nine devices, and a lifetime subscription is on sale for $11 (reg. $169.99). Ads, trackers, and shady pop-ups are on almost every site out there, and free ad blockers rarely catch what’s important. AdGuard’s Family plan blocks all three at once, and a lifetime subscription is on sale for $11 (reg. $169.99). You’ll get wide protection with the family plan, which supports up to 9 devices at once; it can be installed across laptops, phones, and tablets running Windows, macOS, iOS, or Android without buying separate licenses. AdGuard is highly compatible with the tech you’re already using. It runs on Windows 11 and 10 and macOS 10.15 or later, so it should work with most existing hardware without requiring an investment. Banner ads and disruptive pop-ups are automatically stripped out, and ads that run in front of videos are blocked too. item.title: This free Photoshop alternative runs right in your browser
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.48
It can be tough to justify shelling out for Photoshop if you only need to edit images every now and then. As an alternative, I recommend checking out Photopea. It’s a free image editor that runs right in your browser. You can use it for quick jobs like cropping, resizing, or touching up a photo, but Photopea goes well beyond the basics. It supports layers, masks, filters, smart objects, vector graphics, and AI tools for things like removing backgrounds or replacing parts of an image—and it does a pretty good job of it too. It can also open and save PSD files, which makes it especially useful if someone sends you a Photoshop file and you don’t actually have Photoshop. The layout follows a familiar pattern, too. You’ve got your tools on the left, layers on the right, and menus across the top. If you’ve ever spent any time in Photoshop, you’ll be able to find your way around pretty quickly. Photopea is entirely free and you don’t have to install anything or make an account. Since it’s browser-based, you can simply open the Photopea site and start editing. Your files are also processed locally on your device instead of being uploaded to Photopea’s servers. There are a few catches. The free version has ads, and large or complicated projects can bog things down a bit. But for quick edits, memes, graphics, or the odd PSD file, Photopea is a surprisingly capable tool that I think is worth keeping bookmarked. For more fun and helpful tips, tricks, website and app recommendations, be sure to subscribe to our PCWorld Try This newsletter.

item.title: 8 PC gaming upgrades under $100 that are actually worth it
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.35
Gaming on a budget doesn’t have to mean compromising on quality. Whether you’re a casual player or a dedicated enthusiast, finding the right accessories can make the precious hours you get to spend in front of your computer that much better… without emptying your wallet. We’ve dug around and found some of the best PC gaming accessories under $100. Not only will you get top-notch performance, but you’ll get great value too. Let’s dive into the gear that proves great gaming doesn’t have to come with a hefty price tag. Upgrade your mouse: Razer Basilisk V3 X HyperSpeed Razer One of the main things you need for your gaming setup is a proper mouse. There are so many options out there, but we’re particularly in love with the Razer Basilisk V3 X HyperSpeed. With an 18K optical sensor, nine programmable keys, and Chroma RGB, this one’s speedy, versatile, and gorgeous. The Basilisk V3 is also a solid option with a 26K DPI optical sensor and 11 programmable buttons. If you’re into MMOs, then the Naga V2 HyperSpeed may be better with its 19 buttons and 30K sensor. Elevate your laptop while expanding its ports: Mukiya USB-C Dock Stand Mukiya If you’re on a gaming laptop, then you’ll get a ton of mileage out of a USB-C laptop docking station stand like this one by Mukiya. Not only does it support nine different angles, but it also has an integrated dock with ports for 4K HDMI, two USB-A, one USB-C for data, one USB-C with 85W of passthrough charging, as well as SD and microSD card slots. It’s the ultimate accessory for a decked-out gaming laptop. Add more screens and accessories to your laptop: Anker 14-in-1 Docking Station Anker If you want an even more versatile docking station than the Mukiya above and you don’t need the laptop stand feature, then this Anker 14-in-1 Laptop Docking Station is a great option. It comes with two 4K HDMI ports and another 1080p VGA port, enabling you to add three displays to your gaming laptop. It also has several USB ports, a USB-C PD port with 100W max charging power, SD and microSD card slots, and a Gigabit Ethernet port for stable online gaming. Upgrade your audio quality: Creative Pebble Pro Desktop Speakers Creative Laptops (and monitors) don’t come with high-quality integrated speakers, so you’re going to need a proper pair if you want to properly enjoy the movies and TV shows you watch and the games you play. For their price, these Creative Pebble Pro Desktop Speakers are absolute gold. They have a minimalist design, they come with Bluetooth 5.3 support, and they have customizable RGB lighting. Chat online in ultimate comfort: Turtle Beach Stealth 600 Wireless Headset Dominic Bayley / IDG If you’re into online multiplayer games, then you need to be able to keep in touch with friends on Discord. The Turtle Beach Stealth 600 Wireless Headset is one of our favorites, not only for PC gaming but also while working, while on your phone, and even while gaming on the Xbox One and PS5.
