AI leaders have been promising that AI is the key to curing human disease. Dario Amodei opined just last week: “I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years.” To do that, an LLM would have to have methods to test its theories in real life. “We believe that to do biology, the final test is still, and will be for a while, in real lab work,” Anthropic’s head of life sciences, Eric Kauderer-Abrams, told Reuters. “We absolutely are doing that today.” He added that the lab operates like most biotech labs: Anthropic conducts some research there while also working with external partners. This news probably shouldn’t be shocking. Anthropic bought Coefficient Bio, a stealth AI biotech, in April. While Anthropic declined to give specifics on what the wet lab is working on, it did say the main focus was fundamental biology, not drug discovery. Anthropic doesn’t want to give the appearance of competing with the pharma industry, where it has numerous major customers and partners (e.g., it just announced a deal to work with Novo Nordisk on joint drug discovery). Anthropic has already faced backlash for launching products perceived to compete with those of its customers. To that end, Anthropic also launched a Life Sciences Verification Program this week, to give vetted bio researchers access to its most powerful models. It has also published recent reports on some of the research it’s doing to support drug discovery. This includes one report on accelerating protein design and one on uplifting bimolecular modeling. But the world is still reeling from the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who warned that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Anthropic’s own alignment lead gave the odds at greater than 10% that AI could exterminate humanity within the next decade. The fervor has grown so intense that CEO Dario Amodei published a post last weekend calling on the industry to slow down and institute self-regulation. He has repeatedly called bioterrorism one of AI’s biggest risks. The juxtaposition of these dire warnings and the wet lab has not gone unnoticed in the tech industry. As investor and AI coding startup founder Chamath Palihapitiya posted on X, somewhat tongue in cheek: “The group behind such hits as: ‘We’re All Going To Die’ and ‘Regulate Me Now’ are building a wet lab in SF. I do not recommend this.”

item.title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 3.48
This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale. At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence, so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems. But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.” To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities. That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me. Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out? No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs, and even OpenAI and Anthropic. In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building. Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario: If you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention.

item.title: Automattic names interim CFO after exec departures
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 3.40
Automattic has a new interim chief financial officer: Jeremy Klaperman, the CFO of the company’s WordPress VIP Enterprise business unit. The news, shared internally on Friday, follows last week’s attempted ouster of Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg, which ultimately resulted in the departure of the board members who voted him out and other executives, including then-CFO Mark Davies. Davies was briefly interim CEO before Mullenweg retook the position. In a Slack post, Mullenweg shared that Klaperman had previously acted as Automattic CFO when Davies had been on sabbatical. He noted that the board — whose new members have yet to be announced — will still need to evaluate internal and external candidates for the position before a final decision is made. In addition, Mullenweg said in the post that a candidate to become the company’s chief legal officer had also just verbally accepted the position, replacing Chief Legal Officer Andy Missan, who has also since left the company alongside Davies. TechCrunch recently reported that Davies and Missan had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s 33-hour leave of absence before he returned as CEO. “I have 100% confidence in our cash and financial position,” Mullenweg’s post concluded, adding “There is still work to do, but everything is within our control and depends only on Automattic’s ability to execute.” In subsequent updates, Mullenweg also said to “stay tuned” for board announcements, and noted that special advisor and creator of Wolfram|Alpha, Stephen Wolfram, will continue in his position. The company’s next board meeting is scheduled for September 23.

item.title: Vals, backed by Andreessen Horowitz, is looking to become the gold standard for AI benchmarking
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 3.26
Benchmarking has become the industry norm for how AI companies validate their models’ capabilities and, when the metrics swing in their favor, stand out from competitors and advertise their superiority. In other words, good benchmarks pretty much always mean good PR. Unfortunately, companies have also figured out how to outwit legacy benchmarking systems — many of which are older, and not built to measure the capabilities of modern models. Vals, a startup formed in 2024, says that it is on a mission to fix this very imperfect system. In the span of less than two years, the company has established itself as a notable presence in the tech industry and, last year it managed to secure a seed round led by 8VC and Bloomberg Beta. Then, last month, after a period of rapid growth, it raised $40 million in a series A led by Andreessen Horowitz. Rayan Krishnan, the company’s 25-year-old co-founder, previously interned at Palantir, and, as an undergraduate at Stanford, worked for Microsoft and the school’s much lauded artificial intelligence lab. Krishnan says Vals was born from his own observations about how benchmarking was falling behind the advances of the industry it was designed to measure. “We were seeing a bunch of new, very capable models come to market quickly, and the academic benchmarks [were] not keeping up with that frontier advance,” Krishnan shares. With AI being integrated into every part of society, benchmarks should really exist to verify that models can do what companies advertise they can do, Krishnan said. Last week, the young founder showed me around his company’s two-floor office on San Francisco’s Folsom Street — an old brick building that, a century ago, served as the site of a large brewery. Instead of an industrial output of beer, the historical structure is now home to a number of different startups looking to ship the future of the tech industry. “Historically, I think evaluation has been done to evaluate intelligence in a very abstract way,” Krishnan tells me. “Like, do models know enough information to be able to take a bar exam type test?” Here, Vals seeks to differentiate itself. While many benchmarking systems offer tests that are publicly available (this can allow a company to train its model against those tests, thus arguably cheating on their exam), Vals doesn’t publicly disclose its specific test materials. Instead of measuring an AI model’s general knowledge, Vals also evaluates models on their ability to complete complex tasks associated with specific industries like law, finance, and coding. “What we’re doing is actually looking at what are the real impacts of the models,” said Krishnan. “Can they do work that produces a product of the same quality as a human within every domain?” The idea is to check not just for positive outcomes but also for negative ones, he says. The hope is to analyze how, “if these models ran wild in the world, what the negative implications would be.” The capabilities that Vals is measuring are growing. In additional to more traditional industries, the startup continues to push into more unique terrain. “We have a benchmark on recursive self improvement. We’re doing some work in mental health, cybersecurity, biosecurity, and even law of armed conflict to models to understand how to apply the Geneva Convention,” Krishnan shares. Companies pay Vals to test their models, which can be an odd concept to wrap your head around. Why would a company pay to learn its model isn’t performing well? But having an effective measurement helps companies troubleshoot and improve over time. Krishnan compares their revenue model to how a student might pay the College Board to take the SAT. In turn, these evaluations are becoming key decision-making factors for companies looking to acquire new AI models. The startup recently revealed that its revenue is currently eight times what it was last year. Its staff is also growing. Vals, which started the year with only eight people, has already tripled to a team of 25. Krishnan said that as the startup grows, the plan is to relocate to a significantly bigger office, as well as to bring on an additional 10 to 15 people. The company also recently launched a program centered around providing model evaluations to federal agencies. Krishnan sees his company’s system of benchmarking as the future of how AI companies think about growing their businesses and establishing public trust. “AI companies are starting to go public. SpaceX went public. Anthropic is slated for later this year. I suspect OpenAI will be public soon. I think as AI models become a core part of the economy and are diffused more broadly, the types of benchmarks and evaluations that we do are going to drive their usage and be a central part of how these companies submit public filings or talk about the prospective investments they’re going to make in AI,” he said.

item.title: Security researchers used Claude to help them hack into OpenAI
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 5.91
A team of three independent security researchers at Hacktron says it took less than 72 hours for them to hack into OpenAI employee accounts using Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 and 5, The Wall Street Journal reports. They were able to access OpenAI’s GitHub repository, called “Monorepo,” which reportedly contains “OpenAI’s algorithmic secrets,” according to The Wall Street Journal’s sources. Security researchers used Claude to help them hack into OpenAI A three-person team of researchers used a corrupted image file and forum software to hack into OpenAI. They stopped short of accessing internal code in Monorepo themselves, but sent a pull request from an employee’s Codex account to prove they gained access. They were able to get in through Discourse, the third-party service that hosts OpenAI’s community forums, by exploiting an issue with the system it uses to process HEIF images. According to Hacktron, Claude Opus 5 launched in the evening on July 24th, and by 10AM the next day they had used it to achieve RCE on Discourse Cloud and accessed OpenAI’s instance. Their HEIF Heist project took “only one or two days” to adapt to different companies, including OpenAI, Slack, Meta, GitHub Ent, Rails, Next.js, ImageMagick, and others, using less than $3,000 in tokens, and to their knowledge, was only detected by one target, Shopify. The vulnerabilities Hacktron reported to Discourse and OpenAI have since been fixed, and Hacktron says OpenAI paid it $6,500 for finding the bug, but as Hacktron CTO Mohan Pedhapati said to the WSJ, “I don’t think we are as strong as Chinese threat actors… We’re just three guys with Claude and Codex subscriptions.”

item.title: This cartridge-playing Game Boy clone is smaller and cheaper than Analogue’s Pocket
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.78
FunnyPlaying, a Chinese company known for its Game Boy and GBA upgrade kits, has announced a new handheld that plays original Nintendo cartridges and ROMs. The FPGB Mini’s cartridge support is limited to the Game Boy and Game Boy Color so it isn’t as capable as the Analogue Pocket that’s also compatible with the GBA and Sega Game Gear. What still makes the FPGB Mini a tempting alternative is its extremely pocketable design resulting in a handheld only slightly wider than a Game Boy cartridge, and its cheaper price. This cartridge-playing Game Boy clone is smaller and cheaper than Analogue’s Pocket The FPGB Mini is only slightly wider than the original Nintendo cartridges it plays. Following recent price hikes the Analogue Pocket is now $239.99 while the FPGB Mini is currently discounted from $89.99 to $69.99 for the first batch of just 20 units that quickly sold out. However, the company is potentially planning to release more following some hardware improvements, according to Retro Dodo who’s been testing the handheld for a few days and so far seems impressed with its design and capabilities. Like the Pocket the FPGB Mini uses field-programmable gate array (FPGA) technology to play Game Boy and GBC games as accurately as Nintendo’s original hardware does. But the FPGB Mini brings improvements like a 2.98-inch, 800x720-pixel LCD display, an 1,800mAh rechargeable battery, and a microSD slot for storing game saves, screenshots, or ROMs that can be played through emulation. The handheld’s compact size does prevent cartridges with rumble motors or other hardware additions from being used, but otherwise the FPGB Mini looks to be about as small as the Game Boy is ever going to get.

item.title: Disney’s first CTO is Character.AI’s former CEO
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.42
You would think that a multimedia conglomerate as large as Disney would have a few chief technology officers by now, but the company has just appointed someone to the position for the very first time. Disney’s first CTO is Character.AI’s former CEO The House of Mouse has poached Karandeep Anand from the chatbot company. Today, Disney announced that Karandeep Anand is joining the company as its new CTO. Anand will report directly to recently appointed CEO Josh D’Amaro, and he will head up the company’s infrastructure, product, engineering, and data / AI platforms teams. Anand comes to Disney from chatbot startup Character.AI, where he served as CEO for just over a year and oversaw the company’s push into microdramas. Anand jumping ship to Disney comes as a bit of a surprise considering how this time last year, the company was sending Character.AI cease and desist letters due to the startup’s tools infringing on copyrighted IP. But Anand’s hiring could be a sign of how Disney wants to move forward with AI now that its partnership with OpenAI has fallen apart.

item.title: The real story of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.65
It’s one of the most fascinating years in a while when it comes to iPhone camera upgrades. The big story of the iPhone 18 Pro is the variable aperture main lens, which lets you open the aperture up wider for better low light shots and make the aperture smaller for better depth of field in group photos. But all I can get anyone to talk about is the software upgrades: it turns out, they’re a lot more useful day to day than the aperture on a camera this small. The real story of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera On The Vergecast: an iPhone 18 Pro camera deep dive, the state of the AI safety debate, and more. This week on The Vergecast, David Imel and Allison Johnson are here for a deep dive into the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera. There’s a lot to explore here, from the aperture, to the camera app’s new manual controls, to the updated imaging pipeline and the improvements to ProRAW. After that, Hayden Field is on the show to discuss the state of the AI safety debate. Concerns are still boiling over after an Anthropic researcher quit his job to warn about the dangers of AI, and any chance for policy solutions seems to have hit a dead end. We discuss whether what’s likely to happen in the interim — third-party evaluators being embedded within the big AI labs — has any teeth, and where the safety conversation goes from here. Finally, it’s time for a Lightning Round. We discuss Waymo’s ability to call the cops, a new ereader from Boox, and a couple of tiny retro-style cameras. If you want to learn more about any of the topics we discussed, you can check out the stories below:

item.title: Anamanaguchi has ‘too goddamn many’ browser tabs open right now
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.39
Anamanaguchi, the band consisting of Peter Berkman, James DeVito, Luke Silas, and Ary Warnaar, are most known for their chiptune music. Like me, you might have first heard them in game soundtracks like 2010’s Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The Game or know of their collaboration with Hatsune Miku (which even made its way into Fortnite). They’ve gone through different eras of breakneck chiptune beats and dance-y pop songs, but their 2025 album Anyway took an indie rock departure — written at the American Football house and filled with fuzzy guitars. Anamanaguchi has ‘too goddamn many’ browser tabs open right now The chiptune rock band formed in 2004 on forums and remains very online to this day. Anamanaguchi has ‘too goddamn many’ browser tabs open right now The chiptune rock band formed in 2004 on forums and remains very online to this day. They’re also a band that’s terminally online and very plugged into the video game scene as well as the weirder sides of the internet — just listen to Peter and Luke’s guest spot on the Panic World podcast talking about Etsy witches. Anamanaguchi has a new single, “Yeah I Guess,” continuing in the musical direction of Anyway. And if it’s a precursor to a new album dropping soon, I’m sure I’ll be looping it endlessly just as I did the tracks “Magnet,” “Fall Away,” and “Valley of Silence.” (Seriously, I’ve at times had Anyway set on repeat for hours straight.) Not only did all four members of Anamanaguchi agree to answer our weekly questionnaire, but they answered all our questions. What is your most indispensable tool? Luke Silas: I think my most used tool is Ableton Live Operator, it is simple and powerful and can make basic things happen incredibly quickly. I usually open it up just for writing or getting ideas down, but more often than not the sounds I get with it tend to make it to the final product! Which is the most underappreciated? Ary Warnaar: Built-in laptop mic and cellphone mic aren’t exactly slept on, but def underappreciated. They’re great for just getting ideas down fast, but now they sound so good that I find myself not even re-recording what I thought would be “scratch” vocals. Peter Berkman: Right now it’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S. Best mouse I’ve ever had. It has a sideways scroll. It has a button to switch between notched and smooth scroll wheel. The click is satisfying but still really quiet. It’s really sensitive & responsive on whatever surface I happen to have it on. It feels really good in my hand. It charges directly into a USB-C port without external batteries so it gets to look like a mouse with a tail after it’s worked really hard. When I’m at a different computer, or if I’m on a laptop having to use a trackpad, I feel like I’ve lost so much gestural fidelity. I love the keyboard but let’s be real Douglas Engelbart cooked when he invented the mouse. But he didn’t have the recipe of the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and he didn’t even live to see it. The LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S wasn’t even invented until June 2022. I have seen two friends recently using the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and I say “Hey man that’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S” I use that thing too. James DeVito: Lately it’s been an app called “Amphetamine” that keeps your computer from going to sleep for a set amount of time. It’s great when starting an export/render or other task that may take a while and then being able to throw my laptop in my bag and have it work while I head elsewhere… Just gotta make sure the laptop doesn’t ’splode in your bag from overheating. LS: I love metronomes! Strengthening time is so important, and getting more comfortable with a metronome means you get to play around with time more confidently! I would love people to love metronomes the way I do! What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer? LS: Probably Discord? Let’s say Discord. What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone? AW: Would kill to get a normal 1/8-inch headphone out again. I’ve been constantly replacing dongles ever since Apple ditched the headphone out. Because they break or or get misplaced. Frustrating and wasteful. JD: A wise friend of mine once taught me to increase the key-repeat on my computer beyond what is normally allowed via the UI. It feels insane at first but your hand/brain coordination catches up with the speed eventually and then you can tttttttttttttttype and deleeeeeeete things so much quicker. LS: The only thing I’d like to add to my iPhone SE is a USB port so I can type with a keyboard because I suck at typing on my phone. What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar? LS: I have never done this before! I probably should!! PB: There’s a new radio aggregator called vvorldwide.com. It’s amazing. It’s like having a radio dial in your car except it pools the feeds from NTS, The Lot, dublab, KEXP, loads of different places from all over the world. It’s one of those products that’s like: Wow. Why did nobody think to make this before? It’s so useful, lightweight, and beautiful. It’s amazing to me how detached from reality and human use the big companies are (and have been for a long time). It’s one of those refreshing things you see, it reminds me of The Unfinished Revolution by Michael Dertouzos. You can just build things you want to see! JD: Gmail :( How many tabs do you have open right now? PB: Tab grouping from Firefox has become an artform for me. I don’t see tabs anymore just folders of memory I can recall like a PSX save file. LS: 46 and 31 between two windows. Too goddamn many. Most of them are meant to be shared with others or read/watched, every weekend I do a cleanout but there are truthfully a few that have been sitting for months. I can’t be the only one. JD: I like when Chrome on my phone stops displaying the number of open tabs and just shows a smiley face :) Which social media platform do you use the most? LS: Staying detached from social media tends to be better for my mental health on the day-to-day, but scrolling following on Twitter is the easiest way for me to stay connected to games or news still. Instagram stresses me out lately more than ever before. YouTube definitely counts and I do love it very much, but shorts are a rare treat; I tend to watch long-form stuff mostly or have different content with no dialogue on a second monitor, like either a video game longplay or lots of restoration or cooking videos. What is your happy place online? AW: Facebook marketplace. Specifically low-balling “I know what I got” type mfs. No one ever accepts my offers, but I think it’s important to keep people humble, and long term, I’d like to think that I’m contributing to keeping the prices low for the next buyers. PB: I’ve just discovered clothes. So I’m hunting a lot on places like Grailed or Depop or whatever. It’s a lot like the way I treat musical equipment on Reverb. It’s fun to sell stuff and buy stuff… when it’s equal amounts it feels more like barter and temporary sharing. LS: Video game speedruns! Twitch streams like GDQ or RPG Limit Break are very comforting to me and a very sweet community of fun personalities. What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned? JD: 3D printers. I’ve been 3D printing for a long time now, and it’s gotten so so so much more reliable/easy at this point. The fact that I can design a bracket etc. for stage production and have it in hand within an hour really is the future. LS: I’m going to say my Game Boy counts for this question. I use it less for sound design than I used to, but I bought new flash cartridges recently for the first time in years, and I’m ready to get cooking with it again very soon! It’s a perfect little self-contained workstation. Which was the most disappointing? LS: I’ve bought a few different effects plugins that tend to have some distinct effects but end up not giving me what I’m looking for, or feel far too specific to a use case for me to reach for generally speaking. I’ve found more exciting results from stacking and tweaking stock effects than I have reaching for dedicated single-use stuff. PB: I’m not gonna hate on here… but they exist. What game do you have the fondest memories of? PB: Return of the Obra Dinn was so much fun. Any game that feels like detective work is the kinda thing that gets me going, and instantly creates a moment of excitement for me that stays frozen that I can always go back to. I think about playing [the original] Resident Evil for the first time, the first three Phoenix Wright games: I can tell you everything about where I was and what I was feeling when I first played those games. It’s not even a nostalgia based thing. I played Parasite Eve II for the first time two years ago and it was an instant deep love. LS: I think my favorite video game of all time is Chrono Trigger. It was a world I really wished I could experience in real life and the atmosphere of every place you go is special to me. I have been trying to rip off Yasunori Mitsuda and Nobuo Uematsu every time I write for the last 30 years. It’s the first game I think of when I want to start a new playthrough of something familiar to me! Which tech trend do you wish would go away? AW: I don’t like forced two step authentication or even worse, the upper case + number + symbol extra long type passwords. Like if I want my password to just be the letter “a,” that’s on me. I’m comfortable with that choice. I’m comfortable with that level of vulnerability. Shit maybe I don’t even want a password sometimes. Just leave it all out there for the people. LS: Using AI to make music! Blue check accounts on twitter talking about using AI to make music! Write your own fucking music, have fun learning a skill that will continue to give and build and bloom until the day you die!!! What is one thing you wish you had created? LS: “Show Me Love” by Robin S. is a perfect song, and every time I hear it I think “God, I wish that could have been mine.” The combination of the M1 organ, that 909 groove, and Robin S.’ top line is like a simple meal where the right ingredients add up to something far greater than the sum of their parts; a perfect BLT, a chocolate/vanilla/peanut butter milkshake, the freshest sushi you’ve ever eaten. JD: The Black Eyed Peas performed at the 2020 VMAs and they all had light up crotches that sync’d up to the show. Why the f didn’t they call me to do that? What creation are you most proud of? PB: Going back and listening to our album Anyway always surprises me. I love it so much. I think it’s the kinda thing that people who didn’t get it will eventually come around on. Sleeper classic even for me ha. LS: I think the song “Really Like To” from our latest album Anyway is a song that accomplishes a lot of the things I want to when writing for the band! It’s loud and fast, has fun drum parts, fun to sing along to, and I got to do an ambient section at the end; I like showing it to people as an indication of where we’re at right now. JD: Anyway as well — the entire process was so collaborative throughout. A lot of really great memories writing at the house and recording at Tarbox Road Studios. Which are you least proud of? LS: In 2023 I tried to get good at baking cookies, and in the process made a batch of not only the worst cookies I’ve ever had, but some of the worst food I have ever experienced. They looked great, but on a first bite tasted like absolutely nothing and had a texture of chewing damp sand, and on a second bite a bitter taste began to crawl across my tongue that practically gagged me. The only other human who tasted them was my next-door neighbor, just so I could have a witness to the crime that I’d committed. To this day I’m still not sure how I fucked up that bad, and I’ll never forget that taste. What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received? AW: When I was a kid I met Steve Lukather, the guitarist of Toto, and I told him I wanted to be a guitarist in a band when I grow up. He told me that if I wanted to get the girls I had to either lift weights or get good at guitar solos. I’ve done neither and I’ve been suspicious of all advice ever since. PB: My dad told me to “never give up” when I was playing Zelda in my basement as a kid. It gave me a big affinity for puzzles, very encouraging. My dad still gives me important advice at all the big moments in my life — I am very grateful to have him. LS: Progress, not perfection. What is your current obsession? PB: Investigating criminal networks of the 1990s! More of a hobby than an obsession. LS: I’ve unfortunately found myself going further down the rabbit hole of Deltarune theory videos. I don’t buy into the majority of the speculation shared, but I love the game and there is lots of incredible insight shared into the design of it and aspects of it mechanically and narratively that I didn’t even realize I was missing. What do you do when you need to focus? AW: Modafinil. Jk lol, I try not to force focusing and just let it be a byproduct of inspiration/motivation. I wait for the focus to come. If I’m having trouble focusing on something then I probably shouldn’t be doing it. Like driving a car. And if you attach rituals to focus it just invites the possibility of not being able to focus without said rituals. LS: I wait until about 8pm, charge my phone on the other side of my studio, get a large cup of black coffee, put on my second monitor a very long playthrough of a game I’m already familiar with (most recent one was Grandia II), and keep my door shut as long as possible. What do you do when you’re feeling stuck? LS: Take a walk down the Venice boardwalk, get a two-dollar salad from Chairman Mao’s, and eat while listening to music and watching people skate at the Venice bowl. PB: It’s very important to fuck off for a minute. I will go out to a Smash tournament in the Dallas area. There’s a very lively scene that’s super competitive and full of great people. I can always go back from that feeling fresh. When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone? PB: My phone’s dead half the time so it’s a moment that can happen anytime. LS: I legitimately don’t remember and that depresses me!! I don’t like that!! What’s the last piece of physical media you bought? LS: About a month ago I picked up a used copy of Only Theatre of Pain by Christian Death at Headline Records, great shop I’ve been going to since I was a kid! JD: I recently bought a record of a band called “Schlong” at Permanent Records in LA. I love finding stuff that isn’t available on streaming. It can be really easy to get complacent with what’s available online but there’s so much out there in the real world!!! What do you think is worth splurging on? LS: I think the most consistent answer for me is special meals. Something unique in another country, or something really special to which I don’t get to treat myself often. It’s always food! AW: Vacation/travel/time off/adventure etc... I wish it wasn’t considered so much of a splurge. The same way you wouldn’t really call going on a hike a splurge, but in a world where just existing can be expensive, I think it’s something that’s tremendously good for the ~soul~, and worth regularly “splurging” some time/money on. I want to talk to my friends about what cool missions they went on this summer, not what new shoes they bought or whatever. PB: Gonna agree 100% with Ary. The value of travel can’t be overemphasized. What would the tagline for your biopic be? AW: “If you cant handle him at his fastest, you don’t deserve him at his furiousest” JD: “Better to waste than to have not” PB: “You know he had to do it to em” LS: “Life is Hectic.” What’s the last GIF or meme you used? PB: I’m very GIF-averse. There’s something about it that feels like wearing someone’s skin. But here’s a pic I like. AW: LS: Correction September 19th, 2026: This story originally stated that Anyway was recorded at the American Football house. It was written there, but recorded elsewhere.

item.title: Meta’s Muse is creepy, but maybe not for the reasons you think
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.14
Meta’s Muse is apparently an effective AI assistant, but one that’s a little creepy. Part of that is because of its new Mac app, which can access Messages, Calendar, and Notes. But for all its smarts, Muse doesn’t actually know how to describe itself. Jason Aten, a contributing editor at Inc Magazine, posted on Threads screenshots of an interaction he had with Muse in which the assistant asks him some questions about a conversation he was having in Messages. Meta’s Muse is creepy, but maybe not for the reasons you think Muse probably can’t ‘see’ your notifications. But it also has no idea how it works. The problem is that Aten says he didn’t give Muse access to his messages. When asked how it knew about the contents of his messages, Muse replied, “I saw the notification previews, not your message history. I haven’t been reading your texts.” Aten continued to push, asking how Muse was receiving message previews, it didn’t have a good answer. “Honest answer: I can’t give you the exact plumbing,” it said. “What I know is that the paired Mac app exposes notifications as one of its capabilities, and they arrive to me through the device sync. Obviously, not great. Meta Superintelligence Labs’ David Singleton chimed in below the post to try to explain. First, he walks through all the permissions Muse needs to read messages, including granting the Mac app full disk access. He states that the features are opt-in. The more interesting part comes in towards the end of the thread in which Singleton says that Muse, “does not watch notifications on your Mac, but rather syncs data from Messages only after the user has specifically enabled access.” He suggests that the issue isn’t Muse illicitly reading Aten’ texts, but simply that Muse has no idea what it’s talking about: In the conversation with his Muse in Jason’s screenshots, when Muse said it synced “device notifications”, it was confused about how to explain the feature and gave an incorrect explanation. That’s on us. We apologize for the incorrect response from Muse and we’re working to improve Muse’s understanding of its own internals so that it gives correct answers to questions about how it functions more consistently. That might not be particularly reassuring, but it also makes some sense. We already know chatbots won’t tell you their secrets and will instead tell you what you want to hear.

item.title: Lenovo’s Yoga Slim 7X is the most laptop that $1,000 can currently buy
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.04
Anyone shopping for a Windows laptop with a $1K budget should head to Best Buy, where for the rest of the day you can get a great deal on a capable Lenovo laptop. The Yoga Slim 7X is a slim 14-inch machine with a 2K 16:10 OLED touchscreen, Snapdragon’s high-end X2 Elite processor with 12 cores, plus 16GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. The specs are about the best you can get these days for $1,000, as worthwhile laptop deals are in short supply during RAMageddon. Lenovo’s Yoga Slim 7X is the most laptop that $1,000 can currently buy It features an OLED screen and a Snapdragon X2 Elite CPU. Also, get a $25 DoorDash gift card with the new Fire Emblem. The Yoga Slim 7X seems like a great alternative to spending more (and getting less) with Microsoft’s latest Surface Laptop. In fact, you’d spend $1,549 on a similar model and still get half the storage that’s in this particular Yoga Slim 7X configuration. Its Arm-based processor can run most Windows apps very well, and yields superior battery life compared to laptops with x86 processors. The laptop includes three USB-C ports, and a hardware switch for disabling the webcam. It supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.3. It seems like a great machine for work, watching movies, or playing some games that aren’t too graphically intensive. More great Verge-approved deals - The PlayStation 5 version of Starfield hasn’t been available for as long as the Xbox and PC version, so it’s been a little slower to see major discounts. However, it recently hit $29.99 (originally $49.99) at Amazon and Best Buy, making now a good time to pick up the RPG. While Starfield didn’t have nearly as large of a cultural impact as Bethesda’s other first-person RPGs, it’s still worth playing if you love space, guns, and quests. It’s probably the studio’s most polished game yet. Buyers will be able to download the Free Lanes update that hit alongside its PS5 debut in April, and there are multiple paid expansions available if you want more. Read our review. - As mentioned in a previous deal roundup, DoorDash is offering DashPass members a $25 DoorDash digital gift card when they spend $50 or more on a game (non DashPass members get $10). Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave just came out, and that’s a great game to use this promotion for if you have a Switch 2 and enjoy turn-based tactics gameplay. The digital title costs $69.99. Those who have had success with this deal note on Slickdeals that the gift card should arrive within a few days of making your purchase. Read our review of the game. - The Baseus VD1 Pro dash cam recently dropped in price by $20, selling for $99.99 at Amazon. There are so many dash cams out there, but this one’s unique in a few ways. It includes both a 4K front- and 1080p rear-facing camera to record multiple angles, and the front camera includes a battery that can be recharged via its built-in solar panel to keep it going even when your car is off. It captures continuous footage while your car is giving it power, though it can detect incidents for up to 14 days with its built-in battery while your car is parked. A long USB-C cable connects the two cameras, so you’ll need to get clever with how you hide it in your trim. Read more about the camera’s features here.

item.title: OpenAI and Microsoft knew they were starting a ‘doom loop’ for the web
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 2.95
Recently unsealed court documents in the New York Times’ case against OpenAI and Microsoft are pretty damning. The companies’ own documentation warned that it was starting a “doom loop” that would damage the web, characterized its scraping of data to train its models as the “largest theft of labor in human history,” and that it made a “complete mockery of the idea of fair use.” OpenAI and Microsoft knew they were starting a ‘doom loop’ for the web The companies knew they were driving us toward Google Zero, and did it anyway. Many of the most eye-catching quotes from the document come from Microsoft’s Director of Applied Science, Brent Hecht. Though, the company has tried to distance itself from Hecht’s assertions. Microsoft spokesperson Alex Haurek told The Verge that “These comments reflect one employee’s individual perspective, are not a legal analysis, and do not represent the company’s views.” In a separate court filing, Jordan Usdan, GM for Data Strategy and Ops at Microsoft AI, characterized Hecht’s role as adversarial. He said that Hecht “holds divergent, academic, and forward-looking views about how data ecosystems for AI should operate and is employed at Microsoft to bring asymmetrical, futuristic, and academic points of view … nor is he someone who speaks for Microsoft specifically as to his theoretical views on AI’s potential effect on content creators.” But whether or not Microsoft wants to own these comments, it’s clear that this came true. Google Zero is real! AI is eating the web! There are plenty more wild statements in NYT’s filing from a variety of figures, including Satya Nadella, Sam Altman, and other OpenAI employees. Here are some highlights from the 92 page document. “An astonishing theft” The introduction quotes Hecht and OpenAI’s Head of ChatGPT (presumably Nick Turley) in a way that seems to show the companies knew they posed an “existential threat” to publishers like the New York Times. Hecht calls ChatGPT and Copilot’s harvesting of data the “largest theft of labor in human history” and says that Microsoft’s defense makes a “complete mockery of the idea of ‘fair use.’” It’s a “doom loop” Satya Nadella admits that chatbots have basically replaced search and removed the need to go straight to the source for info. But perhaps more damning is an internal Microsoft document that says, “Our AI content strategy has started a ‘doom loop’ that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time: It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain.’” That’s not even a real number Don’t be fooled by OpenAI or Microsoft’s claims of altruistic intent. OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman is more interested in the “gazillions” of dollars it he could potentially make through commercial AI. Paywall shmaywall Despite Nadella later being quoted as saying, “anything that is paywalled should be licensed,” An OpenAI representative admitted that he was “unaware” of any effort to detect or remove paywalled content from training data. “Insanely good at regurgitation” Internally, it seems that OpenAI was well aware of ChatGPT’s tendency to simply reproduce copyrighted material “verbatim.” Even though it acknowledged that the “prevention of memorization” was important to “minimize copyright violations,” employees admitted that GPT-4 “memorized a ton of data and therefore will be insanely good at regurgitation.” The filing then goes on to cite several examples of ChatGPT outputting long strings of copy straight from articles in the Times, Mercury News, The Denver Post, LifeHacker, and Eurogamer in response to queries. “‘Hoovering up’ all their work” Microsoft knew how its wholesale scraping of the internet would be perceived and admitted that “almost no one intended for they [sic] content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use.” A “substitute for the labor of people” OpenAI Policy Director Jack Clark saw the writing on the wall, saying that it was “creating systems that substitute for the labor of the people that define the ‘culture’ of society.” Internal documents described ChatGPT as “the modern newsstand.” OpenAI’s Nick Turley is later quoted as saying that once you get an answer from its chatbot, there is “no good reason to click” on a link to the source. Destroying their own supply chain Microsoft is quoted as admitting that “LLMs are a product that destroys its own supply chain” because it’s a substitute for its own training data in many cases. OpenAI knows its killing referral traffic OpenAI’s own media and economic experts attributed the drop in referral traffic for sites like the Times directly to AI summaries like Google’s AI Overviews. They’ve speculated that search referrals may be down as much as 60 percent. Microsoft spokesperson Haurek cautioned that “Satya’s testimony and Microsoft’s position in this case are perfectly consistent. He spoke to broad principles and changes underway in how people find and consume information. Those observations should not be confused with conclusions about copyright questions before the Court, which Microsoft addresses in its filings.” But it seems pretty clear based on this newly unsealed document that both Microsoft and OpenAI knew they were going to irreparably harm the publishing industry, the “millions of people” it employs, and, by extension, damage their own product, but carried forward anyway in pursuit of “gazillions” of dollars — doom loop be damned.

item.title: The AI regulation smackdown isn’t over
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 2.16
At the start of this week, the who’s-who of AI seemed — at least tentatively — on the side of AI regulation. Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had proposed a three-step plan for slowing AI development, including by embedding third-party evaluators in labs, coordinating across the domestic industry, and forging international agreements potentially with government assistance. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk publicly seemed to agree on aspects of all three things. The AI regulation smackdown isn’t over It’s AI CEO against AI CEO, and things are changing by the day. The AI regulation smackdown isn’t over It’s AI CEO against AI CEO, and things are changing by the day. Anthropic and OpenAI had already been dropping hints that they and other labs were working on some kind of industry framework. Appearing pro-regulation looked like both a good PR move and, potentially, a way for companies to address fallout from progressively more concerning hacking incidents. For now, any government involvement in this process looks like a non-starter. The Trump administration has attacked the idea of a safety crisis in AI, calling it a “hoax.” The AI world itself is also divided. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg quickly came out against limiting companies’ autonomy, and earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported that Zuckerberg, Musk, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang scuttled proposals for an industry-funded independent regulator for the AI industry — akin to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), a private nonprofit regulator in finance. But parts of the industry aren’t giving up on the idea, including OpenAI. “People want to know AI is being developed safely,” Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s global affairs chief, told The Verge. “That begins with the steps companies like ours take on our own, but government has an important role too. The AI policy window is open, with growing bipartisan support for mandatory national safety standards for frontier AI. Congress should turn that momentum into a framework that strengthens safety, supports American innovation, and keeps the U.S. leading in AI.” An AI venture capitalist, who requested anonymity due to their current investments, agreed that regulation was necessary. “You see these moments in every technology, whether it was electricity, cars, or airplanes, where, at some point, the industry had to come together to find a way to say, ‘How do we collectively embrace what safety means?’ Cars were unsafe, airplanes were unsafe, and then we had to create safety standards that everybody embraced that actually made technology more widespread. But the early days are always a little wild and unruly, and that’s how technology unfolds.” Anthropic declined to comment, but Amodei wrote in his essay that the company has “always … advocat[ed] for well-considered regulation of AI, even when this gets us accused of hype, ‘doomerism’, or regulatory capture.” Other companies have remained quiet. Safe Superintelligence Inc., SpaceX, and Google didn’t respond to a request for comment. Thinking Machines Lab declined to comment. And Meta pointed to an X post by Zuckerberg, in which he distanced himself from the calls for a slowdown and regulation, writing, “Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens.” Zuckerberg’s line of thinking appears in vogue with Trump right now. The president made headlines last week for calling recent fears about AI risks a “hoax.” He called Huang while the latter was onstage at a conference and told a crowd over speakerphone that “The robots will not be taking over.” That same day, he also posted on social media that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He added that the Trump administration has already “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’” using its existing “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” He denounced a “SICK conspiracy” going on against both AI and data centers and that whoever wins AI wins overall. “Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!” he wrote. For Nick Reese, an adjunct professor at New York University and the Department of Homeland Security’s former director of emerging tech policy, Trump’s current anti-regulation statements about AI are confusing because he worked with the first Trump administration to develop Executive Order 13960 — which Trump signed and has not been repealed. The order was centered on creating a set of principles for federal AI use that would protect “privacy, civil rights, [and] civil liberties.” “Six years ago, the Trump Administration signed executive action on AI safety, so there is a real change in the president’s position on the topic,” Reese said. “AI safety requires more than the intellectual abilities of one elected official.” As AI-industry blogger Zvi Mowshowitz put it, Trump isn’t necessarily fully anti-regulation — after all, he’s the one who slapped some restrictions on frontier labs, like pre-release testing by the government. But he’s driven more by, in Mowshowitz’s words, “vibes” than consistent policy. “Trump’s not yet buying this ‘existential risk’ thing, that’s ‘negative forces,’” Mowshowitz wrote. So government guardrails aren’t exactly ruled out, but they may bear little resemblance to what OpenAI or Anthropic want — let alone the plans of less-powerful, independent AI safety advocates. Overall, the administration’s positions on AI regulation have been “wobbly and inconsistent,” Reese said. “The result of that is that we are now framing AI safety in this doomsday scenario where the robots are coming to get us. But framing it as ‘robots are coming to get us’ really distorts what the core problem actually is. The core problem is that we have AI that is not physical or embodied in a robot that is hurting humans now.” Trump wrote in his post on Truth Social that the administration currently has both criminal and regulatory power over AI labs, but Reese said we’re nowhere near sufficient regulatory authority over the AI industry. As the technology advances, and the general public continues to push back — protests, boycotts, and outcry over the AI industry’s concentrated power in the hands of few — calls for regulation are only increasing, and that pressure could influence Trump’s current position. Reese said the opposition to regulation boils down to a “tired” idea that it’s always bad for innovation. Instead, he says, it’s important to think about why anything gets regulated. “We regulate things that we can tolerate no failure on … like the financial sector or airlines,” he said. “We build systems and checks and quality assurance and fallback mechanisms to make sure that those things don’t harm life or harm us systemically. But somehow we’re exempting AI from that.”

item.title: How Adaptive Beauty Tools Make Makeup Easier for Everyone
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 4.42
Listen and follow The Wirecutter Show Apple Podcasts | Spotify | Amazon Music | YouTube | iHeartRadio Applying mascara or eyeliner can be difficult even when you don't have a disability. For people with arthritis, tremors, low vision, or other mobility issues, beauty routines can feel nearly impossible. This episode, Wirecutter beauty writer Ayanna Redwood-Crawford explains how accessible makeup tools can make those routines easier for everyone. She shares what makes a makeup tool genuinely accessible, why universal design benefits more than just the people it was created for, and how some brands have made products easier to use without sacrificing their formulas or affordability. This episode covers: - Why accessible makeup is useful for everyone. Products designed for people with arthritis, tremors, or low vision can also help beginners, parents with their hands full, or anyone who finds makeup tools difficult to use. Testers appreciated products that were easier to grip and control, and many of them also had great formulas and finishes. - What makes a makeup tool genuinely accessible. It’s not enough for a product to be labeled adaptive. Look for tools that address specific challenges, like gripping a mascara tube, controlling a brush, or applying makeup with limited hand movement. - Why makeup doesn’t always have to be perfectly precise. Look for products that simplify tricky steps, like eyeliners with built-in wing stamps or buildable multisticks for color control and flexibility. Products we recommend These chunky foam tubes slide onto brushes, pencils, and slim cases, giving you added control. The inexpensive sets (six or nine pieces) come with tubes in three sizes, but they don’t fit every product perfectly. This makeup brush has an ergonomic grip, a flat base so it stands on its own, and bristles that evenly distribute face makeup like foundation, concealer, and blush. But the company is based in the United Kingdom, so shipping may take up to 10 days. This brush has a smooth, bell-shaped handle with a ring that slips between two fingers for a more secure grip. Plus, its short length allows for just-close-enough eye makeup application. This mascara has a short wand with a rubbery coating that makes it easy to grip and maneuver, and the curved brush reaches every lash. But you may need multiple coats to achieve a thicker lash look. This eyeliner has a smooth-flowing pen and two built-in stamps for creating tiny wings on outer corners. But the tube is slim, which made it hard for some testers to grip. This multiuse makeup stick is perfect for anyone who has trouble creating precise or detailed makeup looks. The sheer, buildable colors look great on eyes, cheeks, and lips, and they’re easy to blend with fingers. But the small case may be difficult to open for people with limited hand dexterity. This brightly lit vanity mirror has three light temperatures and comes with a removable magnetic magnifying mirror. But you have to twist in a screw (with a provided tool) to attach the mirror to its stand the first time you use it. Additional reading Episode transcript CAIRA: I'm Caira Blackwell. ROSIE: I'm Rosie Guerin, and you're listening to The Wirecutter Show. ROSIE: Caira, quick, pop quiz. CAIRA: No, I didn't study. ROSIE: Yeah, that's why it's pop, dude. What do audiobooks, bendy straws, and cordless vacuums all have in common? Quick. CAIRA: I use them all occasionally. ROSIE: That might be true, but what I was going for is that they were all originally designed for people with disabilities. CAIRA: That's really cool. ROSIE: It is really cool. These are tools that worked so well. They've now become mainstream, universal tools many, many, many people use. But there’s one product that still hasn't reached that status. It’s makeup. CAIRA: Yeah, that makes sense. I feel like ease and accessibility has just never been a top priority in the beauty industry. I mean, I wear makeup pretty much every day and I find it hard to use these tools still. But one of our staff writers on the beauty team, Ayanna Redwood-Crawford, recently wrote an article about how beauty brands are now launching more and more accessible makeup and adaptive tools. ROSIE: It's a really, really interesting piece. You might remember Ayanna from our previous episode, which was all about self-tanners. CAIRA: Enlightening. ROSIE: Enlightening. Now we've got her back to talk about how she tested these tools and what she thought of them. Ayanna, welcome back. AYANNA: Hi, thanks for having me back. ROSIE: Good to see you. Tell us how this piece first came to be. AYANNA: So I got to know our paid testers really well from when I worked on the sleep team. CAIRA: Can you tell us a little bit more about the paid testers? ROSIE: Yeah, who are our paid testers? AYANNA: Okay, so our paid testers are a diverse group of people with different abilities, different genders, ages, and they come in and they test pretty much everything for us. On the sleep team, they tested everything, just about everything I've covered. And so we got to know each other pretty well. And then when I moved over to the beauty team, they were very comfortable with telling me exactly what their pain points were with beauty products. And that mixed with my own curiosity about accessibility and making sure that the topics that I cover are universally designed and they work well for everyone. That's how this piece came to be. CAIRA: And when you say accessible here in terms of things in the makeup industry, what does that mean exactly? What kinds of challenges were you looking for these brands to be designing for? AYANNA: I was specifically looking for brands that made products that would work well for people with hand mobility issues like arthritis or tremors and also people with low vision. I think your hands and your eyes are the things you need the most when you're putting on makeup and also for people with joint pain of any kind. It was really cool to find brands that solely created adaptable, universally-designed products that are actually good. CAIRA: And what kind of products were you looking for? Or were you even looking for any specific products? Because there are a billion makeup things and tools for mascara, eyeliner, anything. So were you kind of hoping to solve specific pain points for your testers? AYANNA: First, I was looking for products that can make things easier for everyone. So I was thinking about people who had joint pain. I was thinking about people with arthritis. I was thinking about folks who have tremors. I was also thinking about people who have temporary disabilities like, "Oh, I just broke my arm and it's my dominant arm." And I was also thinking about someone who usually has their hands full, like a parent. CAIRA: Oh, that's good. AYANNA: So I was like, "Okay, what are the products that someone can use possibly one-handed or if they don't have a lot of time, or even if they're a beginner and they need something that is kind of foolproof?" CAIRA: God, teenage me would've loved that. ROSIE: I want to know what surprised you most during this testing. AYANNA: What surprised me was that universal design is accessible design. It's all the same. And whenever I'm writing about something, I always think about the person who needs it the most and then I start from there. So when thinking about accessible beauty tools, I was like, "Okay, who needs this the most?" And it's obviously people who want to maintain these beauty rituals, but it's just a literal pain for them or it's just really uncomfortable or a hassle. So I was like, "Okay, I think that these things that I'm finding are also things that make my life easier and I'm not disabled." So I was like, "Oh, well, this is absolutely amazing." And on top of things being easier to hold, easier to grip, and easier to apply, they're also really good formulations that look pretty and wear well. ROSIE: Yeah. I'm curious through your reporting, did you get a sense that companies are thinking about accessibility or thinking about design? AYANNA: I think that more brands are starting to understand the value and being accessible to everyone. And I also thought that it was very cool to see brands that solely make adaptive makeup and cosmetics and tools. That was very cool to see. There are also brands like Rare Beauty that have accessible line or products that are accessible within them. CAIRA: That's pretty cool. AYANNA: Yeah. They were very good about letting me know which ones I should be testing and which ones wouldn't make sense. ROSIE: So some progress and then also- AYANNA: Some progress. ROSIE: ... some space for improvement. AYANNA: Yeah. And I think that what more brands need to realize is that they can make more accessible packaging and cosmetics without sacrificing their aesthetic or even price. ROSIE: And it could be a net positive because like you said, accessibility is universal. AYANNA: Yeah. CAIRA: We're going to take a quick break and then when we're back, we're going to talk with Ayanna about some of the accessible tools she loves and why. Be right back. ROSIE: Welcome back. In this episode, we are talking about accessible makeup with our colleague, Ayanna Redwood-Crawford. Ayanna, a lot of your picks are designed to solve the basic problem of gripping and controlling makeup tools. So can you talk about some of the products you think did particularly well for that and why? AYANNA: Oh my God, I would love to. So first is the Lyforx's grip tubing, which is a foam tubing that our testers loved. CAIRA: A foam tubing? AYANNA: Yes. CAIRA: What is tubing? AYANNA: It's a cylindrical tube that has a little hole in it and the holes come in different diameters. So you can stick different things inside of them and it makes it easier to grip onto something that's hard and cold and long, like a mascara tube or an eyeliner pen. CAIRA: Oh. AYANNA: Yeah. CAIRA: So it's an accessory that you put on top of your makeup? AYANNA: So let's say you didn't want to use an accessible beauty product because you already have an eyeliner or a lipstick or a mascara that you love, it's just hard for you to hold it. This will make it easier for you to do that. CAIRA: Cool. AYANNA: So what our testers liked about the foam tubing was that it allowed for them to have freedom of movement. So they could use a blush brush at any angle that they wanted and they can apply as much pressure as they usually would. And then they're also really inexpensive. So you can buy multiple packs of these and have foam tubing for literally everything you own if you wanted to. CAIRA: That's amazing. AYANNA: And you can cut them to the size you need them to be. CAIRA: So you don't have to keep transferring them to a different makeup whatever. AYANNA: Not if you don't want to. CAIRA: You can just keep them on and they live there now. ROSIE: That's so cool. CAIRA: Yeah. AYANNA: Okay. So another product that I loved was the Kohl Kreatives Medium Circle Brush, which really changed the way that I thought about makeup brushes in general. Kohl Kreatives is an accessible beauty line. So everything they make is for accessibility purposes. CAIRA: Wow. ROSIE: That's really cool. AYANNA: So instead of holding a brush like you would a pencil by pinching it, which can be really uncomfortable for people with hand mobility issues, you can instead just hold the brush in your fist and use it vertically. CAIRA: Wow. ROSIE: Like you're holding an ice cream cone or something. AYANNA: Yeah, exactly. And then the next one that was really great for gripping was the Guide Beauty Blend & Crease Brush. This one is specifically for eyeshadow. So Guide is another adaptive cosmetics line, much like Kohl Kreatives. And this brush is really cool because it has this guide ring that you can slip between two fingers, whichever ones are most comfortable for you, allowing you to apply your eyeshadow more comfortably and with a bit more control. CAIRA: I think I need this. AYANNA: I mean, in my research, I saw that people were doing a DIY hack, which is putting a spoon up to their eye so that they can have the perfect cut crease or apply eyeshadow that way. And I was like, oh, okay. Well, maybe this might help them have more control over what they're doing. CAIRA: Yeah. ROSIE: In testing, did you find that it was pretty intuitive for people to use or was there a little bit of a learning curve for that one? AYANNA: There was a tiny bit of a learning curve, but once I was just like, "Oh, you just slip between your fingers." Everyone was like, "Oh, oh my God. Yeah, of course. You can just do it like this? Oh, this is great." Yeah. CAIRA: That's so cool. Another theme that I noticed in your guide is products that take some of the precision out of makeup application. So for me personally, I have a really hard time with eyeliner because you have to be so sharp and precise about it without messing up. So what did you find that makes it easier to get a polished look without having to be perfect, like with a perfectly steady surgeon's hands? AYANNA: Okay. Well, the Tilt mascara for one. This is actually my favorite mascara. I legit use it every day. CAIRA: And your eyelashes look amazing. AYANNA: Thank you so much. ROSIE: What do you like so much about it? AYANNA: Well, not only is the formula amazing, testers loved how good it feels to hold and apply. So unlike some other mascaras, the wand isn't bendy at all. It's also shorter and it curves upward at the tip. So that makes it really easy to get those inner corner lashes without getting mascara on your lids at all. It's great. ROSIE: That's really cool. So you don't have to necessarily use as much hand movement when you're going sort of down to up? AYANNA: Yeah. With a straight mascara wand, you really have to be careful when you're going to your inner corner of your lashes because you can get that wand on the bridge of your nose. CAIRA: Do it every day. AYANNA: Exactly. ROSIE: Yeah. I have a little bit of a hand tremor and I think when I'm trying to get right in that spot you're talking about, that's when I have the most trouble. AYANNA: Yeah. Yeah, I get that, because it's also, you get a little nervous when you're like- ROSIE: When you're that close to your eye. AYANNA: ... "I don't want to poke myself in the eye." ROSIE: Absolutely. AYANNA: The Sheglam eyeliner is also a good one. This product actually changed my life. ROSIE: What is it? AYANNA: I'll say it. First of all, I didn't know eyeliner stamps even existed. That's what it is. It's an eyeliner stamp. ROSIE: What does that mean? AYANNA: So let me be more specific. It's not an eyeliner stamp, it's a wing stamp. So basically you just put the stamp on the corner of your eye and the wing is there. You don't have to draw it on. I am a person who has been using liquid eyeliner forever and I prefer a wing and I fight for my life every day trying to make sure they match And this eyeliner stamp, it's just like you don't have to struggle. You just stamp it on and you're good on the first go. You just have to make sure that the placement is correct for both of them. CAIRA: Right. So they're even? AYANNA: Exactly. We like the sheglam because you can do everything with one pen. So basically you have two sides of the pen, one for your left eye, one for your right, and then you can detach it in the middle and there is an eyeliner marker. It is not like a little thin pen that we're used to using. The marker makes it so much easier to line your eye. CAIRA: Wow. AYANNA: Yeah, it's great. CAIRA: This is life-changing stuff. AYANNA: I know, and it saves so much time. And I think this would also be really great for beginners. CAIRA: Yeah. Again, teenage me would've loved that. ROSIE: What about lip products? Was there anything that you tested there that you liked? AYANNA: We loved the Tilt sheer lip treatment. So first of all, a sheer Lipstick, which doesn't necessarily offer hydration or a tinted lip balm, which definitely offers hydration but doesn't have to offer you any color, those are always going to be the best go-tos for a person who wants to add a pretty pop of color on the go without having to look in the mirror or be especially proficient in applying it. So the Tilt sheer lip treatment has a bit of a mixture of both. It's not quite a lipstick. It is a balm that offers hydration, but it does add enough color that you're like, "Oh, yeah, I've put something on, but I don't have to be beholden to it all day if I don't want to be." CAIRA: Yeah. I think you've actually let me try this one because I'm one of those people who can't do a lipstick because I don't want to reapply and I get it everywhere. And it just makes you look a little more alive, for lack of a better word. You don't have to worry about it smearing everywhere and looking goofy. AYANNA: Exactly. It doesn't have to be perfect. ROSIE: Ayanna, accessibility isn't of course always about finding the specific tool itself. It can also be about simplifying an entire routine. So what did you find that worked well for people who just wanted to use fewer products overall in their routine or eliminate some of the more complicated steps? AYANNA: Yeah, absolutely. So we are in the stickification of everything in cosmetics. And so we were able to find a really great multi-stick in the e.l.f. Monochromatic Multi Stick. So it is a stick that you can get in different colors. It's short and it's thick and you can use it on your eyes as an eyeshadow, you can use it as a blush and as a lipstick. So you can throw it in your bag or have it on your vanity and do three things at once. And it's sheer, so it's buildable. So you don't have to put it on and be like, "Well, I'm stuck with this, this really, really deep orange or something." You can just build it to where you feel comfortable. It's great. CAIRA: And was there a product or a specific category of products that you were really hoping to find an accessible tool for, but you ended up not being able to? AYANNA: Well, there was a makeup organizer that I really wanted to find that could be helpful for people with certain cognitive disabilities. The occupational therapist I spoke with, they told me that if you have your tools organized in a way where you can easily see them and pick them up without having to think too much about it, that's probably the best case scenario. And frankly, I want that for myself too. CAIRA: Me too. AYANNA: Yeah. CAIRA: I just dig through a pouch. AYANNA: I also really wanted to find a great vibrating brush that I had seen during my research. ROSIE: What is that? AYANNA: So it's an adaptive beauty tool that smooths and blends out makeup without the user having to exert too much effort. This is great for people with tremors or joint pain. ROSIE: So interesting. AYANNA: The one that we tried, the FlexiBrush, worked pretty well, but it's expensive. And I wish there were more out there that are just as good as that one. CAIRA: And then there's the challenge of actually being able to see what you're doing. You mentioned earlier that you wanted to find some tools for people who have low vision as well. So you did test a bunch of different vision aids, but what did you learn about what makes a makeup mirror, for example, genuinely useful for someone who does have low vision? AYANNA: I learned a lot through our testers and their feedback. So they all loved the Fancii Vera Vanity. It was really a favorite because it was hands-free and that is a really important feature. We tried things that were like a handheld mirror that had lights on it and we thought that would be good. And people were like, "No, I need my hands to do things." We also tried these glasses with different magnifications, but it was just too much of a hassle to find the magnification that worked best for you. And so people really love the fancy vanity mirror for that. Our testers also preferred it because it had an adjustable LED light where you can adjust not only the warmth, but the brightness. CAIRA: Love. AYANNA: That was great. CAIRA: And it stands on your desk, I'm assuming, yeah? AYANNA: Yes. It stands on the desk. And it also comes with a smaller magnetic magnifying mirror that you can just plop onto the bigger one if you really need to get in there and see what you're doing close up. CAIRA: The name is Fancii. It's called the Fancii mirror. Does it have a fancy price as well? AYANNA: Yeah. So this mirror costs about $140, but we did test this against our budget pick for lighted mirrors, and people just preferred this one because it does get brighter. CAIRA: Okay. ROSIE: Since we're talking about cost and prices of these products, I was curious whether you noticed that these adaptive tools, that they're on the whole more expensive? AYANNA: I would say that they're not. And actually the products on our roundup range everywhere from $5 to 24. CAIRA: So that's like normal pricing. ROSIE: Pretty commensurate with pricing. AYANNA: Yeah. ROSIE: Ayanna, thank you so much for joining us. This was really fun. AYANNA: Thanks for having me. It's great. ROSIE: Congrats on the piece. It's really cool. AYANNA: Thank you. ROSIE: That's it for us for today. If you want to check out any of the products Ayanna recommended today, we will link those in our show notes as well as a link to her guide. Thanks for joining us. Talk soon. The Wirecutter Show is executive produced by me, Rosie Guerin, and produced by Abigail Keel. Engineering support from Maddie Mazziello and Nick Pittman. Today's episode was mixed by Catherine Anderson. Original music by Dan Powell, Marion Lozano, Elisheba Ittoop, Rowan Niemisto, Catherine Anderson, and Diane Wong. Cliff Levy is Wirecutter's deputy publisher and general manager. Ben Frumin is Wirecutter's editor in chief. CAIRA: I'm Caira Blackwell. ROSIE: And I'm Rosie Guerin. Thank you for listening. Credits The Wirecutter Show is executive produced by Rosie Guerin and produced by Abigail Keel. Engineering support from Maddy Masiello and Nick Pitman. Episodes are mixed by Catherine Anderson, Efim Shapiro, Rowan Niemisto, Sophia Lanman, and Sonia Herrero. Original music by Dan Powell, Marion Lozano, Elisheba Ittoop, Catherine Anderson, Rowan Niemisto and Diane Wong. Wirecutter’s deputy publisher and general manager is Cliff Levy. Ben Frumin is Wirecutter’s editor-in-chief. Hosted by Rosie Guerin, Caira Blackwell and Christine Cyr Clisset. Meet your guides Caira Blackwell is a senior staff writer covering sleep, and co-host of our podcast, The Wirecutter Show. She has spent countless hours testing more than 50 mattresses and has slept on nearly a dozen at home. Her work has been published in Nylon magazine, Okayplayer, and Narratively. When she isn’t busy sleeping (for work), she’s busy trying new recipes in the kitchen or reading in the sun. Rosie Guerin is a creative executive, an editor, a showrunner, and a producer foremost, with a background in news and politics and a great love of pop culture. She specializes in new-show development and has produced for television and radio, and she now resides in the world of podcasting as the executive producer and co-host of the brand-new podcast, The Wirecutter Show. She has developed and produced shows for Apple, Audible, Gimlet, New York Public Radio, Spotify, Wondery, and beyond. Rosie is from Maine and especially loves the beach in winter. I research and report on everything from cosmetics to self-tanners, and most hair products in between. Wirecutter’s podcast features interviews with journalists from our newsroom about their reporting and testing. I help choose what the podcast will cover and edit the episodes that appear on the show. I also read the emails that listeners send to the show to make sure we investigate their biggest questions and concerns. Further reading - by Ellen Lee and Nancy Redd From deodorant and face wash to first bras and period underwear, reliable personal-care items can make puberty easier and help your kid form lasting habits. - by Ayanna Redwood-Crawford We tested 41 beauty products and tools designed for people with dexterity challenges and/or low vision. Our nine favorites make applying makeup easier. - by Samantha Schoech Whether the traveler on your list prefers spa weekends away, or roughing it through multiple countries we’ve got a gift to make their trips more stylish, more memorable, and more comfortable.
